# Agent Templates `bxAgents new` creates a project one of three mutually exclusive ways - see [CLI Reference](/cli-reference/index.html#new) for the exact flag syntax and validation rules. This page goes deep on all three: exactly what each built-in `--template` generates, what a `--repo`/`--forgebox` source needs to look like to work as a project source, and how to build and publish one of your own. A template is the **shape** a project starts from. The [new wizard](/guides/new-wizard/index.html) lets you pick one (a single agent, a team, a scheduled agent, an MCP server) and then adds the tools, MCP servers, channels and deploy target you choose on top, so a template and those choices combine. The channel starters below (`slack-bot`, `telegram-bot`, `github-bot`, `webui-chat`) are the same thing as picking that channel in the wizard. ```bash bxAgents new my-agent --model=openai/gpt-5 --template= # a built-in starter bxAgents new my-agent --repo=owner/repo-name # clone a GitHub repo bxAgents new my-agent --forgebox=some-package-slug # install a ForgeBox package ``` Every path lands on the same thing: a directory containing an agent definition (an [`Agent.yaml`](/conventions/agent-yaml/index.html), or a class-based `Agent.bx`) at its root, ready for `bxAgents build`. What differs is where that definition (and everything around it) comes from. ## The 8 built-in `--template` starters Every template starts from the exact same base skeleton - `Agent.yaml`, `instructions.md`, a root [`Application.bx`](/conventions/application-bx/index.html) and [`box.json`](/conventions/box-json/index.html), the empty convention folders (`tools`, `skills`, `subagents`, `gateways`, `schedules`, `mcp`, `interceptors` and `modules`), a ready-to-run [`tests/`](/conventions/testing/index.html) folder, a `.env` (declaring `BOXLANG_HOME=.build/runtime`, with room for your API keys), a `.gitignore` and the standard dotfiles - then layers a small, specific amount of pre-wired content on top. Add `--class` to any `--template` to get the class-based `Agent.bx` form of the root definition (and of the subagents the `multi-agent` template scaffolds) instead of `Agent.yaml`; everything else is unchanged. None of them need a validator change: each one's extra content reuses a config shape [`ProjectValidator`](/conventions/agent-bx/index.html) already accepts, so a scaffolded project of any template validates cleanly by construction. [](#minimal)
[minimal](#minimal) [The bare skeleton. Nothing extra.](#minimal) [](#minimal)[
webui-chat A browser chat UI at /chat.](#webui-chat)[
slack-bot A Slack Socket Mode channel adapter.](#slack-bot)[
telegram-bot A Telegram long-poll channel adapter.](#telegram-bot)[
github-bot A GitHub issue/PR webhook adapter.](#github-bot)[
mcp-server An example tool exposed as an MCP server.](#mcp-server)[
scheduled A real ColdBox Scheduler calling the agent.](#scheduled)[
multi-agent Two subagents, wired via subAgents.](#multi-agent)
### `minimal` The default when `--template` is omitted entirely. This IS the base skeleton described above - no extra files. Use it when you're starting from a blank agent and adding conventions yourself as you need them. ### `webui-chat` Adds `gateways/webui.bx`, exposing the built-in [web chat UI](/conventions/web-ui/index.html) at `/chat`: ```javascript // gateways/webui.bx class { function configure() { return { exposes : "webui", path : "/chat" }; } } ``` After `bxAgents build && bxAgents serve`, the agent is reachable at `http://localhost:8080/chat` - a real static chat page backed by a generated SQLite-based conversation store. No `apiKeyEnvVar`/`users` are configured out of the box, so the page is open by default; see [The web chat UI](/conventions/web-ui/index.html) for locking it down. ### `slack-bot` Adds `gateways/slack.bx`, a push-style [Slack](/conventions/gateways/slack/index.html) channel adapter (Socket Mode - a persistent websocket, no public webhook needed): ```javascript // gateways/slack.bx class { function configure() { return { type : "slack", botTokenEnvVar : "SLACK_BOT_TOKEN", appTokenEnvVar : "SLACK_APP_TOKEN" }; } } ``` Also appends matching stub lines to `.env`: ```bash # Slack gateway (gateways/slack.bx) - see https://api.slack.com/apps SLACK_BOT_TOKEN=xoxb-... SLACK_APP_TOKEN=xapp-... ``` Fill in both real values from a Slack app with Socket Mode enabled before `bxAgents serve` - see [Slack](/conventions/gateways/slack/index.html) for the app-configuration steps. ### `telegram-bot` Adds `gateways/telegram.bx`, a push-style [Telegram](/conventions/gateways/telegram/index.html) channel adapter (long-poll via `getUpdates`): ```javascript // gateways/telegram.bx class { function configure() { return { type : "telegram", botTokenEnvVar : "TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN" }; } } ``` Also appends a matching stub line to `.env`: ```bash # Telegram gateway (gateways/telegram.bx) - from @BotFather TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN=... ``` Get a token from [@BotFather](https://core.telegram.org/bots#botfather) and drop it in before serving. ### `github-bot` Adds `gateways/github.bx`, a push-style [GitHub](/conventions/gateways/github/index.html) channel adapter (webhook-driven, `@mention`-gated issue/PR comment threads): ```javascript // gateways/github.bx class { function configure() { return { type : "github", tokenEnvVar : "GITHUB_TOKEN", webhookSecretEnvVar : "GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET", botNameEnvVar : "GITHUB_BOT_NAME" }; } } ``` Also appends matching stub lines to `.env`: ```bash # GitHub gateway (gateways/github.bx) - a PAT with repo/issues+PR read+write scope GITHUB_TOKEN=... GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET=... GITHUB_BOT_NAME=... ``` `GITHUB_TOKEN` needs a PAT with repo + issues/PR read-write scope; `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET` is whatever you set the repo's webhook signing secret to; `GITHUB_BOT_NAME` is the account name the bot replies as, used to gate on `@mention`. See [GitHub](/conventions/gateways/github/index.html) for the webhook setup. ### `mcp-server` Adds an example [MCP](/conventions/mcp/index.html) tool server plus a gateway entry exposing it: ```javascript // mcp/exampleServer.bx class { function configure() { return { description : "Example MCP tool server", version : "1.0.0" }; } } ``` ```javascript // gateways/mcpExpose.bx class { function configure() { return { exposes : "mcp", path : "/mcp", target : "exampleServer" }; } } ``` `target` names the `mcp/*` entry to expose - here, the example server above. After `build`/`serve`, any MCP-speaking client can connect at `/mcp`. The example server registers no tools yet: write `@AITool` functions under `tools/` and list their names in a `tools: [ ... ]` array in `mcp/exampleServer.bx` (or add more `mcp/*.bx` files), per [mcp/](/conventions/mcp/index.html). ### `scheduled` Adds a [BoxLang scheduler](/conventions/schedules/index.html) calling the agent on a cron schedule: ```javascript // schedules/Example.bx class { function configure() { task( "example" ) .cron( "0 0 * * *" ) .call( () => run( "Give me a status update" ) ) .withNoOverlaps() } } ``` (`run()` sends the message to the project's default agent, the root agent. The build gives the class its helpers, so there is no `extends`.) This is real [`schedules/`](/conventions/schedules/index.html) content, not a placeholder - edit `configure()` to add or change tasks with BoxLang's task DSL (`cron(...)`, `every(...)`, `everyDayAt(...)`, etc.), or add more files. ### `multi-agent` The one template that changes the root `Agent.yaml` itself, rather than only adding files alongside it. It declares two [subagents](/conventions/subagents/index.html) with a `subAgents` list: ```yaml # Agent.yaml name: my-agent provider: openai model: gpt-5 subAgents: [ researcher, writer ] environments: # `bxAgents test` builds against this override by default (see # BaseAgentSpec.bx) so a fresh project's tests need no API key or # network access - swap the model to test against a real provider. test: model: mock/mock-model ``` ...and scaffolds both as real, working subagent folders: subagents/ ├── researcher/ │ ├── Agent.yaml │ └── instructions.md └── writer/ ├── Agent.yaml └── instructions.md Each subagent's own `Agent.yaml` is a complete, buildable agent (always against the `mock` provider - a subagent here is a demonstration of the delegation shape, not a working agent out of the box): ```yaml # subagents/researcher/Agent.yaml name: researcher description: "Gathers facts on a topic. Does not write final prose - that's the writer's job." model: mock/mock-model ``` `researcher` gathers facts; `writer` turns findings into final prose - a minimal two-role delegation example. See [subagents/](/conventions/subagents/index.html) for how the `subAgents` list (folder names to wire) differs from `super.init()`'s own `subAgents` argument in a class-based `Agent.bx` (already-built `AiAgent` instances), and the [multi-agent-team example](/guides/example-multi-agent-team/index.html) for a fuller walkthrough. ## Sourcing a project from GitHub (`--repo`) ```bash bxAgents new my-agent --repo=owner/repo-name # or a full URL: bxAgents new my-agent --repo=https://github.com/owner/repo-name.git ``` Instead of scaffolding from a built-in template, `--repo` clones an existing repository and uses it as the new project directly. Cloning is done with a bundled [JGit](https://www.eclipse.org/jgit/) dependency (`org.eclipse.jgit:org.eclipse.jgit`, from Maven Central) - **no `git` binary needs to be installed or on `PATH`**; the git client ships inside the module's own jar. **What makes a repo a valid template:** an `Agent.yaml` (or `Agent.bx`) at the repository's root, same as any scaffolded project. Beyond that, there's no special manifest or marker file to add - any BxAgents project (yours, a colleague's, an example from `examples/`) is already a valid `--repo` source as-is. **What happens on clone, in order:** 1. `owner/repo-name` shorthand resolves to `https://github.com/owner/repo-name.git`; a value already containing `://` or starting with `git@` is used as-is (so a self-hosted GitLab/Bitbucket/etc. HTTPS URL works too, not just GitHub). 2. Refuses to run if the target directory already exists and is **not empty** - nothing is ever cloned over existing files. 3. Clones **shallow** (`--depth=1` - only the current state, no history) via JGit's `cloneRepository()`. 4. **Always deletes the resulting `.git` folder afterward, unconditionally - no flag to keep it.** This is deliberate: a template repo's own git history and `origin` remote have no legitimate reason to survive into a fresh project, and leaving them in place is a real foot-gun (your project's first `git init`/commit/push could otherwise interact with the *template's* upstream repo instead of your own). If you genuinely want the source repo's git history, clone it manually with `git clone` instead of using `bxAgents new --repo`. 5. Verifies an `Agent.yaml` or `Agent.bx` exists at the cloned root - if not, the whole operation fails with a clear error naming what's missing, rather than leaving behind a half-usable, non-BxAgents directory. > **Warning** > > Cloning is **anonymous HTTPS only** - no credentials are passed to JGit today, so a private repository will fail to clone. Use a public repo, or clone a private one manually and `bxAgents new` isn't the right tool for that case yet. `--model`, `--name`, and `--description` are **not** required or used with `--repo` - the cloned project already defines its own `Agent.yaml` or `Agent.bx` (and therefore its own name/model). Passing `--name`/`--description` anyway produces a warning in the output rather than an error, and is otherwise ignored. The scaffolded-`tests/`'s automatic `box install` step (and `--skipInstall`) also don't apply here - a cloned project's own `tests/` folder, if it has one, is left exactly as cloned. ## Sourcing a project from ForgeBox (`--forgebox`) ```bash bxAgents new my-agent --forgebox=some-package-slug ``` Installs a [ForgeBox](https://www.forgebox.io) package - CommandBox's package registry, which can host a full app/project template, not just a library - and uses it as the new project. This talks to ForgeBox's own public REST API (`https://www.forgebox.io/api/v1`) directly, using BoxLang's native `bx:http`/`http()` support - **no `box` CLI is required**. **What makes a ForgeBox entry a valid template:** an `Agent.yaml` (or `Agent.bx`) at the root of its published archive (or nested exactly one folder deep - see the unwrapping note below). ForgeBox has a dedicated `bxagents` entry type for exactly this ("BxAgents" in the ForgeBox UI) - browsing it is the fastest way to find a starting point - but `bxAgents new --forgebox` itself doesn't filter or care about an entry's declared `type` at all when installing; it only cares whether the downloaded archive, once extracted, contains an `Agent.yaml` or `Agent.bx`. **What happens on install, in order:** 1. Refuses to run if the target directory already exists and is **not empty**. 2. `GET /entry/` looks up the package. A slug that doesn't exist fails clearly and immediately - no download is attempted. 3. Resolves the current release's download URL from the entry's own `latestVersion.downloadURL` (falling back to the newest entry in its `versions` array if that's somehow missing). 4. Downloads the archive and extracts it with BoxLang's own built-in `extract()` BIF (zip support - no bespoke unzip code involved). 5. **Unwraps one level of nesting automatically**, if present: many ForgeBox archives (matching a typical GitHub zip export) wrap their entire contents in one top-level folder. If extraction produces exactly one top-level entry and it's a directory, its contents are moved up so the target directory itself ends up as the project root. 6. Verifies an `Agent.yaml` or `Agent.bx` exists at the (possibly unwrapped) root - if not, the whole operation fails, since a ForgeBox slug could just as easily be an unrelated library rather than a project template. Same as `--repo`: `--model`/`--name`/`--description` are not required (warned-and-ignored if passed anyway - the installed project defines its own), and the auto-`box install`/`--skipInstall` step doesn't apply. ## Publishing your own template A BxAgents template - whether you'll share it via GitHub, ForgeBox, or both - is just an ordinary BxAgents project (an `Agent.yaml` at its root, plus whatever conventions it uses) with the specifics filled in for someone else to copy and adapt, rather than left as placeholders for you personally. ### 1. Build the project Start from any of the 8 built-in starters above (or from scratch) and shape it into what you want people to start from: ```bash bxAgents new my-template --model=openai/gpt-5 --template= ``` A few things worth doing deliberately, since someone else will `bxAgents new --repo=...`/`--forgebox=...` this and expect it to just work: * **Keep `Agent.yaml` generic and buildable out of the box.** Don't hardcode a real API key or point at a paid-only model by default - the `test` environment's `mock/mock-model` override (already scaffolded) means `bxAgents test` still works with zero setup even if the real `model` needs a key nobody but you has yet. * **Ship a real `instructions.md`** describing the agent's actual purpose, not the generic "You are a helpful AI agent" placeholder `new` scaffolds by default. * **Document required env vars in `.env`** as commented stub lines (`SLACK_BOT_TOKEN=xoxb-...`, etc.) exactly like the `slack-bot`/`telegram-bot`/`github-bot` templates do above - it's the first thing someone reads after cloning. * **Verify it from cold** , the same way a stranger would receive it: `rm -rf .build dist`, then `bxAgents build && bxAgents test` (and `bxAgents doctor` to catch anything env/dependency-related) from a completely fresh checkout. * **Never commit `.build/`, `dist/`, or a real `.env`** - the scaffolded `.gitignore` already covers all three; keep it. ### 2a. Publish it to GitHub Nothing BxAgents-specific is needed - push the project to a public GitHub repository with `Agent.yaml` at the root (or push a subtree; `--repo` only unwraps ForgeBox's own single-nesting convention, not arbitrary repo layouts, so keep `Agent.yaml` at the actual repo root). Anyone can then run: ```bash bxAgents new my-agent --repo=your-org/your-template-repo ``` A short "Getting Started" section in the repo's own `README.md` (what env vars to set, which model to point at) goes a long way, since `--repo` doesn't read or surface anything from the README itself - it's purely for the human cloning it. ### 2b. Publish it to ForgeBox ForgeBox packages are described by a `box.json` at the project root - the same file CommandBox's own package system uses everywhere else. At minimum: ```json { "name": "My BxAgents Template", "slug": "my-bxagents-template", "version": "1.0.0", "type": "bxagents", "shortDescription": "A short description of what this agent template does", "private": false } ``` * **`slug`** is the unique name people install with (`--forgebox=my-bxagents-template`) - it's also what `getEntry()` looks up, so pick one you're happy to keep. * **`type`** should be `bxagents` - ForgeBox's own dedicated entry type for BxAgents projects/templates (run `box forgebox types` to see it alongside every other type). `bxAgents new --forgebox` itself never inspects `type` when installing, but declaring it correctly is what gets your template listed under ForgeBox's own "BxAgents" category instead of a generic one, so people can actually find it by browsing. Add descriptive `keywords` too (e.g. `"boxlang"`, `"ai-agent"`), since that's what full-text search uses. * **`version`** should be bumped (`box bump --patch`/`--minor`/`--major`, from inside the template's own folder) each time you publish a change - `bxAgents new --forgebox` always installs whatever `latestVersion` currently resolves to. Then, from inside the project: ```bash box forgebox register # once, if you don't already have a ForgeBox account box publish ``` `publish` reads `readme`/`instructions`/`changelog` files from the folder by convention and publishes them as the entry's description/installation notes/changelog - worth having a real `README.md` for the same reason as the GitHub path above. Once published, anyone can run: ```bash bxAgents new my-agent --forgebox=my-bxagents-template ``` > **Info** > > `bxAgents new --forgebox` already unwraps one level of nesting automatically (see above), so you don't need `box.json`'s `createPackageDirectory: false` setting for this specific path to work - that flag only matters for `box install`'s own separate install conventions, not this module's installer.

title: Agent.bx
body: Agent.bx Most agents use Agent.yaml instead The default way to define an agent is a plain Agent.yaml . Reach for Agent.bx when the definition itself needs code: hooks, dynamic instructions, tools registered in code, an overridden method, or detectEnvironment() . A folder holds one or the other, never both. The sections on the model slug , environment overrides , merge semantics and the always-on agent route below apply to both. Agent.bx is the advanced way to define an agent. A BxAgents project needs an Agent.yaml or an Agent.bx . It extends bx-ai's own AiAgent , so it is the agent - the build instantiates it rather than rebuilding one from a config struct, so what you write is what runs. Inherit and add whatever you need: private helpers, overridden methods, tools registered in code. Because it's a real class rather than a struct-returning descriptor, an IDE can introspect it like any other BoxLang class - jump to definition, autocomplete on inherited methods, the works. class extends="bxModules.bxai.models.runnables.AiAgent" { function init() { super.init( name : "my-agent", description : "A helpful assistant", instructions: "You are a helpful assistant.", model : aiModel( provider: "openai", params: { model: "gpt-5" } ) ) return this } } bxAgents new --class scaffolds exactly this shape (without --class , new scaffolds an Agent.yaml ). instructions.md is optional - set instructions directly in super.init() , or drop the file beside Agent.bx and let the build wire it in for you (see the table below). What the build layers on top of the class The rule: an explicitly declared convention wins; otherwise the class is in charge. So an agent that sets everything in its own init() gets nothing imposed on it, while one that sets the bare minimum still picks up the conventions it didn't speak for. Everything below is optional - declare a configure() returning any of these keys to override what the class itself set, or the matching instructions.md / tools/ / subagents/ convention folder: You declare The build emits If you don't declare it instructions.md withInstructions( fileRead( ... ) ) the class's own instructions stand model in configure() setModel( aiModel( ... ) ) the class's own model stands name / description in configure() setName() / setDescription() the class's own stand memory in configure() setMemory( ... ) the class's own stands the tools/ folder withTools( ... ) with that folder's tools always - withTools() appends in bx-ai rather than replacing, so tools your class registered itself are kept and the agent's own tools/ are added tools / toolOptions in configure() withTools( ... ) with each item@module / *@module listed, built with the module's options no module tools; see Tools and Tool options subAgents on the class, or subagents/ on disk addSubAgent( ... ) per child appended the same way checkpointer in configure() withCheckpointer( ... ) injected anyway if the class set none - see below Info The checkpointer is the one thing the build fills in unasked. An agent reachable from a gateway with no checkpointer has silently broken human-in-the-loop, so a class that set none still gets the cache default. A class that sets its own is left alone. Warning Deliberately not implemented by comparing your instance against bx-ai's DEFAULT_AGENT_* values. "Did the author mean this, or is it just the default?" is unanswerable, and an author who genuinely wanted the default name would find it silently replaced. Presence of an external declaration is a fact; intent behind a default value is not. The class is copied into the generated app at agent/classes/ and instantiated there by its own absolute file path (never a relative lookup that would depend on a registered mapping), exactly as tools/ , skills/ and mcp/ are copied - so a packaged .bxa carries it, and chat / invoke / serve all instantiate it the same way whether or not a real ColdBox container is booted. configure() (optional) - overriding what the class set A configure() method is entirely optional. Declare it only to override specific fields from outside the class - useful for keeping deployment-specific values (a different model per environment, say) out of the class body itself: class extends="bxModules.bxai.models.runnables.AiAgent" { function init() { super.init( name : "with-mcp-servers-agent", model : aiModel( provider: "openai", params: { model: "gpt-5" } ) ) return this } function configure() { return { mcpServers : [ "https://example.com/mcp", { url : "https://other.com/mcp", name : "other" } ] }; } } Field Type Notes name string Also becomes this agent's config/WireBox.bx binding key at build time ( getInstance( name ) , or agent( name ) in a scheduler) - see schedules/ - so it must be unique across the whole project (root + every subagent); build fails if two agents share a name. model string A provider/model slug or a bare provider name. A profile (see Models and profiles ) can stand in for it. See below. description string Optional. subAgents array of strings Names of sibling folders under the root project's subagents/ . See subagents/ . mcpServers array MCP servers - each entry a URL string, or a mapping with url (or command ), name and the credentials the server wants. See mcp/ . security struct Forwarded verbatim into the generated app's bxai module settings; bx-ai's own SecurityDirector turns it into guardrail middleware. Passthrough only - BxAgents has no own guardrails convention. memory string or struct The agent's conversation memory. A bare string is shorthand for the type ( "cache" ); a struct is { type, ...config } and is passed through to aiMemory() verbatim - e.g. { type: "cache", maxMessages: 50 } , or with summaryProvider / summaryModel / summaryThreshold to make the web UI's /compact functional. Applies per node, so a subagent can declare its own. checkpointer struct { type: "cache"\|"file"\|"jdbc", ...config } . Defaults to { type: "cache" } if omitted. Always applied - without one, human-in-the-loop approval flows through any gateway other than cli fail outright. gatewaySession struct { policy, maxQueueDepth, attachments, commands } , all optional (default "queue" / 50 / true / a safe set of slash commands ). Only meaningful if the project has at least one push-style gateway entry - controls the generated GatewaySession 's policy for a second inbound message arriving on a thread that already has a turn in flight. policy must be one of reject / queue / steer / interrupt . agentApi struct { enabled, access, tokenEnvVar, tokens, profiles, path, allowedIPs, rateLimit, manageTokens } , all optional. Controls the always-on agent route, at /__bxagents unless path moves it. See The always-on agent route below. tools , toolOptions array, struct Module tools and their options. See Tools and Tool options . provider , params , options , providers , profiles , defaultProfile , profile , contextWindow , vision , embeddings , speech , transcription , image various The model settings, with the same shape and checks as in Agent.yaml . A subagent may not set params , options , providers , profiles , defaultProfile or the four capabilities: they apply to the whole app and belong to the root. See Models and profiles . notes struct Short notes the agent keeps. See Notes . usage boolean Records what each model call used. Root only. See usage . tui struct How the terminal chat looks. Root only. See tui . extensions struct Values for the project's extensions . Root only. any other key any Merged and available in the resolved config struct, but not interpreted by BxAgents itself. The model slug model is BxAgents' own convention - bx-ai itself takes provider and model as two separate arguments to aiModel() . BxAgents splits the slug on the first / only , so a provider that itself contains a slash (like OpenRouter's openrouter/anthropic/claude-x ) still parses correctly: model value provider model openai/gpt-5 openai gpt-5 openrouter/anthropic/claude-x openrouter anthropic/claude-x mock/mock-model mock mock-model If model has no / at all, it must be a known core provider name (the provider's default model) - validation rejects anything else. The recognized core providers are: bedrock , cartesia , claude , cloudflare , cohere , deepseek , docker , elevenlabs , gemini , grok , groq , huggingface , minimax , mistral , mock , ollama , openai , openai-compatible , openrouter , perplexity , voyage (kept in sync with bx-ai's own CORE_PROVIDERS ). mock is a real provider, useful for tests and CI - it never makes a network call. This slug-splitting convention is what a configure() -declared model string goes through - super.init() 's own model argument instead takes a real AiModel instance directly ( aiModel( provider: "...", params: { model: "..." } ) ), since the class already speaks bx-ai's own API. Environment overrides Agent.bx may declare a method named after an environment (e.g. production() , development() , or any custom name) returning a struct of overrides - this works whether or not the class also declares a configure() : class extends="bxModules.bxai.models.runnables.AiAgent" { function init() { super.init( name : "override-agent", description : "An agent with an environment override", model : aiModel( provider: "openai", params: { model: "gpt-5" } ) ) return this } function production() { return { model : "openai/gpt-5-mini" }; } } The active environment is resolved with this precedence (highest wins): --environment CLI flag ( bxAgents build --environment=production ) Agent.bx 's own detectEnvironment() method, if it declares one BX_AGENTS_ENV environment variable "development" (default) detectEnvironment() For anything the first and third tiers can't express, Agent.bx may declare a detectEnvironment() method and decide for itself. Whatever it returns is taken as the environment name verbatim: class extends="bxModules.bxai.models.runnables.AiAgent" { function init() { super.init( name : "my-agent", model : aiModel( provider : "openai", params : { model : "gpt-5" } ) ) return this } function detectEnvironment() { return fileExists( expandPath( "/.production-marker" ) ) ? "production" : "development"; } } This mirrors ColdBox's own tier-1 convention (a config declaring detectEnvironment() has its return value taken verbatim), with two deliberate differences, both because this runs at build time: An explicit --environment flag outranks detectEnvironment() here, where ColdBox puts its own detect method first. A flag someone typed is the most specific statement of intent available. ColdBox's other detection tier - an environments struct of regexes matched against CGI.HTTP_HOST - is not supported. It cannot work here: the build runs in a CLI process with no HTTP host, so it would only ever describe the machine doing the building (a CI runner would resolve development for a production build). Returning a blank string, or anything that isn't a string, means "no opinion" and falls through to the next tier - so a project computing its environment from something absent on this machine degrades to the default rather than failing the build. A detectEnvironment() that throws is a different matter: that's a real bug in the project's own code, and build fails and says so. This is a build-time decision only, distinct from ColdBox's own runtime environment detection (the generated app reads getSetting("environment") on its own, per ColdBox's environments convention) - this precedence only decides which environment() override method on Agent.bx , and which boxlang-{env}.json / miniserver-{env}.json files, the build pipeline applies. If no method matching the active environment exists, no override is applied. Merge semantics The full resolution order (lowest to highest precedence) is: configure() (optional) the matching environment-override method, if any boxlang.json boxlang-{environment}.json miniserver.json miniserver-{environment}.json Struct keys are merged recursively - a nested struct in a higher-precedence source only overrides the keys it actually sets, leaving sibling keys from a lower-precedence source intact. Arrays and all scalar values are replaced whole , never appended or concatenated. boxlang.json / boxlang-{env}.json / miniserver.json / miniserver-{env}.json are all optional project-root JSON files, useful for config that's easier to express as data than as BoxLang code (e.g. model defaults): // boxlang.json { "modelDefaults": { "temperature": 0.7, "maxTokens": 1000 } } // boxlang-production.json { "modelDefaults": { "temperature": 0.2 } } Building with --environment=production here yields modelDefaults: { temperature: 0.2, maxTokens: 1000 } - the recursive merge kept maxTokens from the base file since boxlang-production.json never mentioned it. Warning Secrets (API keys, tokens) are never read or merged by BxAgents at build time - they stay external (an OS environment variable, .env , a platform secret manager) and are resolved live by bx-ai itself at runtime. See Deployment & Secrets . The always-on agent route Every built project exposes its root agent over HTTP at a fixed reserved path, whether or not it declares any gateways/ entries: POST /__bxagents/invoke POST /__bxagents/stream # SSE POST /__bxagents/batch GET /__bxagents/info They answer in the shape ColdBox's toAi() terminator gives, but they are routes of the agent API's own handler, so the same access setting covers them and every other route. (ColdBox route middleware does not reach toAi() 's routes, which is why they are not used.) The route exists so this module's own tooling always has an address to talk to - it's the service entrance, not your project's public API. A project's own public surface belongs in gateways/ , at whatever paths you choose. A route reached with a verb it does not take (a GET to /invoke ) answers 405 with the usual JSON body, { "success": false, "error": "...", "code": "method_not_allowed" } , not an error page. Run control Beside those four, a generated handler ( handlers/AgentApi.bx ) serves what a chat client needs to control a run. It is what chat --server and chat --connect use: POST /__bxagents/events # SSE: like /stream, plus tool and suspended frames. Body may carry # attachments: [ { name, mime, data (base64) } ], at most 4 pictures of 5 MB POST /__bxagents/cancel # { threadId, reason? } POST /__bxagents/steer # { threadId, input } GET /__bxagents/pending # ?threadId= POST /__bxagents/resume # { threadId, decision } -> SSE, like /events GET /__bxagents/tools GET /__bxagents/profiles # the profiles a client may ask for GET /__bxagents/agent # name, model, what it can do GET /__bxagents/sessions # the caller's recent conversations (?source=terminal for those that started there; ?all=1 lists everyone's, with whose each is, for an admin) POST /__bxagents/sessions # { title? } start one: { conversationId } POST /__bxagents/sessions/rename # { conversationId, title } name one POST /__bxagents/sessions/fork # { conversationId, title? } copy one, messages and all POST /__bxagents/sessions/delete # { conversationId } its row and the agent's messages for it GET /__bxagents/export # ?conversationId=&format=md|html the conversation as a file to save GET /__bxagents/whoami # who the server takes the caller to be: { id, name, scope, source, agent } GET /__bxagents/volumes # the folders the agent may use: { volumes: [ { name, mode, description } ] }, never a path on the machine GET /__bxagents/logs # the agent's logs, admin only: which there are, or ?area=&tail=&level=&q= for the last lines GET /__bxagents/gateways # the chat apps and their state, admin only: { gateways: [ { name, type, state, credentials, lastActiveAt, lastError } ] } GET /__bxagents/skills # the skills the agent can load: { skills: [ { name, description, origin } ] }, origin is installed, project or agent GET /__bxagents/data # where the agent keeps everything and where each volume is (admin only) GET /__bxagents/users # the sign-in accounts and whether each is an admin (admin only) POST /__bxagents/users/admin # { username, admin }: make an account an admin or take that away (admin only) GET /__bxagents/preferences # what the caller has set: { preferences : { key : value } } POST /__bxagents/preferences/set # { key, value } POST /__bxagents/preferences/delete # { key } GET /__bxagents/history # ?conversationId= what was said in one POST /__bxagents/clear # { conversationId } forget its messages POST /__bxagents/compact # { conversationId } summarize the older messages POST /__bxagents/ping # { profile? } test a model with one tiny question: { ok, model, ms, reply } or { ok : false, model, reason } GET /__bxagents/commands # the slash commands this caller may run, [ { name, hint } ] GET /__bxagents/context # ?conversationId= estimated size of the context: parts, largest tools, total, share of the window GET /__bxagents/status # ?conversationId= what the extensions' status items say: { items : [ { name, text } ] } GET /__bxagents/slots # ?conversationId= what the extensions' slots hold: { items : [ { id, extension, place, html, text } ] } POST /__bxagents/command # { line : "/info", conversationId? } run one, answers { blocks, effects, conversationId } GET /__bxagents/notes # the caller's notes and the agent's, with how full they are POST /__bxagents/notes # { scope : "user" | "agent", text } POST /__bxagents/notes/update # { scope, id, text } POST /__bxagents/notes/remove # { scope, id } /events sends the frames of /stream ( thread first, chunk for each piece of the answer, done last) and adds: Frame Data tool { id, name, arguments, status, ms } , once with status: "running" and once with "ok" and the time it took suspended { threadId, pendingActions : [ { toolName, toolArgs } ] } when the run waits for a human decision error { message } cancel stops the run at its next checkpoint (before the next model call or tool call, not in the middle of a token). steer splices a message into a run in flight. resume takes approve , approve_session or reject and streams the rest of the turn. A run belongs to whoever started it: pending answers "nothing pending" and resume answers 403 to anyone else. Send a conversationId with /events to keep the turn in a conversation: the server lists it under the caller (the name of the token used, or local on an open route) and the agent's memory keeps its messages under the same id. sessions , history , clear and compact work on the caller's own conversations only; someone else's id is a 404 , the same as one that does not exist. They answer 404 when the server has no shared chat database, and compact reports available: false when the agent's memory has no summary model. The notes routes answer 404 for an agent that has no notes block. Each caller reads and changes their own user notes (the owner is the name of the token they used, or local on an open route) and the agent's notes. Any caller can add to either scope or edit a note; removing a note of the agent needs an admin token (a 403 otherwise), because it changes what every user's agent knows. These routes sit behind the same x-bxagents-token gate as the other four (a missing or wrong token is a 401 ), and agentApi.enabled: false removes all of them. Answers, errors and who is calling Every answer is JSON with success . A failure is { "success": false, "error": "text for people", "code": "machine_code" } with the status the code means: Status Codes 400 bad_request , bad_profile , bad_attachment 401 unauthorized 403 forbidden , csrf , not_your_run 404 not_found , no_notes 409 busy , conflict 429 rate_limited 500 internal On a route that is open, everyone is the one user local , on every surface, so the terminal chat, the web page and a script share conversations and notes. A caller can say which surface it is with the x-bxagents-source header ( web , terminal , or any plain lower case name; api when it sends none). The conversation list records it: GET /__bxagents/sessions returns a source for each conversation, and ?source=terminal lists only those. Conversations that were made before this was recorded have a blank source. Because the path is reserved, build rejects any gateways/ entry whose path is /__bxagents or sits underneath it. Two routes on one mount is a genuine conflict: one would silently shadow the other, and yours would be the one that never answers. agentApi configure() may return an agentApi struct to control it: Key Type Notes enabled boolean Default true . Set false to omit the route entirely - for a build going somewhere it has no business existing. access open or token Whether callers must prove who they are. Left out, it follows the next two keys: a tokenEnvVar or tokens: true means token , nothing means open . open with either of those set, or token with neither, is a build error. tokenEnvVar string The name of an environment variable holding a shared secret. When set, every route requires a matching x-bxagents-token request header. tokens boolean Default false . true also accepts the access tokens made with bxAgents token create . path string Default /__bxagents . Where the whole API is served, e.g. /agent-api : a rooted path of plain segments (letters, digits, _ , - , ~ ). Everything on this page that says /__bxagents means this path. A gateways/ entry may not sit on it. The web page, serve and chat --server follow it by themselves; chat --connect to a server that moved it needs --api-path=/agent-api . allowedIPs list Default none (anyone). The addresses and networks that may call at all, e.g. [ "10.0.0.0/8", "203.0.113.7", "::1" ] . It is cbSecurity's own AllowedIPs route middleware in front of every route, so anyone else gets 403 ( { "error": true, "messages": [ "Your IP address is not allowed" ] } ) before any token is looked at. It checks the address of the connection, never a X-Forwarded-For header the client chooses; behind a reverse proxy every caller has the proxy's address unless you set cbSecurity's middleware.trustedProxies . /health stays open. rateLimit struct Default none. { requests, perSeconds } : at most requests calls from one address in each window of perSeconds seconds. It is cbSecurity's own Throttle route middleware, one counter for the whole API, kept in CacheBox. Over the limit answers 429 with a Retry-After header; every answer carries X-RateLimit-Limit and X-RateLimit-Remaining . manageTokens boolean Default false . true lets an admin make, list and revoke access tokens over the API ( GET / POST /__bxagents/tokens , POST /__bxagents/tokens/revoke ) and shows a Tokens panel in the web page. Needs tokens: true and a token API; a chat token gets 403 . The secret of a new token is in the answer to the create call and nowhere else. Off, the routes do not exist and tokens are made only with bxAgents token create . profiles list Default none. The profiles a client may ask for with options.profile on /events , and what GET /__bxagents/profiles lists (never a key). Any other profile is a 400 , so a caller cannot pick a model you did not offer. chat --connect uses this list for /profile . Each name must be declared in Agent.yaml , or default . function configure() { return { name : "my-agent", model : "openai/gpt-5", agentApi : { tokenEnvVar : "BXAGENTS_API_TOKEN" } }; } Because this comes from configure() , it scopes per environment with an environment override like any other key - so a project can leave the route open locally and require a token in production: function production() { return { agentApi : { tokenEnvVar : "BXAGENTS_API_TOKEN" } }; } Who may stop a run POST /cancel and POST /steer take a threadId , which is not a secret (the first frame of every stream carries it). A run can only be stopped or steered by the caller who started it: anyone else gets 403 with code: "not_your_run" . A run no caller here started (one a chat platform's gateway runs) can only be touched by an admin ; anyone else is told cancelled: false , the same answer an unknown thread id gets. Open or token access: open (the default when nothing else is set) asks nobody anything: everyone is the one local user. It is meant for your own machine. When serve is told to listen on an address other machines can reach ( --host=0.0.0.0 , say) and the API is open, it prints a warning at start: WARNING: the agent API is open and this server listens on every network interface (port 8080). Anyone who can reach it can chat with the agent, use its tools and read its conversations. Set agentApi.access to token ... access: token puts every route of the API behind one check, made before any action runs, by ColdBox route middleware. That includes invoke , stream , batch and info , and the same four routes of any gateway that exposes the agent ( exposes: "agent" ), which follow this one switch. A request that carries neither the shared secret nor an issued token is answered 401 and never reaches the agent. The gate fails closed : if the named variable is unset or blank at runtime, nothing matches - it never degenerates into comparing "" to "" and letting every caller through. A request without a valid token gets a 401 with a small JSON body ( code: unauthorized ), and never reaches the agent. Warning tokenEnvVar names a variable , never the secret itself. build rejects a value that isn't a valid environment-variable name, precisely so a literal token can't be committed here by mistake. Only the variable's name is ever written into generated source. Access tokens for a deployed agent One shared secret ( tokenEnvVar ) is enough for a single caller. To let several people or machines in, each with a name you can revoke, turn on issued tokens: # Agent.yaml agentApi: tokens: true Make them where the agent's database is: on the server, or in the project before you pack it. bxAgents token create --name=laptop --expires=90d bxAgents token create --name=ci --scope=admin bxAgents token list bxAgents token revoke --name=laptop A token is shown once , when it is made. Only its SHA-256 is stored, so a stolen database file cannot be used to call the agent. The caller sends it in the x-bxagents-token header, or bxAgents chat --connect=<url> --token=<token> (or BXAGENTS_TOKEN ) does. The name is who is calling. A run belongs to the token that started it, and one token cannot answer another's pending approval. The scope is chat or admin . Revoking takes effect on the next request, without a restart. A token can also expire ( --expires=90d , 12h , 2w or a date). With tokens: true and no tokenEnvVar , a server with no tokens yet refuses everyone. With both, the shared secret works as an admin token, so a fresh deployment can be reached before the first token exists. The tokens live in the shared chat database ( data/chat.db ). On a deployed server run token with BXAGENTS_DB pointing at the file the app uses. Put HTTPS in front of any server a token travels to: a token on plain HTTP can be read on the wire. Info The route is bound to whatever host the miniserver is listening on - 127.0.0.1 by default, so nothing is reachable off the machine unless you deliberately expose it. tokenEnvVar is what matters once you do, and for any built .bxa artifact you deploy.
