# CLI Reference Usage: boxlang module:bxAgents [options] (or the shorter `bxAgents [options]` form - see [Installation](/getting-started/installation/index.html).) ## Global flags These are handled before verb dispatch and never reach a verb. | Flag | Effect | |------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `-h`, `--help`, `help` | Print usage (every verb + description) and exit 0. Accepted in **any** position, so `bxAgents clean --help` prints usage rather than running `clean`. Also printed (exit 1) if no verb is given at all. | | `-v`, `--version` | Print `bxAgents v{version}` and exit 0. Only meaningful as the very first token, so it never collides with `package --version=1.0.0`. | ## The banner At an interactive terminal, `bxAgents --help` and the end of the `new` wizard greet you with the BxAgents name in block letters, painted in a gradient picked at random from eight themes (Ocean, Fire, Sunset, Purple, Mint, Gray, Forest, Gold), the same idea as the ColdBox CLI's banner. It is never written to a pipe or a file. | Setting | Effect | |-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `NO_COLOR`, `--no-color` | Same shape, no color | | `TERM=dumb`, output that is not UTF-8, or a terminal narrower than the art (75 columns) | One plain line instead | | `--no-banner`, or `BXAGENTS_BANNER=off` | No banner | | `BXAGENTS_BANNER_THEME=Ocean` | Pin a theme instead of a random one, for a recording that comes out the same every time | ## Every verb accepts `--projectRoot=` (or a bare positional path as the first non-flag argument) to target a project other than the current directory. Precedence: `--projectRoot` flag \> first positional argument \> current working directory. ## Argument syntax Follows BoxLang's own documented CLI conventions: | Form | Result | |----------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------| | `--option` | `true` | | `--option=value` / `--option="quoted value"` | `value` (surrounding quotes stripped) | | `-o=value` | short form with a value | | `-o` | short form, `true` | | `-abc` | combined shorthand: `a`, `b`, `c` all `true` | | `--!option` / `--no-option` | negation, `false` | | anything else | a positional (the first becomes the project-root fallback) | Repeated options: last one wins. Note the first row: a bare `--option` is a **boolean** , not a way to pass the next token as its value. A flag that requires a value (`--model`, `--message`, `--password`, `--environment`, `--port`, ...) is therefore rejected with an error when written bare, rather than silently becoming `true`: $ bxAgents new my-agent --model openai/gpt-5 Error: --model requires a value - write it as `--model=`. Always use the `--flag=value` form. The space-separated form is not supported. ## Tab completion `completions/` holds ready-made completion scripts for bash, fish and PowerShell. See [Installation](/getting-started/installation/index.html#tab-completion) for the one-line setup of each. ## Verbs [](#new)
[new](#new) [Scaffold a new agent project.](#new) [](#new)[
add Add a tool, interceptor, schedule, MCP server, gateway, subagent, skill, extension and more to an existing project.](#add)[
skills Find, install, update and remove skills from skills.boxlang.io.](#skills)[
build Run the full build pipeline.](#build)[
test Run your project's own tests/specs via TestBox.](#test)[
serve Launch a real boxlang-miniserver process.](#serve)[
chat Interactive REPL against the built agent.](#chat)[
invoke One non-interactive turn - for scripting/CI.](#invoke)[
package Package a built project into a .bxa.](#package)[
deploy Ship to a real deployment target.](#deploy)[
hash-password Hash a plaintext password for a webui users entry.](#hash-password)[
token Issue, list and revoke access tokens for a deployed agent.](#token)[
users List the web page's accounts and choose who is an admin.](#users)[
notes Read and manage the notes an agent keeps.](#notes)[
models List the models a project can talk to and test that they answer.](#models)[
sessions List, rename, fork, delete, export and import the conversations in the chat database.](#sessions)[
stats What the model calls used: tokens by model, provider, day or user, once the project turns usage on.](#stats)[
inspect Report how the agent is composed, from its source.](#inspect)[
extensions List the extensions the chat loads, and install, update, remove or link more.](#extensions)[
clean Remove a project's .build/ and dist/ output.](#clean)[
doctor Diagnose the runtime and project before build/serve surprise you.](#doctor)
### `new` Create a new agent project one of three mutually exclusive ways: scaffold it (answering questions at a terminal, or with flags), clone a GitHub repo, or install a ForgeBox package. ```bash # At a terminal: answer questions (see the new wizard guide) bxAgents new my-agent # Scaffold from flags (default template: minimal) bxAgents new my-agent --model=openai/gpt-5 [--template=minimal|webui-chat|slack-bot|telegram-bot|github-bot|mcp-server|scheduled|multi-agent] [--name=...] [--description=...] [--class] [--skipInstall] # The same, adding what the wizard would have offered bxAgents new my-agent --model=claude --with=time,search --search=brave --mcp=github --channels=web,telegram --guard=flag # Clone an existing GitHub repo bxAgents new my-agent --repo=owner/repo-name # Install a ForgeBox package bxAgents new my-agent --forgebox=some-package-slug ``` * With no `--model`, no `--repo` and no `--forgebox`, at a terminal, `new` runs the [wizard](/guides/new-wizard/index.html). `--no-wizard` or `--yes` turns it off, `--wizard` turns it on even with a `--model`, and `--no-tui` asks the same questions as numbered lines. A `--model` on its own never starts it, since scripts have always had to pass one. The wizard's flags (`--with`, `--search`, `--files`, `--files-dir`, `--temperature`, `--max-tokens`, `--timeout`, `--memory`, `--mcp`, `--channels`, `--web-auth`, `--guard`, `--prompt`, `--widgets`, `--widgets-bottom`, `--deploy` and the deploy details) are listed in the [wizard guide](/guides/new-wizard/index.html#without-the-wizard); a bad value names the flag and what it accepts. They need `Agent.yaml`, so they cannot be combined with `--class`. * `--template`, `--repo`, and `--forgebox` name three different project SOURCES - exactly one applies. Combining any two of them is an error. * **`--template` mode** (the default when no source flag is passed at all - `minimal`): * `--model` is **required** when no questions are asked - a `provider/model` slug (see [the model slug](/conventions/agent-bx/index.html#the-model-slug)). * `--name` defaults to the target directory's own basename. * Refuses to run if the target already contains an `Agent.yaml` or an `Agent.bx`. * Creates [`Agent.yaml`](/conventions/agent-yaml/index.html), `instructions.md`, a root [`Application.bx`](/conventions/application-bx/index.html) (extends the class every build generates; never overwritten), every convention folder (empty), a root [`box.json`](/conventions/box-json/index.html) (`testbox` as a development dependency, installed into `lib/testbox`), a ready-to-run [`tests/`](/conventions/testing/index.html) folder (`tests/specs/AgentSpec.bx`), a `.env` declaring `BOXLANG_HOME=.build/runtime` (matching `serve`'s own scoped runtime home), a `.gitignore` (`.env` and `.env.*`, `.build/`, `dist/`, `data/chat.db*`, `lib/`, `boxlang_modules/`, `.agents/skills/`, editor files), and the standard dotfiles `.editorconfig`, `.gitattributes`, `.bxlint.json`, `.markdownlint.json` and a `.boxlang.json` listing every bx-ai setting at its default (the BoxLang runtime reads it when run from the project root; edit the values there). Never overwrites a file that already exists. BoxLang and `boxlang-miniserver` load a `.env` from the project root themselves, so the file also works for your API keys; BxAgents never reads, copies or packages it. * `--class` (a bare boolean flag, like the others described above) writes the class-based [`Agent.bx`](/conventions/agent-bx/index.html) instead of the default `Agent.yaml`, for agents whose definition needs code (hooks, dynamic instructions). It applies to the root and to any subagents a template scaffolds, and only to `--template` mode - not to `--repo`/`--forgebox`. * `--template` picks one of 8 built-in starters, each layering a bit of pre-wired content on top of the base skeleton above (see [Agent Templates](/agent-templates/index.html) for every generated file in full, plus how `--repo`/`--forgebox` sources work and how to publish your own): * `minimal` - the bare skeleton, nothing extra. * `webui-chat` - adds a `gateways/webui.bx` exposing the [web chat UI](/conventions/gateways/index.html) at `/chat`. * `slack-bot` - adds a `gateways/slack.bx` channel adapter, plus matching `SLACK_BOT_TOKEN`/`SLACK_APP_TOKEN` stub lines in `.env`. * `telegram-bot` - adds a `gateways/telegram.bx` channel adapter, plus a matching `TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN` stub line in `.env`. * `github-bot` - adds a `gateways/github.bx` channel adapter, plus matching `GITHUB_TOKEN`/`GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET`/`GITHUB_BOT_NAME` stub lines in `.env`. * `mcp-server` - adds an example `mcp/exampleServer.bx` tool server and a `gateways/mcpExpose.bx` entry exposing it as an MCP server at `/mcp`. * `scheduled` - adds a [`schedules/Example.bx`](/conventions/schedules/index.html) scheduler calling the agent on a daily cron schedule. * `multi-agent` - adds a `subAgents` list to the root `Agent.yaml` declaring two [subagents](/conventions/subagents/index.html) (`researcher`, `writer`), each scaffolded as its own real `subagents//Agent.yaml` + `instructions.md`. * Also runs `box install` in the new project root, so `bxAgents test` works immediately with no separate install step. This is best-effort: if `box` isn't on `PATH` or the install fails, `new` still succeeds - the message just tells you to run it yourself. Pass `--skipInstall` to opt out of this step entirely. * **`--repo` mode** (`--repo=owner/repo-name` or a full URL): clones the repo via a bundled [JGit](https://www.eclipse.org/jgit/) dependency - no `git` binary needs to be installed. Always clones shallow (depth 1) and always strips the resulting `.git` folder afterward, so the new project starts with a clean history rather than staying tied to the template repo's own remote. Refuses to run into a directory that already exists and is non-empty, and fails clearly if no `Agent.yaml` or `Agent.bx` is found in the cloned repo. * **`--forgebox` mode** (`--forgebox=`): installs a [ForgeBox](https://www.forgebox.io) package by talking to ForgeBox's own REST API directly (no `box` CLI required). Fails clearly if the slug doesn't exist, the download fails, or the installed package has no `Agent.yaml` or `Agent.bx` at its root (unwrapping one level of nesting first, since many ForgeBox archives wrap their contents in a single top-level folder). * Only `--template` mode needs `--model`; `--repo`/`--forgebox` never require it, since the source project already defines its own. * `--name`/`--description` are ignored (with a warning in the output) when `--repo`/`--forgebox` is used - the cloned/installed project defines its own. * The `box install` convenience step (and `--skipInstall`) only ever apply to `--template` mode - a cloned/installed project's own `box.json` (if it has one at all) is left untouched. ### `add` Add one thing to a project that already exists, asking the same questions `new` asks. Today that is a `tool`, an `interceptor`, a `schedule`, an `mcp` server, a `gateway`, a `subagent`, a `skill`, a `profile`, a `provider`, a `capability` or an `extension`. ```bash bxAgents add # pick what to add bxAgents add tool # asks for the name, function, description and arguments bxAgents add tool WeatherTools --function=getWeather --description="Get the weather for a city" --args="city, days:numeric" bxAgents add tool Pinger --agent=researcher # into subagents/researcher/tools/ bxAgents add tool Pinger --dry-run # show the file, write nothing ``` * The positional arguments are the kind and the name, so the project is found by `--projectRoot=` or the current folder only. * At a terminal, whatever is not given as a flag is asked, in the full-screen UI (or numbered lines with `--no-tui`). With `--yes`, in a pipe or in CI nothing is asked: flags and defaults are used, and a required answer that is missing names the flag to pass. * Questions end on a review of the files that will be written. Cancelling, with Esc or Ctrl+C, changes nothing. * **Nothing is overwritten.** If a file already exists none are written and the error names it; `--force` replaces it. At a terminal the review offers to replace instead. * `--dry-run` prints each file with its text and writes nothing. #### `add tool` Creates `tools/.bx` with one `@AITool` function in the shape [bx-ai documents](/conventions/tools/index.html): a docblock describing each argument, the annotation carrying the description the model reads, and typed `required` arguments from which bx-ai builds the tool's schema. | Flag | Meaning | |------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `--name=` | The file name, or the second positional. Letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter. | | `--agent=` | Whose tool it is. Asked only when the project has subagents; `.` (the default) is the root agent. | | `--function=` | The function the model calls. Defaults to the file name with a lower-case first letter. | | `--description=` | What the tool does. The model reads it to decide when to call the tool. Without it, and with nothing to ask, the file gets a `TODO` description and the output reminds you to replace it. | | `--args=` | Comma separated, each `name` or `name:type` (`string` by default; `numeric`, `boolean`, `array`, `struct`, `date` and `any` also work). | A tool belongs to the agent whose folder it is in and is attached to that agent automatically. Two tool files of one agent may not share a name, even in different subfolders, so a clash is refused here instead of at the next `build`. Check the result with `bxAgents inspect --section=tools`. #### `add interceptor` Creates `interceptors/.bx` with one method for each interception point you pick, and the `@scope` that [the build splits on](/conventions/interceptors/index.html). ```bash bxAgents add interceptor AuditLogger --points=preProcess,onException --description="Log every request" bxAgents add interceptor AiWatch --scope=runtime --points=beforeAIModelInvoke,onAIError ``` | Flag | Meaning | |--------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `--name=` | The file name, or the second positional. A name another interceptor already uses is refused. | | `--scope=agent\|runtime` | `agent` (the default) is a ColdBox interceptor registered with the generated app when it starts; its methods take `( event, interceptData, rc, prc )`. `runtime` listens to the events bx-ai announces in the BoxLang runtime and takes the event data as its one argument; BxAgents copies it to `.build/runtime-interceptors` but does not register it for you. | | `--points=` | Comma separated interception points. The picker offers the common ones; any ColdBox core point (`agent`) or bx-ai event (`runtime`) can be named here, and a name that is not a point for that scope is refused. Defaults to `preProcess` (`agent`) or `beforeAIModelInvoke` (`runtime`). | | `--description=` | One line for the class's docblock. Optional. | #### `add schedule` Adds a [scheduler](/conventions/schedules/index.html) to `schedules/` that sends an agent a message on a schedule. Three things are asked: when it runs, what it says to the agent, and which agent. Overlapping runs are always prevented (`.withNoOverlaps()`). Each schedule is its own file, `schedules/.bx`, so adding one never edits another. ```bash bxAgents add schedule --when="weekdays 08:30" --prompt="Summarize yesterday's findings" bxAgents add schedule digest --when="0 9 * * 1-5" --prompt="Check for new tickets" --agent=researcher bxAgents add schedule # asks how often, the details, a name, and what to say ``` | Flag | Meaning | |---------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `--when=` | When it runs: one of the phrases below, or a cron expression. At a terminal, leave it out and you are asked how often, then the details. | | `--prompt=` | The message sent to the agent each time. | | `--name=` | The task's name, or the second positional. It also names the file: `daily-digest` writes `schedules/DailyDigest.bx`. Defaults to a name made from the phrase. A task name already used in `schedules/` is refused. | | `--agent=` | Which agent runs it. Asked only when the project has subagents; `.` (the default) is the root agent, which the file calls with `run()`. Another agent is called with `agent( "name" ).run()` by its declared `name`, so renaming the agent means editing the file. | | Phrase | Runs | Written as | |-------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `every 15 minutes`, `every 2 hours`, `every 1 days` | At that interval | `.cron( "*/15 * * * *" )` where the step divides the hour or day evenly, otherwise `.every( n, "unit" )` | | `hourly`, `hourly :15` | Every hour, on the hour or at that minute | `.cron( "0 * * * *" )`, `.cron( "15 * * * *" )` | | `daily 09:00` | Every day at that time | `.cron( "0 9 * * *" )` | | `weekdays 08:30`, `weekends 10:00` | Monday to Friday, or Saturday and Sunday | `.cron( "30 8 * * 1-5" )`, `.cron( "0 10 * * 0,6" )` | | `weekly mon 09:00` | Once a week (`mon` `tue` `wed` `thu` `fri` `sat` `sun`) | `.cron( "0 9 * * MON" )` | | `monthly 1 09:00` | Once a month on that day, 1 to 28 so that no month skips it | `.cron( "0 9 1 * *" )` | | `first-business-day 09:00`, `last-business-day 17:00` | On that business day of each month | `.onFirstBusinessDayOfTheMonth( "09:00" )` (cron cannot say it) | | `0 9 * * 1-5`, `0 30 8 * * MON-FRI` | Any cron expression: five fields, or six with seconds in front | `.cron( "..." )`, checked by BoxLang's own parser | Times are 24 hour `HH:mm` in the scheduler's timezone. * An existing file of the same name is a conflict and nothing is written; `--force` replaces it. * Schedulers run while the app is served (`bxAgents serve`). Check the result with `bxAgents inspect --section=schedule`. #### `add mcp` Adds an MCP server in either direction: one the agent **calls** (written into `Agent.yaml`), or one the project **hosts** (`mcp/.bx`). ```bash bxAgents add mcp client github # a server from the catalog the new wizard uses (or --direction=client) bxAgents add mcp client --url=https://mcp.acme.dev/mcp --name=acme --auth=bearer --env=ACME_TOKEN bxAgents add mcp server tools --description="My tools" bxAgents add mcp # asks which way ``` **`add mcp client`** adds an entry to the agent's `mcpServers:` list. A name from the catalog (`github`, `stripe`, `notion`, `atlassian`, `cloudflare`, `supabase`, `git`) fills in the address and the sign-in, or for a server that runs as a program on this machine (`git`) the `command` to start it and what it needs on the PATH; otherwise give `--url`. Without a terminal, name the server as the positional or give `--url`. | Flag | Meaning | |--------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `--server=` | A catalog server by name, instead of the positional. | | `--url=
` | A server not in the catalog. An address with a user name, password or key in it is refused: the secret belongs in an environment variable. | | `--name=

# Connect: services that ask each person to sign in

Some [MCP servers](/conventions/mcp/index.html) do not take a fixed key. Mail, calendars and ticket systems ask **each person** to sign in with OAuth, and then accept a token that expires and is renewed. Add `oauth` to the server's entry in `Agent.yaml` and BX Agents does the rest: the person signs in once, their tokens are **sealed in the chat database** with the [vault](/conventions/vault/index.html) key, and the agent uses **their** tokens when it acts for them. The model never sees a token.

```yaml
# Agent.yaml
mcpServers:
  - name: mail
    url: https://mail.example.com/mcp
    oauth:
      scopes: [ mail.read ]
```

`oauth: true` is enough for a server that tells us what we need. The entry needs a `name`, because people type it.

The sign in above is real, against a small fake mail service ([`tools/demo/fake-oauth-mcp.bxs`](https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/bx-agents/tree/development/tools/demo)); the agent's first answer is scripted.

![The Connections panel with mail connected](/assets/webui/connections.png)

## What you write

|     Key under `oauth`      |                                                                                                      Meaning                                                                                                       |
|----------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `scopes`                   | A list of scopes to ask for. Left out: what the server asks for, else everything it supports                                                                                                                       |
| `clientId`, `clientSecret` | A client you registered with the provider yourself. Left out: the client registers itself. `clientSecret` must be an ``${env.NAME}` or `${vault.NAME}`` placeholder: a secret written in the file is a build error |
| `clientMetadataUrl`        | The `https` address of your Client ID Metadata Document, for providers that support them                                                                                                                           |
| `clientName`               | The name shown on the sign in page when the client registers itself                                                                                                                                                |
| `redirectUri`              | Where the provider sends the person back. Left out: your public address, the [API path](/guides/agent-api/index.html) and `/connect/callback`                                                                      |

A server with `oauth` cannot also have `token`, `user` or `password`. Everything is checked when the project is built.

## Signing in

Each way asks the same questions of the same place, so they never disagree about who is connected.

|     Where      |                                                                           How                                                                            |
|----------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Web page       | **Connections** in the settings menu: a row per service with *Connect* or *Disconnect*. The sign in opens in a new tab; the page notices when it worked  |
| Terminal chat  | `/connect` lists the services, `/connect mail` prints an address and waits for the browser in the background, `/connect mail remove` forgets it          |
| Command line   | `bxAgents connect` lists, `bxAgents connect mail` signs in, `bxAgents connect mail --remove` forgets. See [`connect`](/cli-reference/index.html#connect) |
| Chat platforms | `/connect mail` sends an address that works once, for ten minutes. Open it in a browser and sign in                                                      |
| HTTP           | `GET /connect`, `POST /connect`, `POST /connect/remove` on the [agent API](/guides/agent-api/index.html)                                                 |

![The terminal chat after /connect: not connected, the address to open, then connected](/assets/tui/connect-chat.png)

When a person has not signed in to a service, the agent is told which one and how to connect, in one short line, so it can say so instead of "I cannot read your mail". The tools of a service appear in the same running agent once somebody has signed in; there is no restart.

## Trying it on a chat platform

A person reaches the agent from Telegram, Slack and the other [gateways](/conventions/gateways/index.html), and `/connect` works there too. The browser is the part to plan for: the provider sends it back to **your server**, so the server needs an address the person's browser can open. On your own machine, give it one with a tunnel.

1. **A gateway.** For Telegram, `gateways/telegramChannel.bx` with `type: "telegram"` and `botTokenEnvVar: "TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN"` (see [Telegram](/conventions/gateways/telegram/index.html)). Make the bot with @BotFather and `export TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN=...`.
2. **A service that asks people to sign in** , with `oauth` on its `mcpServers` entry as above.
3. **A public address.** Start a tunnel to the port you serve on, `export BXAGENTS_PUBLIC_URL=https://your-tunnel.example.com`, and register `https://your-tunnel.example.com/__bxagents/connect/callback` with the provider.
4. **Build and serve:** `bxAgents build` then `bxAgents serve`.
5. **In the chat with the bot:** send `/connect`, then `/connect mail`. The bot answers with an address that works once, for ten minutes. Open it in a browser, allow access, and send `/connect` again: the service is *connected*.

The person is the platform's own id for them (a Telegram user id, a Slack member id). Their tokens are kept under it, so each person on the platform signs in once. Send `/connect` in a private chat with the bot, not in a group: anyone in a group can open a link posted there.

## Where the browser comes back to

After the person signs in, the provider sends their browser to an address you register with it.

* **A served agent** receives it at `<your public address><API path>/connect/callback`, for example `https://agent.example.com/__bxagents/connect/callback`. Set `BXAGENTS_PUBLIC_URL` to the address people reach the server at, and register that callback with the provider.
* **The terminal** has no public address. `bxAgents connect` and `/connect` open a small listener on `127.0.0.1`, on a free port, for a few minutes, catch the one redirect and close it. Providers that follow RFC 8252 accept any port on the loopback address. For one that does not, give the port you registered: `bxAgents connect mail --port=8765`.

The callback is the one public route of the connect routes. It is safe because it carries no person: the **single use `state`** that the sign in started with says who it was for, and it is used once and expires after ten minutes. Nothing in the address names anyone.

## Whose tokens

A turn runs as the person who asked, so the agent uses that person's tokens. A person never uses another's. A run with nobody behind it, such as a [schedule](/conventions/schedules/index.html), finds no tokens and gets no tools from that service.

The list of a service's tools is the same for everyone, so when the app starts it is asked for as **the person who signed in last**. If nobody has, the agent starts without those tools and gets them when the first person signs in.
> **Note**
>
> Signing in on the web page does not sign the same human in on a chat platform: each place knows the person by its own id (`local`, a Slack user id), so each is its own sign in. Say so to the people who use both.

## Where the tokens are

Tokens, the client registration and a sign in waiting for its callback are rows of the `oauth_records` table, each **sealed with the vault key** (AES-256-GCM) and bound to its row, so a value copied onto another row does not open. The key is the vault's: `BXAGENTS_VAULT_KEY`, or the key file beside the database. Losing the key means everyone signs in again, and a changed key is reported by name. `bxAgents vault status` says where it comes from.

bx-ai's own token stores keep tokens as plain text; this is why BX Agents brings its own.

## Limits

* OAuth is for web servers (HTTP). A server that runs as a program takes its credentials from its environment.
* A link sent in a group chat can be used by anyone in it: ask people to use `/connect` in a private chat with the bot.
* The sign in follows the [MCP authorization specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/basic/authorization): PKCE (S256) is required, and a provider that does not offer it is refused.

title: data and volumes
body: Data and volumes An agent keeps its state in one place, the data home , and reaches the rest of your machine only through volumes : folders you name in Agent.yaml . bxAgents data shows both, and bxAgents backup and restore keep the data safe. The data home <data home>/ README.md what this folder is, written once chat.db conversations and the agents' memory of them, notes, access tokens, secrets and usage counts files/ what the agent writes (the `files` volume) skills/ skills the agent saves routines/ reports saved by routines, one folder each (see routines) logs/ what the agent logs, one file per area (see logs) backups/ written by bxAgents backup There is always a home. Where it is, first match wins: The environment variable BXAGENTS_HOME . data.home in Agent.yaml . The folder of BXAGENTS_DB when that names a file called chat.db (what serve and chat set). data/ in the project, when it already holds a chat.db . A project from before this convention keeps its data. ~/.bxagents/<agent name> , the convention. It is outside the project and outside the build, so a new build never replaces it, and it is the same place in development and when deployed. data/ in the project, only for an agent that has no name. # Agent.yaml name: nanobox data: home: ~/.nanobox # an absolute path, one starting with ~, or one relative to the project BXAGENTS_DB keeps working and names the database file on its own. The agent name is turned into a safe folder name: letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores, the rest become a dash. Two projects with the same agent name share one home, so give them different names, or set data.home on one. The folders and the README are made the first time the app or chat starts. Nothing is made just by asking where the home is. Volumes A volume is a folder on this machine that the agent's file tools may use, under a name. # Agent.yaml volumes: notes: path: ~/Notes mode: rw # rw (read and write) or ro (read only, the default) description: My notes # optional, up to 200 characters downloads: path: ~/Downloads Every agent also has files : the files/ folder of its data home, always read and write. Rule Detail Names Lowercase letters, digits and dashes, 1 to 32 characters. files is taken. At most 32 volumes path Absolute, starting with ~ , or relative to the project. It must exist when the app starts Too wide The whole disk or the whole home folder is refused. So is the data home itself Keys path , mode , description . Anything else is refused When Volumes are fixed when the app starts. The agent cannot add one, and neither can an API An agent that lists bx-ai's file tools ( readFile@bxai , writeFile@bxai , and so on) gets the project's volumes with no further setting. An agent that sets toolOptions.bxai.allowedPaths itself keeps those full paths instead, and cannot also use volumes. How the agent sees them The agent writes a path as volume:path , for example notes:todo.md . A path with no volume is in files . A full path on the machine is refused, and so is anything that climbs out of its volume with .. or a symbolic link. A read only volume can be read, listed and copied from, but not written to, moved, or deleted from. Results and error messages name volumes. The agent never sees where a volume is on the machine. listAllowedDirectories answers with the volumes, their modes and their descriptions. Seeing them In chat: /volumes lists the volumes by name, mode and description, in the terminal, the web page and chat apps. It never shows a folder on the machine. Over the API: GET /volumes answers the same list to anyone who may call the API. GET /data answers the data home, the size of each part and the folder of each volume, and is for admins only, since it shows paths. In doctor : it reports the data home, where it came from, and whether it can be written. It makes nothing. Skills the agent saves A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md : instructions the agent loads by name when a task calls for them. There are three levels: Level Where Written by origin Installed .agents/skills/ in the project The registry tools ( npx skills , bxAgents skills install ), restored at build time installed Ships with the agent skills/ in the project, and the skills extensions carry You project The agent's own skills/ in the data home The agent, with its skill_save tool agent The build copies the first two into the app, and the app loads the third at start and the moment a skill is saved. A diagram of the levels is on the skills page . A skill that ships with the agent wins over an installed one of the same name. After a task that took real steps and is likely to come up again, the root agent can call skill_save( name, description, content ) . The skill is written to the data home and is in the agent's skill list at once, with no restart. Subagents are given the skills when they are built; they cannot save any. The first two levels win. The agent cannot take the name of an installed skill or one that ships with the agent, or replace it. It can save over a skill it wrote itself, to improve it. Approval. Each save is approved by a person, as for any tool that needs approval, unless skills.autoApprove: true . Limits. A name is a folder name (letters, digits, . , _ , - ). A description is up to 500 characters and the content up to 20,000. The agent keeps up to 50 skills; saving over one it has is always allowed. Off switch. skills.agentCanSave: false takes the tool away. skills: agentCanSave: true # default true; the root agent only autoApprove: false # default false A saved skill is part of the data home, so backup and restore carry it. To remove one, delete its folder. Seeing the skills In chat: /skills lists every skill with its level: installed, project or agent. Over the API: GET /skills answers { skills: [ { name, description, origin } ] } ( origin is installed , project or agent ) to anyone who may call the API. It never shows a folder on the machine. Routine reports routines/ holds one folder per routine, <name>-<first 8 of its id> , with the report files the routine saved. Nothing in it is ever deleted automatically: a person removes old reports. They are part of a backup. See routines . Logs The logs/ folder of the data home holds the agent's log files, one per area. They are not part of a backup. See logs . bxAgents data bxAgents data [--json] Prints the data home and where it came from, the size of the database and each folder, and the volumes with their modes. Backups bxAgents backup [--to=FILE] bxAgents restore FILE [--home=DIR] [--force] backup writes one zip with the chat database, files/ , skills/ and routines/ , plus a small backup.json . Without --to it goes in the home's backups/ folder as backup-<date>-<time>.zip . The database is copied whole with SQLite's own VACUUM INTO , so it is safe to run while a server is using it. Volumes are not included: they are your folders. restore puts a backup back. What was there is kept beside it as chat.db.before-restore , files.before-restore and skills.before-restore for one restore; the next restore replaces them. It stops when a server or chat looks to have the database open (SQLite leaves a -wal file while one does), unless you pass --force . --home restores into another data home. # Data and volumes

An agent keeps its state in one place, the **data home** , and reaches the rest of your machine only through **volumes** : folders you name in `Agent.yaml`. `bxAgents data` shows both, and `bxAgents backup` and `restore` keep the data safe.

## The data home

```text
<data home>/
  README.md      what this folder is, written once
  chat.db        conversations and the agents' memory of them, notes, access tokens, secrets and usage counts
  files/         what the agent writes (the `files` volume)
  skills/        skills the agent saves
  routines/      reports saved by routines, one folder each (see routines)
  logs/          what the agent logs, one file per area (see logs)
  backups/       written by bxAgents backup
```

There is always a home. Where it is, first match wins:

1. The environment variable `BXAGENTS_HOME`.
2. `data.home` in `Agent.yaml`.
3. The folder of `BXAGENTS_DB` when that names a file called `chat.db` (what `serve` and `chat` set).
4. `data/` in the project, when it already holds a `chat.db`. A project from before this convention keeps its data.
5. **`~/.bxagents/<agent name>`**, the convention. It is outside the project and outside the build, so a new build never replaces it, and it is the same place in development and when deployed.
6. `data/` in the project, only for an agent that has no name.

```yaml
# Agent.yaml
name: nanobox
data:
  home: ~/.nanobox      # an absolute path, one starting with ~, or one relative to the project
```

`BXAGENTS_DB` keeps working and names the database file on its own.

The agent name is turned into a safe folder name: letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores, the rest become a dash. Two projects with the same agent name share one home, so give them different names, or set `data.home` on one.

The folders and the README are made the first time the app or `chat` starts. Nothing is made just by asking where the home is.

## Volumes

A volume is a folder on this machine that the agent's file tools may use, under a name.

```yaml
# Agent.yaml
volumes:
  notes:
    path: ~/Notes
    mode: rw                 # rw (read and write) or ro (read only, the default)
    description: My notes    # optional, up to 200 characters
  downloads:
    path: ~/Downloads
```

Every agent also has `files`: the `files/` folder of its data home, always read and write.

|   Rule   |                                             Detail                                             |
|----------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Names    | Lowercase letters, digits and dashes, 1 to 32 characters. `files` is taken. At most 32 volumes |
| `path`   | Absolute, starting with `~`, or relative to the project. It must exist when the app starts     |
| Too wide | The whole disk or the whole home folder is refused. So is the data home itself                 |
| Keys     | `path`, `mode`, `description`. Anything else is refused                                        |
| When     | Volumes are fixed when the app starts. The agent cannot add one, and neither can an API        |

An agent that lists bx-ai's file tools (`readFile@bxai`, `writeFile@bxai`, and so on) gets the project's volumes with no further setting. An agent that sets `toolOptions.bxai.allowedPaths` itself keeps those full paths instead, and cannot also use volumes.

### How the agent sees them

The agent writes a path as `volume:path`, for example `notes:todo.md`. A path with no volume is in `files`.

* A full path on the machine is refused, and so is anything that climbs out of its volume with `..` or a symbolic link.
* A read only volume can be read, listed and copied from, but not written to, moved, or deleted from.
* Results and error messages name volumes. The agent never sees where a volume is on the machine.
* `listAllowedDirectories` answers with the volumes, their modes and their descriptions.

### Seeing them

* **In chat:** `/volumes` lists the volumes by name, mode and description, in the terminal, the web page and chat apps. It never shows a folder on the machine.
* **Over the API:** `GET /volumes` answers the same list to anyone who may call the API. `GET /data` answers the data home, the size of each part and the folder of each volume, and is for admins only, since it shows paths.
* **In `doctor`:** it reports the data home, where it came from, and whether it can be written. It makes nothing.

## Skills the agent saves

A skill is a folder with a `SKILL.md`: instructions the agent loads by name when a task calls for them. There are three levels:

|        Level         |                           Where                           |                                      Written by                                      |  `origin`   |
|----------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------|
| Installed            | `.agents/skills/` in the project                          | The registry tools (`npx skills`, `bxAgents skills install`), restored at build time | `installed` |
| Ships with the agent | `skills/` in the project, and the skills extensions carry | You                                                                                  | `project`   |
| The agent's own      | `skills/` in the data home                                | The agent, with its `skill_save` tool                                                | `agent`     |

The build copies the first two into the app, and the app loads the third at start and the moment a skill is saved. A diagram of the levels is on the [skills page](/conventions/skills/index.html#the-three-levels). A skill that ships with the agent wins over an installed one of the same name.

After a task that took real steps and is likely to come up again, the root agent can call `skill_save( name, description, content )`. The skill is written to the data home and is in the agent's skill list at once, with no restart. Subagents are given the skills when they are built; they cannot save any.

* **The first two levels win.** The agent cannot take the name of an installed skill or one that ships with the agent, or replace it. It can save over a skill it wrote itself, to improve it.
* **Approval.** Each save is approved by a person, as for any tool that needs approval, unless `skills.autoApprove: true`.
* **Limits.** A name is a folder name (letters, digits, `.`, `_`, `-`). A description is up to 500 characters and the content up to 20,000. The agent keeps up to 50 skills; saving over one it has is always allowed.
* **Off switch.** `skills.agentCanSave: false` takes the tool away.

```yaml
skills:
  agentCanSave: true     # default true; the root agent only
  autoApprove: false     # default false
```

A saved skill is part of the data home, so `backup` and `restore` carry it. To remove one, delete its folder.

### Seeing the skills

* **In chat:** `/skills` lists every skill with its level: installed, project or agent.
* **Over the API:** `GET /skills` answers `{ skills: [ { name, description, origin } ] }` (`origin` is `installed`, `project` or `agent`) to anyone who may call the API. It never shows a folder on the machine.

## Routine reports

`routines/` holds one folder per routine, `<name>-<first 8 of its id>`, with the report files the routine saved. Nothing in it is ever deleted automatically: a person removes old reports. They are part of a backup. See [routines](/conventions/routines/index.html#reports).

## Logs

The `logs/` folder of the data home holds the agent's log files, one per area. They are not part of a backup. See [logs](/conventions/logs/index.html).

## `bxAgents data`

```bash
bxAgents data [--json]
```

Prints the data home and where it came from, the size of the database and each folder, and the volumes with their modes.

## Backups

```bash
bxAgents backup [--to=FILE]
bxAgents restore FILE [--home=DIR] [--force]
```

`backup` writes one zip with the chat database, `files/`, `skills/` and `routines/`, plus a small `backup.json`. Without `--to` it goes in the home's `backups/` folder as `backup-<date>-<time>.zip`. The database is copied whole with SQLite's own `VACUUM INTO`, so it is safe to run while a server is using it. Volumes are not included: they are your folders.

`restore` puts a backup back. What was there is kept beside it as `chat.db.before-restore`, `files.before-restore` and `skills.before-restore` for one restore; the next restore replaces them. It stops when a server or chat looks to have the database open (SQLite leaves a `-wal` file while one does), unless you pass `--force`. `--home` restores into another data home. A zip with an entry that is not part of a backup, or that tries to leave the home, is refused before anything is changed.

body: deploy/ Each deploy/*.bx / .json entry describes one deployment target attempt - a place to ship a built/packaged project to: // deploy/production.bx class { function configure() { return { target : "digitalocean", appName : "my-agent", region : "nyc", registry : { type : "ghcr", repository : "myorg/my-agent" }, httpPort : 8080, instanceSize : "apps-s-1vcpu-1gb", envs : [ { key : "OPENAI_API_KEY", scope : "RUN_TIME", type : "SECRET" } ] }; } } Run it with: bxAgents deploy --name=production deploy/ is deliberately not validated on every build - deployment config never affects the generated ColdBox app or its manifest, so checking it on every build would be pure overhead for projects that never deploy. It's only discovered and validated when deploy actually runs. The simplest case needs no deploy/ folder at all: bxAgents deploy --destination=/path/to/somewhere is shorthand for the local target. Every other target needs more configuration than a couple of flags can reasonably carry, so it requires a named deploy/* entry ( --name=<entry> ). Targets Every target implements the same IDeploymentTarget interface ( struct function deploy( config, context ) ) - the target field picks which one runs. local Copy the newest .bxa to a destination directory. No deploy/ folder needed. ssh Ship over scp , optionally restart the remote service over ssh . docker Build an image from .build/app and push it to a registry. digitalocean Push-and-minimal-provision against the DigitalOcean App Platform API. ftp / sftp Ship the newest .bxa to a remote directory over plain FTP or SFTP. local Copies the newest packaged .bxa (by file modification time, never a lexical filename sort - v9.0.0 would otherwise sort after v10.0.0 ) to a destination directory. { target: "local", destination: "/path/to/somewhere" } Requires a prior bxAgents package . ssh Ships the newest .bxa to a bare server over scp , then optionally runs a remote restart command over ssh . { target : "ssh", host : "example.com", username : "deploy", remotePath : "/srv/apps/my-agent", identityFile : "/home/me/.ssh/id_rsa", // optional restartCommand : "systemctl restart my-agent" // optional } Requires a prior bxAgents package . Shells out to the real scp / ssh binaries - they must be installed and on PATH . docker Builds a Docker image from .build/app and pushes it to a container registry, shelling out to the real docker CLI. { target : "docker", registry : { type : "ghcr", repository : "myorg/my-agent" }, // type: "dockerhub" | "ghcr" | "docr" tag : "1.0.0" // optional, defaults to "latest" } Requires a prior bxAgents build (not package - it builds straight from .build/app ). The built-in Dockerfile template is based on the real, published ortussolutions/boxlang:miniserver image - override it entirely by adding your own deploy/Dockerfile , or point at a different one via dockerfile: "/absolute/path" . docker login only runs when both DOCKER_USERNAME and DOCKER_PASSWORD are set in the environment - a registry an already-authenticated local Docker daemon can reach needs neither. digitalocean Deploys to a DigitalOcean App Platform app - "push and minimal provision": builds/pushes the image exactly like docker (reuses the same registry config shape), then either redeploys an existing app or creates one from scratch if it doesn't exist yet. { target : "digitalocean", appName : "my-agent", region : "nyc", // optional, defaults to "nyc" registry : { type : "docr", repository : "myorg/my-agent" }, // "namespace/repo" form httpPort : 8080, // optional, defaults to 8080 instanceSize : "apps-s-1vcpu-1gb", // optional, defaults to "apps-s-1vcpu-1gb" instanceCount : 1, // optional, defaults to 1 tag : "1.0.0", // optional, image tag, defaults to "latest" envs : [ { key : "OPENAI_API_KEY", scope : "RUN_TIME", type : "SECRET" } ] // optional } registry.repository must be in namespace/repo form (e.g. myorg/my-agent ) - the DigitalOcean App Spec's image block needs the namespace and repository as separate fields. Requires a prior bxAgents build . An existing app is found by name ( GET /v2/apps , filtered client-side on spec.name ) rather than remembering a local app-ID file, so this works identically from any machine or CI runner with no local state to go stale. ftp / sftp Ships the newest .bxa to a remote directory over plain FTP or SFTP, via the real bx:ftp component - bundled with BxAgents as a nested module. remotePath is a remote directory - the uploaded file keeps its own name, the same convention ssh 's scp target uses. // deploy/ftp-production.bx { target : "ftp", host : "ftp.example.com", username : "deploy", passwordEnvVar : "BXAGENTS_FTP_PASSWORD", remotePath : "/uploads/my-agent", port : 21, // optional, defaults to 21 passive : true, // optional, defaults to true timeout : 30, // optional, seconds, defaults to 30 proxyServer : "proxy.company.com:8080" // optional } // deploy/sftp-production.bx { target : "sftp", host : "sftp.example.com", username : "deploy", key : "/home/me/.ssh/id_rsa", // passwordEnvVar OR key required passphraseEnvVar : "BXAGENTS_SFTP_KEY_PASSPHRASE", // optional, only if the key itself is passphrase-protected fingerprint : "SHA256:...", // optional host key verification remotePath : "/uploads/my-agent", port : 22, // optional, defaults to 22 timeout : 30 // optional, seconds, defaults to 30 } Requires a prior bxAgents package . ftp requires a passwordEnvVar ; sftp accepts either a passwordEnvVar or a key (SSH private key file path). passwordEnvVar / passphraseEnvVar name environment variables holding the real secret - never the secret value itself - resolved live at deploy time. The variable they name must sit in the BXAGENTS_ namespace ( ^BXAGENTS_[A-Z0-9_]+$ ); anything else is rejected with a BxAgents.InvalidDeployConfig error. Entry names must be unique across deploy/*.bx and deploy/*.json . Each target's required fields (above) are checked when deploy runs - local needs destination , ssh / ftp / sftp need host / username / remotePath (the same field name across all three), docker / digitalocean need registry.repository , digitalocean also needs appName , ftp also needs passwordEnvVar , sftp also needs passwordEnvVar or key .

# deploy/ Each `deploy/*.bx`/`.json` entry describes one deployment target attempt - a place to ship a built/packaged project to: ```javascript // deploy/production.bx class { function configure() { return { target : "digitalocean", appName : "my-agent", region : "nyc", registry : { type : "ghcr", repository : "myorg/my-agent" }, httpPort : 8080, instanceSize : "apps-s-1vcpu-1gb", envs : [ { key : "OPENAI_API_KEY", scope : "RUN_TIME", type : "SECRET" } ] }; } } ``` Run it with: ```bash bxAgents deploy --name=production ``` `deploy/` is deliberately **not** validated on every `build` - deployment config never affects the generated ColdBox app or its manifest, so checking it on every build would be pure overhead for projects that never deploy. It's only discovered and validated when `deploy` actually runs. The simplest case needs no `deploy/` folder at all: ```bash bxAgents deploy --destination=/path/to/somewhere ``` is shorthand for the `local` target. Every other target needs more configuration than a couple of flags can reasonably carry, so it requires a named `deploy/*` entry (`--name=`). ## Targets Every target implements the same `IDeploymentTarget` interface (`struct function deploy( config, context )`) - the `target` field picks which one runs. [](#local)
[local](#local) [Copy the newest `.bxa` to a destination directory. No `deploy/` folder needed.](#local) [](#local)[
ssh Ship over `scp`, optionally restart the remote service over `ssh`.](#ssh)[
docker Build an image from `.build/app` and push it to a registry.](#docker)[
digitalocean Push-and-minimal-provision against the DigitalOcean App Platform API.](#digitalocean)[
ftp / sftp Ship the newest `.bxa` to a remote directory over plain FTP or SFTP.](#ftp--sftp)
### `local` Copies the newest packaged `.bxa` (by file modification time, never a lexical filename sort - `v9.0.0` would otherwise sort after `v10.0.0`) to a destination directory. ```javascript { target: "local", destination: "/path/to/somewhere" } ``` Requires a prior `bxAgents package`. ### `ssh` Ships the newest `.bxa` to a bare server over `scp`, then optionally runs a remote restart command over `ssh`. ```javascript { target : "ssh", host : "example.com", username : "deploy", remotePath : "/srv/apps/my-agent", identityFile : "/home/me/.ssh/id_rsa", // optional restartCommand : "systemctl restart my-agent" // optional } ``` Requires a prior `bxAgents package`. Shells out to the real `scp`/`ssh` binaries - they must be installed and on `PATH`. ### `docker` Builds a Docker image from `.build/app` and pushes it to a container registry, shelling out to the real `docker` CLI. ```javascript { target : "docker", registry : { type : "ghcr", repository : "myorg/my-agent" }, // type: "dockerhub" | "ghcr" | "docr" tag : "1.0.0" // optional, defaults to "latest" } ``` Requires a prior `bxAgents build` (not `package` - it builds straight from `.build/app`). The built-in Dockerfile template is based on the real, published [`ortussolutions/boxlang:miniserver`](https://boxlang.ortusbooks.com/getting-started/running-boxlang/docker) image - override it entirely by adding your own `deploy/Dockerfile`, or point at a different one via `dockerfile: "/absolute/path"`. `docker login` only runs when both `DOCKER_USERNAME` and `DOCKER_PASSWORD` are set in the environment - a registry an already-authenticated local Docker daemon can reach needs neither. ### `digitalocean` Deploys to a [DigitalOcean App Platform](https://www.digitalocean.com/products/app-platform) app - "push and minimal provision": builds/pushes the image exactly like `docker` (reuses the same `registry` config shape), then either redeploys an existing app or creates one from scratch if it doesn't exist yet. ```javascript { target : "digitalocean", appName : "my-agent", region : "nyc", // optional, defaults to "nyc" registry : { type : "docr", repository : "myorg/my-agent" }, // "namespace/repo" form httpPort : 8080, // optional, defaults to 8080 instanceSize : "apps-s-1vcpu-1gb", // optional, defaults to "apps-s-1vcpu-1gb" instanceCount : 1, // optional, defaults to 1 tag : "1.0.0", // optional, image tag, defaults to "latest" envs : [ { key : "OPENAI_API_KEY", scope : "RUN_TIME", type : "SECRET" } ] // optional } ``` `registry.repository` must be in `namespace/repo` form (e.g. `myorg/my-agent`) - the DigitalOcean App Spec's `image` block needs the namespace and repository as separate fields. Requires a prior `bxAgents build`. An existing app is found by name (`GET /v2/apps`, filtered client-side on `spec.name`) rather than remembering a local app-ID file, so this works identically from any machine or CI runner with no local state to go stale. ### `ftp` / `sftp` Ships the newest `.bxa` to a remote directory over plain FTP or SFTP, via the real [`bx:ftp`](https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/bx-ftp) component - bundled with BxAgents as a nested module. `remotePath` is a remote **directory** - the uploaded file keeps its own name, the same convention `ssh`'s `scp` target uses. ```javascript // deploy/ftp-production.bx { target : "ftp", host : "ftp.example.com", username : "deploy", passwordEnvVar : "BXAGENTS_FTP_PASSWORD", remotePath : "/uploads/my-agent", port : 21, // optional, defaults to 21 passive : true, // optional, defaults to true timeout : 30, // optional, seconds, defaults to 30 proxyServer : "proxy.company.com:8080" // optional } ``` ```javascript // deploy/sftp-production.bx { target : "sftp", host : "sftp.example.com", username : "deploy", key : "/home/me/.ssh/id_rsa", // passwordEnvVar OR key required passphraseEnvVar : "BXAGENTS_SFTP_KEY_PASSPHRASE", // optional, only if the key itself is passphrase-protected fingerprint : "SHA256:...", // optional host key verification remotePath : "/uploads/my-agent", port : 22, // optional, defaults to 22 timeout : 30 // optional, seconds, defaults to 30 } ``` Requires a prior `bxAgents package`. `ftp` requires a `passwordEnvVar`; `sftp` accepts either a `passwordEnvVar` or a `key` (SSH private key file path). `passwordEnvVar`/`passphraseEnvVar` name environment variables holding the real secret - **never the secret value itself** - resolved live at deploy time. The variable they name must sit in the `BXAGENTS_` namespace (`^BXAGENTS_[A-Z0-9_]+$`); anything else is rejected with a `BxAgents.InvalidDeployConfig` error. That keeps a deploy entry - which is plain data, and easy to wave through in review - from naming an unrelated secret already in the environment (say a provider API key) and having it sent to whatever host the same entry points at. `key` stays a plain path, since it's already not secret material itself. Every `bx:ftp` action throws on failure (connection refused, auth rejected, a negative server reply) rather than returning a soft failure - this target catches that and re-throws it as a clear `BxAgents.DeployFailed`, always closing the connection afterward even on error. ## Secrets stay external No target ever reads a secret (API token, SSH key, registry password) from `deploy/*` config - every credential is resolved from an environment variable at deploy time, matching this project's existing rule that provider API keys are never embedded in a build or package (see [Deployment \& Secrets](/deployment-and-secrets/index.html)): | Target | Env var(s) | |----------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `ssh` | none required - `identityFile` is a path to a key file you manage yourself | | `docker` | `DOCKER_USERNAME`, `DOCKER_PASSWORD` (both optional - only used if set) | | `digitalocean` | `DOCKER_USERNAME`/`DOCKER_PASSWORD` (for the image push) + `DIGITALOCEAN_TOKEN` (required) | | `ftp` / `sftp` | whichever `BXAGENTS_`-prefixed env var(s) `passwordEnvVar`/`passphraseEnvVar` name - the entry itself only ever holds the env var's NAME, never its value (`key` is a path, same as `ssh`'s `identityFile`) | ## Validation * `target` must be one of `local`, `ssh`, `docker`, `digitalocean`, `ftp`, `sftp`. * Entry names must be unique across `deploy/*.bx` and `deploy/*.json`. * Each target's required fields (above) are checked when `deploy` runs - `local` needs `destination`, `ssh`/`ftp`/`sftp` need `host`/`username`/`remotePath` (the same field name across all three), `docker`/`digitalocean` need `registry.repository`, `digitalocean` also needs `appName`, `ftp` also needs `passwordEnvVar`, `sftp` also needs `passwordEnvVar` or `key`.

title: Deployment & Secrets
body:
Deployment & Secrets Secrets never enter the artifact - they are supplied to the process , at the far right of this chain: flowchart LR P["your project"] -->|"bxAgents build"| B[".build/app/
a plain ColdBox app"] B -->|"bxAgents package"| A["dist/name-version.bxa
+ .sha256 + redacted manifest.json"] A -->|"bxAgents deploy"| T["a target:
local / ssh / ftp / sftp
docker / digitalocean"] T --> RUN["boxlang-miniserver runs the unzipped app"] ENV["environment variables
OPENAI_API_KEY, CLAUDE_API_KEY,
every *EnvVar a gateway names"] -->|"read at RUNTIME by bx-ai"| RUN style A fill:#eaf6ec,stroke:#155724 style ENV fill:#fff3cd,stroke:#856404 Nothing on the left of ENV ever holds a secret value: .env /dotfiles are excluded from the zip unconditionally, and the manifest is redacted on top of never carrying one. Packaging bxAgents package zips .build/app/ into a portable .bxa artifact: bxAgents package --version=1.0.0 produces, in dist/ : {agentName}-{version}.bxa - the zipped app {agentName}-{version}.bxa.sha256 - its checksum manifest.json - a redacted copy of the build manifest (see below) Packaging twice in a row over the same build produces byte-identical zip bytes (deterministic entry order/timestamps) - useful for verifying a CI-built artifact matches a locally-built one. The .bxa is relocatable : it carries every file the agent reads at runtime (including each agent node's own instructions.md , copied into agent/ at build time), and the generated agent/GeneratedAgentFactory.bx resolves those paths relative to its own location on disk rather than the absolute paths of the machine that built it. So a .bxa built on CI runs unchanged when unzipped anywhere else - which also means a .bxaignore broad enough to match *.md will strip the agent's own instructions out of the artifact. package requires a prior build (it reads .build/manifest.json ) and refuses to run - producing no .bxa - if manifestVersion is unset or malformed. Excluding files: .bxaignore An optional .bxaignore at the project root, one glob pattern per line ( # -prefixed lines are comments), excludes matching paths from the packaged .bxa . Patterns are matched against paths inside the built app ( .build/app ): a pattern with no / matches at any depth, one with a / is anchored at the app's root, a trailing / names a folder and everything under it, and * also crosses / . # .bxaignore *.log scratch/ This is on top of a hard-coded, always-on exclusion of .env / .env.* /dotfiles at the packaging layer - even if .bxaignore doesn't mention them, and even if they somehow ended up inside .build/app , they never make it into the zip. Secret redaction Secrets are never written into manifest.json in the first place - the manifest's agent block only ever contains safe, structural fields ( name , description , model , environment ). As defense-in-depth, package additionally walks the manifest recursively and replaces any struct key that looks like a secret with [REDACTED] : (apikey | api_key | token | secret | password)$ (case-insensitive, any prefix) This guards against a future field - or a caller passing a richer struct into package some other way - accidentally leaking a value, even though today's manifest never puts one there to begin with. Where real secrets live BxAgents never resolves, stores, or embeds provider API keys, tokens, or passwords anywhere in a build or package. That's entirely bx-ai's job, at runtime : it reads them from the process environment following its own _API_KEY -style convention (e.g. OPENAI_API_KEY , CLAUDE_API_KEY ). Set them however you normally manage secrets for a deployed process - an OS environment variable or your platform's secret manager. For local development, BoxLang and boxlang-miniserver both load a .env from the project root themselves, so bxAgents new 's .env is the easy place for them; BxAgents never reads, copies or embeds it, and it is never committed (the scaffolded .gitignore covers it) or packaged. # Deployment \& Secrets Secrets never enter the artifact - they are supplied to the **process**, at the far right of this chain: ```mermaid flowchart LR P["your project"] -->|"bxAgents build"| B[".build/app/
a plain ColdBox app"] B -->|"bxAgents package"| A["dist/name-version.bxa
+ .sha256 + redacted manifest.json"] A -->|"bxAgents deploy"| T["a target:
local / ssh / ftp / sftp
docker / digitalocean"] T --> RUN["boxlang-miniserver runs the unzipped app"] ENV["environment variables
OPENAI_API_KEY, CLAUDE_API_KEY,
every *EnvVar a gateway names"] -->|"read at RUNTIME by bx-ai"| RUN style A fill:#eaf6ec,stroke:#155724 style ENV fill:#fff3cd,stroke:#856404 ``` Nothing on the left of `ENV` ever holds a secret value: `.env`/dotfiles are excluded from the zip unconditionally, and the manifest is redacted on top of never carrying one. ## Packaging `bxAgents package` zips `.build/app/` into a portable `.bxa` artifact: ```bash bxAgents package --version=1.0.0 ``` produces, in `dist/`: * `{agentName}-{version}.bxa` - the zipped app * `{agentName}-{version}.bxa.sha256` - its checksum * `manifest.json` - a **redacted** copy of the build manifest (see below) Packaging twice in a row over the same build produces byte-identical zip bytes (deterministic entry order/timestamps) - useful for verifying a CI-built artifact matches a locally-built one. The `.bxa` is **relocatable** : it carries every file the agent reads at runtime (including each agent node's own `instructions.md`, copied into `agent/` at build time), and the generated `agent/GeneratedAgentFactory.bx` resolves those paths relative to its own location on disk rather than the absolute paths of the machine that built it. So a `.bxa` built on CI runs unchanged when unzipped anywhere else - which also means a `.bxaignore` broad enough to match `*.md` will strip the agent's own instructions out of the artifact. `package` requires a prior `build` (it reads `.build/manifest.json`) and refuses to run - producing no `.bxa` - if `manifestVersion` is unset or malformed. ## Excluding files: `.bxaignore` An optional `.bxaignore` at the project root, one glob pattern per line (`#`-prefixed lines are comments), excludes matching paths from the packaged `.bxa`. Patterns are matched against paths inside the built app (`.build/app`): a pattern with no `/` matches at any depth, one with a `/` is anchored at the app's root, a trailing `/` names a folder and everything under it, and `*` also crosses `/`. # .bxaignore *.log scratch/ This is on top of a hard-coded, always-on exclusion of `.env`/`.env.*`/dotfiles at the packaging layer - even if `.bxaignore` doesn't mention them, and even if they somehow ended up inside `.build/app`, they never make it into the zip. ## Secret redaction Secrets are never written into `manifest.json` in the first place - the manifest's `agent` block only ever contains safe, structural fields (`name`, `description`, `model`, `environment`). As defense-in-depth, `package` additionally walks the manifest recursively and replaces any struct key that **looks** like a secret with `[REDACTED]`: (apikey | api_key | token | secret | password)$ (case-insensitive, any prefix) This guards against a future field - or a caller passing a richer struct into `package` some other way - accidentally leaking a value, even though today's manifest never puts one there to begin with. ## Where real secrets live BxAgents never resolves, stores, or embeds provider API keys, tokens, or passwords anywhere in a build or package. That's entirely bx-ai's job, at **runtime** : it reads them from the process environment following its own `_API_KEY`-style convention (e.g. `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `CLAUDE_API_KEY`). Set them however you normally manage secrets for a deployed process - an OS environment variable or your platform's secret manager. For local development, BoxLang and `boxlang-miniserver` both load a `.env` from the project root themselves, so `bxAgents new`'s `.env` is the easy place for them; BxAgents never reads, copies or embeds it, and it is never committed (the scaffolded `.gitignore` covers it) or packaged. A deployed `.bxa` has no `.env`, so give that process real environment variables. ```bash export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-... bxAgents serve ``` ## Variables BxAgents reads itself None of these holds a provider secret. `BXAGENTS_TOKEN` is the one credential, and it is only ever read from the environment of the machine you type on. | Variable | Used by | Effect | |--------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `BX_AGENTS_ENV` | `build` | The active environment when `--environment` is not given (default `development`). See [Environments](/conventions/agent-yaml/index.html#environments). | | `BXAGENTS_DB` | the app, `chat`, `token`, `notes`, `sessions`, `stats` | The chat database file. `serve` sets it to `data/chat.db` in the project; a deployed app uses `database.path` inside the app unless it is set. See [the SQLite store](/conventions/web-ui/index.html#the-sqlite-store). | | `BXAGENTS_TOKEN` | `chat --connect` | The token to send, instead of `--token`. | | `BXAGENTS_USER_CONFIG` | `chat`, `extensions` | Another file in place of `~/.bxagents/bxAgents.yml`. | | `BXAGENTS_SKILLS_URL` | `skills` | Another skills registry, instead of `--registry`. | | `BXAGENTS_BANNER`, `BXAGENTS_BANNER_THEME` | `--help`, `new` | `off` hides the banner; a theme name pins its colors. | | `BXAGENTS_` plus a name | `deploy` | The only prefix a `deploy/` entry may name for a password or passphrase (`passwordEnvVar`, `passphraseEnvVar`). | ## Secrets people hand to a running agent Environment variables are for what you deploy with. For a key or login that a person hands to a **running** agent (an API key for Gmail, a ticket system, a customer's own token), use [the vault](/conventions/vault/index.html): values are sealed in the chat database, added from the terminal chat, the web page or `bxAgents vault`, and read by the runtime at the moment a tool or MCP server needs one. # Example: A Minimal Agent

The smallest complete BxAgents project is [`examples/minimal-agent/`](https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/bx-agents/tree/development/examples/minimal-agent) - a few files that show the whole shape of a project: an `Agent.yaml`, instructions, one [tool](/conventions/tools/index.html), and one [skill](/conventions/skills/index.html). Every other example in this guide series builds on exactly this shape.

## The project

    minimal-agent/
    ├── Agent.yaml
    ├── instructions.md
    ├── tools/
    │   └── Greeter.bx
    └── skills/
        └── greeting/
            └── SKILL.md

`Agent.yaml` declares a name, description, and model - the `provider/model` slug (see [The model slug](/conventions/agent-bx/index.html#the-model-slug)) - and nothing else is required. Need code in the definition (hooks, dynamic instructions)? The class-based [`Agent.bx`](/conventions/agent-bx/index.html) is the advanced alternative.

```yaml
name: minimal-agent
description: "The smallest complete BX Agents project: one tool, one skill."
model: mock/mock-model
```

`instructions.md` is the system prompt - a plain Markdown file, copied in as-is at build time:

```markdown
## Minimal Agent

You are a friendly assistant. When someone tells you their name, use the
`sayHello` tool to greet them, and follow the greeting skill's guidance
on tone.
```

## The tool

Any `class` under `tools/` with an `@AITool`-annotated function becomes a callable tool automatically - no registration step, no config entry. `tools/Greeter.bx`:

```javascript
class {

	@AITool( "Say hello to someone by name." )
	function sayHello( name ) {
		return "Hello, " & arguments.name & "!";
	}

}
```

The string passed to `@AITool` is the tool's description, sent to the model exactly as written - see [Tools](/conventions/tools/index.html) for how BoxLang argument types map to the JSON schema the model sees.

## The skill

A skill under `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` is guidance the model can pull in when it decides it's relevant - not always-on like `instructions.md`. `skills/greeting/SKILL.md`:

```markdown
---
name: greeting
description: How to greet people warmly.
---

Always greet the user warmly and use their name if known.
```

See [Skills](/conventions/skills/index.html) for how `description` drives when a skill actually gets used.

## Build and run

```bash
cd examples/minimal-agent
bxAgents build
bxAgents chat
```

`build` assembles everything above into a plain ColdBox application under `.build/app` (see [The Build Pipeline](/build-pipeline/index.html)); `chat` loads the generated agent in-process and opens the [terminal chat](/guides/terminal-ui/index.html). Type `/` to see the commands, and `/tools` to see that `sayHello` is there. Try:

    My name is Ada.

The model should reach for the `sayHello` tool and reply warmly, per the skill's guidance - both from a single sentence of instructions plus a small tool and a one-line skill. With the `mock` model this example ships with, the reply is a fixed one: set a real `provider/model` in `Agent.yaml` to see the tool called. `bxAgents inspect` lists the agent, its tool and its skill without a build.

## Where to go next

* [Example: A Multi-Agent Team](/guides/example-multi-agent-team/index.html) - the same shape, with subagents delegating to each other.
* [Example: A Scheduled Agent](/guides/example-scheduled-agent/index.html) - the same shape, woken by a cron schedule instead of a chat prompt.
* [Tools](/conventions/tools/index.html) and [Skills](/conventions/skills/index.html) for the full conventions these two files follow.

# Example: A Multi-Agent Team

[`examples/multi-agent-team/`](https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/bx-agents/tree/development/examples/multi-agent-team) is a root agent with two [subagents](/conventions/subagents/index.html) - `researcher` and `writer` - each auto-wrapped as a callable tool on the root agent by bx-ai's own `aiAgent()`. Delegation is entirely the model's decision at runtime; nothing in this project hard-codes which subagent handles which message.

## The project

    multi-agent-team/
    ├── Agent.yaml
    ├── instructions.md
    └── subagents/
        ├── researcher/
        │   ├── Agent.yaml
        │   └── instructions.md
        └── writer/
            ├── Agent.yaml
            └── instructions.md

Every `subagents/<name>/` folder is itself a complete mini-agent - its own `Agent.yaml`, its own `instructions.md`, and (not used here, but supported) its own `tools/`/`skills/`.

## Declaring the team

The root `Agent.yaml` names the subagents to wire in with `subAgents`:

```yaml
# Agent.yaml
name: multi-agent-team
description: A root agent delegating to a researcher and a writer subagent.
model: mock/mock-model

# The list of `subagents/` FOLDER names to wire at build time.
subAgents: [ researcher, writer ]
```

`subAgents` is resolved against folder names under `subagents/`; each folder's own `Agent.yaml` declares its own `name`, `description`, and `model` independently:

```yaml
# subagents/researcher/Agent.yaml
name: researcher
description: Gathers facts on a topic.
model: mock/mock-model
```

```yaml
# subagents/writer/Agent.yaml
name: writer
description: Turns research into polished prose.
model: mock/mock-model
```

## Instructions divide the responsibility

Each agent's `instructions.md` is deliberately scoped to its own job - the root coordinates, and each subagent is told explicitly what it does *not* do, so the model doesn't try to do everything in one hop:

```markdown
<!-- instructions.md (root) -->
## Team Lead

You coordinate a small team. Delegate research questions to the `researcher`
subagent and drafting/writing tasks to the `writer` subagent, then combine
their output into a final answer.
```

```markdown
<!-- subagents/researcher/instructions.md -->
## Researcher

You gather and summarize facts on a topic, citing your reasoning. You do
not write final prose - that's the writer's job.
```

```markdown
<!-- subagents/writer/instructions.md -->
## Writer

You turn research notes into clear, polished prose. You do not do your
own research - you rely on what the researcher provides.
```

## How the build wires it up

`ColdBoxAppGenerator` builds the tree **leaf-first** : `researcher` and `writer` are constructed first, and the already-built instances are passed into the root agent's own construction, so the root's `aiAgent()` call receives real subagent objects rather than names to resolve later. See [Subagents](/conventions/subagents/index.html) for the full leaf-first build order and how each subagent gets registered under its own name in WireBox (not just the root).

## Build and run

```bash
cd examples/multi-agent-team
bxAgents build
bxAgents chat
```

Ask something that clearly needs both roles, e.g. `Give me three facts about the BoxLang language, then turn them into a short paragraph.` A real model would typically call `researcher` first, then `writer`, then compose the final answer - the `mock` provider this example ships with won't actually delegate (it returns a fixed response with no tool calls), so swap in a real `provider/model` slug (see [The model slug](/conventions/agent-bx/index.html#the-model-slug)) to see real delegation happen. `bxAgents inspect` prints the agent and subagent tree, with each model and tools, before you build.

## Where to go next

* [Example: A Minimal Agent](/guides/example-minimal-agent/index.html) if you haven't seen the base project shape yet.
* [Subagents](/conventions/subagents/index.html) for cycle detection, nested subagent trees, and per-subagent tools/skills.
* [Example: Building a Slack Bot](/guides/example-slack-bot/index.html) to see a similar agent reachable over a real chat platform instead of the terminal chat.
