title: Example: A Scheduled Agent
body: Example: A Scheduled Agent examples/scheduled-agent/ wakes an agent nightly with a BoxLang scheduler under schedules/ - plain Schedules code with BoxLang's own task DSL and cron syntax. The project scheduled-agent/ ├── Agent.yaml ├── instructions.md └── schedules/ └── Nightly.bx Agent.yaml is the same shape as every other example - nothing special is needed on the agent side to be schedule-driven: name: scheduled-agent description: An agent that wakes up on a cron schedule via schedules/. model: mock/mock-model The scheduler schedules/Nightly.bx is a plain class. The build adds the base class that provides task() and run() : class { function configure() { task( "nightly" ) .cron( "0 0 * * *" ) .call( () => run( "cleanup" ) ) .withNoOverlaps() } } The full BoxLang task DSL is available - cron() , every() , everyDayAt() , withNoOverlaps() , onFailure() and the rest, not a subset BxAgents reimplements (see schedules/ ). run( "cleanup" ) sends the message to the project's default agent, the root agent. To reach a subagent, use agent( "TheAgentName" ).run( ... ) : every agent in a project's tree is registered under its own declared name . Instructions for the scheduled prompt The instructions describe what the agent should do when run( "cleanup" ) fires - there's no difference, from the agent's point of view, between a scheduled wake-up and a chat message; both are just a run() call with some input text: ## Scheduled Agent You run periodic housekeeping prompts. When asked to "cleanup", summarize what a cleanup pass would involve for a typical project. Build and run Unlike a plain bxAgents chat (which loads the agent in the chat process and never boots ColdBox), schedulers only start with the served app, so this one needs serve . bxAgents chat --server also starts the app, as a throwaway local server, and chats with it: cd examples/scheduled-agent bxAgents build bxAgents serve The nightly task fires automatically once serve is running - no separate cron daemon, no OS-level cron entry. BoxLang's own scheduler drives it, on the schedule declared in Nightly.bx . To add another schedule to your own project, run bxAgents add schedule . It asks when (for example daily 09:00 or every 15 minutes ), what to tell the agent and which agent, and writes schedules/<Name>.bx . bxAgents inspect lists the schedules a project has. Info build checks the scheduler's file name and that it is a class, but not the contents of configure() - a typo in an agent() call or a reference to an agent name that doesn't exist will pass build cleanly and only surface once the generated app actually boots. Where to go next Schedules for the helpers a scheduler gets and the cron syntax. Example: A Minimal Agent if you haven't seen the base project shape yet. Example: Building a Web Chat Agent for an agent reachable interactively instead of on a timer.

# Example: A Scheduled Agent

[`examples/scheduled-agent/`](https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/bx-agents/tree/development/examples/scheduled-agent) wakes an agent nightly with a BoxLang scheduler under `schedules/` - plain [Schedules](/conventions/schedules/index.html) code with BoxLang's own task DSL and cron syntax.

## The project

    scheduled-agent/
    ├── Agent.yaml
    ├── instructions.md
    └── schedules/
        └── Nightly.bx

`Agent.yaml` is the same shape as every other example - nothing special is needed on the agent side to be schedule-driven:

```yaml
name: scheduled-agent
description: An agent that wakes up on a cron schedule via schedules/.
model: mock/mock-model
```

## The scheduler

`schedules/Nightly.bx` is a plain class. The build adds the base class that provides `task()` and `run()`:

```javascript
class {

	function configure() {
		task( "nightly" )
			.cron( "0 0 * * *" )
			.call( () => run( "cleanup" ) )
			.withNoOverlaps()
	}

}
```

The full BoxLang task DSL is available - `cron()`, `every()`, `everyDayAt()`, `withNoOverlaps()`, `onFailure()` and the rest, not a subset BxAgents reimplements (see [`schedules/`](/conventions/schedules/index.html)).

`run( "cleanup" )` sends the message to the project's default agent, the root agent. To reach a subagent, use `agent( "TheAgentName" ).run( ... )`: every agent in a project's tree is registered under its own declared `name`.

## Instructions for the scheduled prompt

The instructions describe what the agent should do when `run( "cleanup" )` fires - there's no difference, from the agent's point of view, between a scheduled wake-up and a chat message; both are just a `run()` call with some input text:

```markdown
## Scheduled Agent

You run periodic housekeeping prompts. When asked to "cleanup", summarize
what a cleanup pass would involve for a typical project.
```

## Build and run

Unlike a plain `bxAgents chat` (which loads the agent in the chat process and never boots ColdBox), schedulers only start with the served app, so this one needs `serve`. `bxAgents chat --server` also starts the app, as a throwaway local server, and chats with it:

```bash
cd examples/scheduled-agent
bxAgents build
bxAgents serve
```

The `nightly` task fires automatically once `serve` is running - no separate cron daemon, no OS-level `cron` entry. BoxLang's own scheduler drives it, on the schedule declared in `Nightly.bx`.

To add another schedule to your own project, run `bxAgents add schedule`. It asks when (for example `daily 09:00` or `every 15 minutes`), what to tell the agent and which agent, and writes `schedules/<Name>.bx`. `bxAgents inspect` lists the schedules a project has.
> **Info**
>
> `build` checks the scheduler's file name and that it is a class, but not the *contents* of `configure()` - a typo in an `agent()` call or a reference to an agent name that doesn't exist will pass `build` cleanly and only surface once the generated app actually boots.

## Where to go next

* [Schedules](/conventions/schedules/index.html) for the helpers a scheduler gets and the cron syntax.
* [Example: A Minimal Agent](/guides/example-minimal-agent/index.html) if you haven't seen the base project shape yet.
* [Example: Building a Web Chat Agent](/guides/example-web-chat-agent/index.html) for an agent reachable interactively instead of on a timer.

# Example: Building a Slack Bot

[`examples/slack-gateway-agent/`](https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/bx-agents/tree/development/examples/slack-gateway-agent) connects an agent to a real Slack app via a push-style `gateways/` entry with `type: "slack"`. Slack uses **Socket Mode** - a persistent websocket the gateway holds open itself - so unlike a webhook-driven platform (WhatsApp Cloud, Teams, Twilio, GitHub), there's no public route to expose or `curl`; the gateway reaches out to Slack, not the other way around. See [Push-style gateways](/conventions/gateways/index.html) for how this category differs from `exposes: "agent"`/`"webui"` HTTP exposure.

## The project

    slack-gateway-agent/
    ├── Agent.yaml
    ├── instructions.md
    └── gateways/
        └── slackChannel.bx

`Agent.yaml` is the same shape as every other example:

```yaml
name: slack-gateway-agent
description: An agent reachable as a real Slack app via gateways/, over Socket Mode.
model: mock/mock-model
```

## The gateway

`gateways/slackChannel.bx` declares the platform type and where its credentials come from - **environment variable names**, not the secrets themselves, so nothing sensitive ever lands in the generated app or version control:

```javascript
class {

	function configure() {
		return {
			type          : "slack",
			botTokenEnvVar: "SLACK_BOT_TOKEN",   // xoxb-... - chat.postMessage/chat.update scope
			appTokenEnvVar: "SLACK_APP_TOKEN"    // xapp-... - apps.connections.open scope (Socket Mode)
		};
	}

}
```

At build time, `GatewayGenerator` turns this into a registered `SlackGateway` instance and wires it into the project's single, project-wide `GatewaySession`. At runtime, `SlackGateway.onConnect()` opens the Socket Mode websocket as soon as `GatewaySession` starts.

## Instructions

```markdown
## Slack Gateway Agent

You are a helpful workspace assistant, reachable as a Slack app. Use
Slack-flavored formatting sparingly (bold with `*asterisks*`, not markdown `**`).
```

Nothing here is Slack-API-specific beyond a formatting note - the agent's own logic doesn't know or care which gateway is delivering its replies.

## 1. Create a Slack app

At [api.slack.com/apps](https://api.slack.com/apps), create an app "from scratch":

1. **Socket Mode** - enable it, generate an app-level token with the `connections:write` scope (`xapp-...`) → this becomes `SLACK_APP_TOKEN`.
2. **OAuth \& Permissions** - add the `chat:write` bot scope, install the app to your workspace, copy the Bot User OAuth Token (`xoxb-...`) → this becomes `SLACK_BOT_TOKEN`.
3. **Event Subscriptions** - enable it and subscribe to the `message.im` (and/or `message.channels`) bot event, so the app actually receives message events over the socket.
4. Optional: **Slash Commands** for the chat commands, and the `files:read` scope to let the agent read files people share (see below).

## 2. Configure and run

```bash
export SLACK_BOT_TOKEN="xoxb-..."
export SLACK_APP_TOKEN="xapp-..."
cd examples/slack-gateway-agent
bxAgents build
bxAgents serve
```

DM the bot, or mention it in a channel it's in. Replies stream back token-by-token via a placeholder message that `SlackGateway` posts immediately and then updates in place with `chat.update` as tokens arrive - the same incremental-reveal effect the [web chat UI](/conventions/web-ui/index.html) gives you in a browser, produced here entirely through Slack's own message-editing API.
> **Info**
>
> There's no `curl`-able entrypoint for this one - message the app for real in Slack to see it work. This is true of every persistent-connection gateway (Telegram's long-poll, Slack/Discord's websockets); only the webhook-driven platforms (WhatsApp Cloud, Teams, Twilio, GitHub) generate a route you can hit locally with a hand-computed signature - each of those examples' own README shows how.

## What people can do in the chat

* **Everyone has their own conversation.** The agent is told who is writing (`slack:U123`) and which conversation it is: the channel, plus the thread when there is one. Two people in the same channel do not share a memory, and each Slack thread keeps its own. Conversations are stored in `data/chat.db`, marked with `source` Slack.
* **Commands.** By default the bot answers `/help`, `/tools`, `/model`, `/info`, `/ping`, `/remember`, `/notes` and `/connect` itself, without calling the model. Slack keeps typed `/word` messages for its own commands, so a bot never receives them. Either create a slash command in the Slack app (an umbrella `/agent`, so `/agent model fast` runs `/model fast`, or one per command) and the answer is shown only to the person who typed it, or set another prefix in `Agent.yaml`:

```yaml
gatewaySession:
  commands:
    prefixes: { slack: "!" }     # then type !help
    conversation: true           # also turns on /new, /clear, /compact, /sessions and /resume
```

* **Files.** A text file or a picture shared in a message goes to the agent with it. This needs the `files:read` scope on the Slack app.

See [Commands in a gateway](/conventions/gateways/index.html#commands-in-a-gateway) for every option.

## What's proven, and what isn't

`SlackGatewaySpec.bx` exercises the gateway's inbound/outbound logic - chunking, HITL approvals, reconnect handling - entirely against an injectable test seam, never a real Slack connection; a separate smoke test confirms the BoxLang-to-Java WebSocket interop itself works correctly (a real connection attempt to an unreachable address fails with a plain `ConnectException`, not an interop error). No test in this repo has completed a real Socket Mode handshake against Slack's actual servers. The steps above are exactly the manual verification that gap calls for.

## Where to go next

* [Slack](/conventions/gateways/slack/index.html) for the full gateway convention - reconnect model, HITL correlation, chunking limits.
* [Example: A Multi-Agent Team](/guides/example-multi-agent-team/index.html) to combine a gateway-reachable agent with subagent delegation.

# Example: Building a Web Chat Agent

[`examples/webui-agent/`](https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/bx-agents/tree/development/examples/webui-agent) generates a complete, themed browser chat page for an agent from a single `gateways/*` entry with `exposes: "webui"` - the [v1 web chat UI](/conventions/web-ui/index.html). No frontend code to write, no Node/npm in the build, no separate deploy step for a SPA - the page is a real file BxAgents writes into the generated app.

This is the one example in this guide series with real screenshots, because it's the one kind of BxAgents example whose output is actually a browser page. The images below show the current page layout, captured from a demo app (title "Acme Assistant", blue accent), so the title, tagline and colors differ from this example's own config. The page is the same: only the branding comes from the gateway file.

## The project

    webui-agent/
    ├── Agent.yaml
    ├── instructions.md
    ├── gateways/
    │   └── chat.bx
    └── resources/
        └── webui/
            └── theme.css

`Agent.yaml` is the same shape as every other example:

```yaml
name: webui-agent
description: An agent reachable through the v1 web chat UI via gateways/.
model: mock/mock-model
```

## The gateway: branding and theme, all in config

`gateways/chat.bx` is where the actual page comes from - `exposes: "webui"` is the trigger, and everything else is optional branding:

```javascript
class {

	function configure() {
		return {
			exposes     : "webui",
			path        : "/chat",
			apiKeyEnvVar: "CHAT_UI_API_KEY",   // optional - omit entirely to leave the agent API open (dev-mode)

			// ---------------------------------------------------------------
			// Branding
			// ---------------------------------------------------------------
			title      : "Acme Support",
			subtitle   : "Orders, returns and shipping",
			icon       : "🛟",                 // an emoji, an image URL/path ("/logo.svg", "https://..."), or "phosphor:<name>" ("phosphor:lightning")
			welcome    : "Hi! Ask me about an order, a return, or shipping times.",
			placeholder: "Ask about your order...",
			footer     : "Answers are generated and may be wrong - check anything important.",

			// ---------------------------------------------------------------
			// Stream detail - both default to true
			// ---------------------------------------------------------------
			showReasoning: true,   // the model's thinking, as a collapsed "Thinking" strip
			showToolCalls: true,   // each tool call as a collapsed chip (name + arguments)

			// ---------------------------------------------------------------
			// Theme - every key maps to a CSS custom property on the page.
			// ---------------------------------------------------------------
			theme: {
				accent  : "0f766e",
				accentFg: "ffffff",
				radius  : "10px",
				font    : "Inter, system-ui, sans-serif",
				maxWidth: "68%",

				dark: {
					accent  : "2dd4bf",
					accentFg: "05201c"
				}
			}
		};
	}

}
```

Other branding keys you can add: `suggestions` (up to four short texts, shown as buttons under the welcome message on an empty conversation; one click sends it) and `icon: "phosphor:<name>"` for an icon from the page's own set. With no `icon` the header shows a robot.

```javascript
suggestions: [ "Where is my order?", "How do I return something?" ],
```

Colors are written as bare hex with no leading `#` (`"0f766e"`, not `"#0f766e"`) - BoxLang starts string interpolation at a hash in both single- and double-quoted strings, so a literal one has to be doubled to parse at all. Bare hex sidesteps that entirely; see the comment in the file itself for the full reasoning, and [The web chat UI](/conventions/web-ui/index.html) for anything the theme tokens don't cover (that goes in `resources/webui/theme.css`, inlined last and wins).

## Build and run

```bash
cd examples/webui-agent
bxAgents build
bxAgents serve --port=8080
```

Open **<http://localhost:8080/chat/index.html>** . You get the conversation sidebar on the left, the streaming transcript in the middle, and a header and composer in the colors of your `theme`:

![The generated web chat UI: a conversation sidebar, a multi-turn transcript, and a themed header/composer](/assets/webui-chat-light.png)

### Dark mode

The `theme.dark` overrides (`accent`/`accentFg`) apply automatically when the page switches to dark, from **Settings** or by following the system - everything else is the same generated CSS, just re-tokened:

![The same page and conversation in the dark theme - theme.dark's accent/accentFg tokens carry over, everything else is the same generated CSS](/assets/webui-chat-dark.png)

### Narrow screens

The page is responsive with no separate mobile build - at a narrow viewport, the transcript keeps its full width and the conversation sidebar becomes an overlay instead of squeezing the content:

![The same page at a narrow viewport - the transcript keeps the full width, the sidebar overlays instead of squeezing it](/assets/webui-chat-mobile.png)

## The header and the Settings menu

The header keeps what you use every minute: **Chats** (shows or hides the sidebar), the context ring (click it for what is sent to the model), the model picker (only when the gateway lists `profiles`) and a **Settings** gear. The gear opens one menu with three groups. An item the server does not offer, and a group with nothing in it, is left out.

|      Group       |                                                                    Items                                                                    |
|------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Conversation** | Fork this conversation, Export as Markdown, Clear messages, Compact older messages                                                          |
| **You**          | Notes (when the agent has a `notes` block), Appearance (mode, accent color, text size, density, saved in your browser), Dark or Light theme |
| **Server**       | Password, Access tokens                                                                                                                     |

![The Settings menu open, with the Conversation, You and Server groups](/assets/webui/settings-menu.png)

In the message box, the paperclip attaches a picture or a text file (you can also paste or drop them), the lightning button opens the `/` commands menu, and the arrow sends. While the agent works the arrow steers the run and a stop button appears.

## The optional API key

This example ships `apiKeyEnvVar` **set** . It is the agent API's shared secret, so every call to `/__bxagents` must carry a matching `x-bxagents-token` header - the static shell (`/chat/index.html`) itself stays reachable regardless, since a browser's plain page navigation can't send a custom header, and the shell is exactly what prompts you for the key:

```bash
export CHAT_UI_API_KEY="a-real-secret"
bxAgents build
bxAgents serve --port=8080
```

The page loads fine either way, but a call without the matching key gets a 401 and the page opens its **Password** form by itself - type `a-real-secret` and choose **Save** . A wrong password shows "That password was not accepted". The form is also under **Settings** , **Password** , where **Forget it** removes the saved value. The password is kept in the browser's `localStorage` until you forget it. Delete the `apiKeyEnvVar` line entirely to leave the UI open instead (fine for local dev, never for a public deployment).

## Access tokens for administrators

With `agentApi: { tokens: true, manageTokens: true }` in `Agent.yaml`, a caller with an `admin` token sees **Settings** , **Access tokens** . The panel lists tokens, creates one (a name, a scope of `chat` or `admin`, and how long it lasts, such as `90d`), shows the secret once for you to copy, and revokes tokens. `manageTokens` is off by default and a `chat` token gets `403`. The same thing from a shell is `bxAgents token create|list|revoke`.

![The Access tokens panel: the token list, a new secret shown once, and the create form](/assets/webui/tokens-panel.png)

## One API for the page, the terminal and the gateways

`path: "/chat"` is only where the static shell is served. The page calls the agent API at `/__bxagents`, which derives the visitor's identity **server-side only** , rather than trusting a caller-supplied `userId` the way ColdBox's `toAi()` does, and which the terminal chat and the gateways use too. See [Conversation identity](/conventions/web-ui/index.html#conversation-identity) for the full reasoning.

## What's proven, and what isn't

The generator output itself - the static shell, the templated placeholders, the sign-in pieces when there are accounts, its registration from `Application.bx` - is proven by real generator specs and confirmed to compile and instantiate. Over real HTTP, `runColdBoxIntegrationTests.bxs` proves `/__bxagents/health` and, further, the shared-preferences round trip (`/__bxagents/preferences/set` + `/__bxagents/preferences`) between two independent callers. The screenshots above were captured from the real generated page, not a hand-built mockup - but do at least one real `bxAgents serve` + browser check of your own theme/branding choices before depending on them in production.

## Where to go next

* [The web chat UI](/conventions/web-ui/index.html) for the full picture - human-in-the-loop approvals, compaction, steer-while-streaming, the SQLite-backed conversation store.
* [Example: A Minimal Agent](/guides/example-minimal-agent/index.html) if you haven't seen the base project shape yet.
* [Example: Building a Slack Bot](/guides/example-slack-bot/index.html) for an agent reachable on a chat platform instead of a browser.

title: extensions/
body:
extensions/ An extension adds to BxAgents without changing it: chat commands ( /deploy , /roll 2d6 ), listeners for the events of the chat and of bx-ai, and schedules that run when the agent is served. It is a class that looks and behaves like a ColdBox ModuleConfig : it has a configure() , an onLoad() and an onUnload() , its settings come from Agent.yaml , and things are handed to it with $inject . One file is a whole extension: extensions/ hello.bx /hello roll.bx /roll, /coin standup/ a folder is an extension too Extension.bx commands/Standup.bx schedulers/Reminder.bx A working project with all of these is examples/extensions-agent . The smallest extension extensions/hello.bx . The file name is the extension's name. class { function configure() { variables.settings = { greeting : "Hello" } } @Command( "hello" ) @Hint( "say hello: /hello " ) function greet( agentContext, commandArguments ) { return agentContext.reply().ok( "#settings.greeting#, #commandArguments#!" ) } } Run bxAgents chat and type /hello Ada . /extensions lists what is loaded. A command method is called with the agentContext (the conversation and nothing else; the same object the built-in commands get) and the text after the command name. It returns a Reply ( agentContext.reply().ok( "..." ) , .warn() , .keyValues() , .grid() , .choose() ) or just a string. If it throws, the person sees a warning that names the extension and the chat carries on. Annotations Annotations are normal BoxLang annotations on a method. Each one can be written four ways, and every BxAgents annotation takes all four: Written Means Example bare defaults; the name comes from the method @Command on function roll() is /roll simple the main value @Command( "deploy" ) array several @Alias( [ "dice", "d" ] ) struct every option @Command( { name : "deploy", hint : "plan it", admin : true, aliases : [ "ship" ], transports : [ "tui", "web" ] } ) Shorthand annotations say one option each: @Hint( "..." ) , @Admin , @Alias( ... ) , @Transports( [ "tui", "web" ] ) . A struct option wins over a shorthand, and the clash is shown in /extensions . Annotation names ignore case. transports are where the command runs: tui (the terminal chat), web (the web page and the HTTP command route) and gateway (chat platforms). The default is all three. A chat platform only answers the commands its gateway allows ( gatewaySession.commands.allow ), and a command with @Admin only runs for the people listed as admins there. Settings The extension says its defaults in configure() , as a module does: function configure() { variables.settings = { target : "staging", environments : [ "staging", "production" ] } } The people who use it change them under the extension's name in Agent.yaml : extensions: deploy: target: production A person can set their own values in ~/.bxagents/bxAgents.yml (same extensions: block); the project's values win over theirs. Nested structs merge key by key, arrays and simple values replace. In the extension, settings is the merged struct. Lifecycle Method When configure() once, first. Sets variables.settings . No work here onLoad() after the settings are merged and everything is injected. Open connections, start timers onUnload() when the chat or the server ends. Release them this.title , this.author , this.webURL , this.description , this.version and this.enabled are read as in a module config, and this.dependencies = [ "other-extension" ] loads that extension first. An extension that throws while it loads is shown as failed in /extensions with the reason; the others still load. Injection Every class of an extension has $inject( name, object )`. It puts the object in both the `this` and the `variables` scopes. For private only: `$inject( name, object, "variables" ) . $read( name ) reads a variables entry from outside. BxAgents injects two things before onLoad() : settings and log ( log.info( "..." ) , .warn() , .error() ; what an extension logs is also in /extensions ). To share an object between the files of an extension, create it in onLoad() and $inject it where it is needed. The same call is how a test hands an extension a fake. A folder extension A folder has the same shape as an agent project: extensions/standup/ Extension.bx required: it is what makes the folder an extension (the module config: properties, configure(), onLoad(), onUnload()) commands/ one class per command, like the built-in ones schedulers/ BoxLang scheduler classes, started when the agent is served A class in commands/ extends models.chat.commands.BaseCommand@bxagents and says its name() , hint() , transports() and run( context, args ) . settings and log are injected into it. Schedulers A class in schedulers/ is a BoxLang scheduler : a class with a configure() that defines tasks through the scheduler property BoxLang gives it, like any other BoxLang scheduler. When the agent is served ( bxAgents serve , a .bxa , a deployed server) it starts in the runtime's scheduler service. Like every class of an extension it is given settings (the defaults with the values from Agent.yaml ) and log before configure() runs: class { function configure() { scheduler.task( "standup-reminder" ) .call( () => log.info( "Standup time for #settings.channel#" ) ) .everyDayAt( settings.at ) .withNoOverlaps() } } The BoxLang scheduler lifecycle methods ( onStartup() , onShutdown() , onAnyTaskError() and the rest) work as usual. Each scheduler is registered as extension-- , and a scheduler that fails to start is reported on its extension in /extensions while the others still run. The terminal chat does not start schedulers: they belong to the served agent. Listening to events An extension is also an interceptor. A method named after an event listens to it, exactly like a BoxLang or ColdBox interceptor: class { function onChatInput( data ) { if ( data.text contains "password" ) { data.cancel( "That looks like a password, so it was not sent." ) } } function onAIError( data ) { log.warn( "the model failed" ) } } Two things can be listened to: bx-ai events ( beforeAIAgentRun , afterAIModelInvoke , onAIError , beforeAIToolExecute and the rest). They fire wherever the agent runs. Chat events , announced by BxAgents: Event When data has A listener can onChatSessionStart / onChatSessionEnd the terminal chat opens or closes agent , transport onChatInput before a message is sent text , transport cancel( reason ) , or replace( newText ) onChatTurnStart / onChatTurnEnd around one turn of the agent text , transport ( reply , status at the end) onChatConversationChange /new , /resume , /clear , /fork or /compact changed the conversation line , transport onChatCommandBefore before any command, on every transport line , name , arguments , transport cancel( reason ) onChatCommandAfter after any command, on every transport line , name , reply , transport replace( newReply ) The session, input, turn and conversation events are the terminal chat's; the two command events fire in the terminal, the web page and on chat platforms alike. A listener that throws is caught: it can never stop a turn, the listeners after it still run, and the error is shown in /extensions . @On binds a method with another name, or many events at once, and takes the four forms an annotation takes: @On( [ "beforeAIToolExecute", "afterAIToolExecute" ] ) function toolCalled( data ) { log.info( "a tool ran" ) } @On naming an event the runtime does not know is reported in /extensions , not ignored. interceptors and customInterceptionPoints As in a module config, configure() can name classes from the extension's folder to register, each with its own properties, and points of its own to announce: function configure() { variables.interceptors = [ { class : "interceptors.Audit", properties : { level : "info" } } ] variables.customInterceptionPoints = [ "onAuditRecorded" ] } interceptors/Audit.bx listens with methods named after events and has settings , log and properties injected. Any extension can then listen to onAuditRecorded , and the one that owns it announces it with BoxAnnounce( "onAuditRecorded", { ... } ) . extensions.disable takes extension:method to turn one listener off. ColdBox events ( preProcess , postProcess and the rest) are not part of the terminal chat; they fire only in a served agent. Keys and status @Key binds keys in the terminal chat to a method. On a command method it runs that command, with the same rules and events as typing it; on any other method it calls the method with the agentContext and an empty text and shows what it returns. @Hint (or hint in the struct form) says what it does. @Command @Hint( "count a pulse" ) @Key( "ctrl+g" ) function pulse( agentContext, commandArguments ) { ... } @Key( { keys : [ "ctrl+y", "alt+y" ], hint : "reset the count" } ) function resetPulse( agentContext, commandArguments ) { ... } A key is named extension:method ( pulse:pulse ). /keys lists it with the built-in ones, and a person can give it other keys under chat: keys: in ~/.bxagents/bxAgents.yml . A key a built-in action already uses, or an earlier extension holds, is refused with a sentence that says so. A typed draft stays in the box while a key runs. Keys are for the terminal chat; the web page and chat platforms have commands. @Status is a piece of status next to the size of the context: a method that returns a short text, asked each time the box is drawn in the terminal and after each change to the conversation on the web page (small chips in the header). Return an empty string to show nothing. It must be quick; one that throws is left out and the reason is put on its extension once. @Status function beats( agentContext ) { return variables.beats > 0 ? "beat #variables.beats#" : "" } extensions.disable takes extension:method for a key or a status item too. register( registry ) What annotations cannot say, because it is worked out in code, is said as calls. If the class has a register( registry ) method it is called once, right after configure() : function register( registry ) { registry.command( "deploy", { run : ( agentContext, commandArguments ) => ..., hint : "ship it", admin : true, aliases : [ "ship" ] } ) registry.key( "ctrl+d", "/deploy", { hint : "ship it" } ) // a key that runs a command line registry.key( "ctrl+o", ( agentContext ) => "opened", { name : "open", hint : "open it" } ) // or any function registry.status( "branch", ( agentContext ) => "main" ) registry.on( "onChatCommandAfter", ( data ) => ... ) // an event, or an array of them } Prefixes and @ sources Both are for the terminal chat only. @Prefix claims the start of a line in the message box. The method gets the agentContext and the text after the prefix. It answers one of two ways: a Reply (or a string) is shown and nothing is sent, and { send : "text" } is sent to the agent as the message, after onChatInput has seen it. @Prefix( "%" ) @Hint( "ask for an explanation: % why is the sky blue" ) function explain( agentContext, text ) { return { send : "Explain this in one short paragraph: #text#" } } @Prefix( "=" ) function count( agentContext, text ) { return agentContext.reply().ok( "#text.listToArray( ' ' ).len()# words" ) } / , ! , # and @ are the chat's own, and a lone ? asks for the keys; a prefix that starts with one of them, is empty or has a space is refused with a sentence. The longest prefix wins. Two extensions on one prefix are a warning and the later layer wins. @Source( "ticket" ) brings content along with a message the way @path brings a file. Write @ticket:TCK-1 (or @ticket:"two words" ) and the method is called with the agentContext and the query. It returns { name, content } , an array of them or a string; the content goes with the message and the mention stays in it. @Suggest( "ticket" ) on another method is optional: it returns the values the menu offers as the person types after the colon. It is asked on keystrokes, so it must be quick; one that throws gives no suggestions and the reason is put on its extension once. A source name can be anything that starts with a letter, since files are plain @path . @Source( "ticket" ) function ticket( agentContext, query ) { return { name : "ticket #query#", content : tickets[ query ] } } @Suggest( "ticket" ) function ticketNames( agentContext, query ) { return tickets.keyArray() } Written as calls: registry.prefix( "%", ( agentContext, text ) => ..., { hint : "..." } ) and registry.source( "ticket", ( agentContext, query ) => ..., { hint : "...", suggest : ( agentContext, query ) => [ ... ] } ) . The person chooses the prefix or the name, by the id extension:method , in ~/.bxagents/bxAgents.yml : chat: prefixes: desk:explain: "?%" sources: desk:ticket: issue A choice that cannot be used is reported and the extension's own is kept. extensions.disable takes extension:method for these too. Asking the person A command, key or prefix can put a question to the person while it runs: var title = agentContext.ask( "Title of the ticket?", { default : commandArguments, help : "A short sentence." } ) var priority = agentContext.choose( "Priority?", [ "low", "normal", { value : "high", label : "high", hint : "someone is blocked" } ] ) if ( agentContext.confirm( "Make the #priority# ticket?" ) ) { ... } ask() returns the text, choose() returns the value picked, and confirm() is true only for a yes. Esc gives null ( false for confirm() ). Questions work in the terminal chat only. Where nobody can answer (the web page, chat platforms, a server) they answer at once with null ( false ) instead of waiting, and agentContext.canAsk() tells you beforehand so a command can say so. Reloading /reload loads the extensions again without leaving the chat: it runs onUnload() of what was loaded, reads ~/.bxagents/bxAgents.yml and the extensions: settings of Agent.yaml anew, and loads what is found, with its commands, keys, status items, prefixes, sources and listeners. An extension that fails to load is reported and left out; the others load. It is for admins and works in the terminal chat only: a served app registers schedulers and ColdBox listeners when it starts, so restart it instead. The web page: slots and web/ Two ways to add to the web page. Both are served with the page; the terminal chat has no page, so they are ignored there. Slots put a string in a named place of the page: header (a chip next to the context size), sidebar (a panel under the list of conversations) or composer (next to the Attach button). The method is called with the agentContext and returns the string: @Slot( "header" ) function badge( agentContext ) { return variables.pings > 0 ? "#variables.pings# pings" : "" } @Slot( { place : "sidebar", html : true } ) function about( agentContext ) { return "Panel
Use the Ping button." } The string is shown as text. Only a slot that says html : true has its string put into the page as markup; that is the author saying it is their own markup, so it must never carry what a visitor typed (use encodeForHTML() ). An empty string shows nothing. The page asks for every slot in one request, GET /__bxagents/slots?conversationId= (the agent API's own path, which agentApi.path can move), behind the same sign-in or token as the rest of the API, each time it refreshes the context size. A slot that throws is left out and the reason is put on its extension once. Written as a call: registry.slot( "header", ( agentContext ) => "...", { html : false, name : "badge" } ) . extensions.disable takes extension:method for a slot. web/ is a folder inside a folder extension. The page serves every file in it (images too) at /ext// , read from the extension itself in the built app; nothing is copied next to the page. The *.css and *.js files that sit directly in web/ are linked into the page, in file name order: styles in the head and scripts at the end of the body. An extension turned off by name in extensions.disable brings nothing. extensions/panel/ Extension.bx web/ panel.css panel.js logo.png served at /ext/panel/logo.png The page gives scripts one small object, bxagents : bxagents.slot( place ) a box of your own in header , sidebar or composer , to draw into bxagents.runCommand( "/ping" ) runs a slash command as if it were typed bxagents.onRefresh( fn ) called after each change to the conversation, once the slots are drawn bxagents.refresh() asks the page to refresh now bxagents.conversationId() the conversation in view bxagents.apiBase the page's API path, for your own fetch calls bxagents.icon( "robot" ) markup for one of the page's Phosphor icons , sized by the text around it. The names are in tools/webui-vendor/icons.json Your CSS can use the page's variables so it follows light, dark and the accent: --bg , --surface , --fg , --muted , --border , --accent , --accent-fg , --accent-soft (a light tint of the accent), --accent-ink (the accent as text or an icon), --ring (a focus glow), --radius and --font . Tools and skills A folder extension can carry its own tools and skills: extensions/helpdesk/ Extension.bx tools/Tickets.bx a normal bx-ai tool class skills/triage/SKILL.md a normal skill folder The extension stays as it is. The app reads the folders where they are ( extensions/helpdesk/tools/ in the built app) and gives the tools to the root agent as if they were in the project's own tools/ , and adds the skills to the global skills every agent gets. Nothing is copied or merged into the project's tools/ or skills/ . A tool or skill of the project's own wins over an extension's of the same name, and a later extension wins over an earlier one. extensions.disable takes extension:Tickets (the tool's file name) or extension:ticket-triage (the skill's name) for one, or the extension's name for all of them. Gateway types A class in an extension's gateways/ folder is a gateway type, named after its file in lower case: extensions/matrix/gateways/Matrix.bx is the type matrix . It is an ordinary bx-ai gateway (see the built-in ones, which extend ScheduledGatewayBase ); its getName() must be the same as its file, lower case, because that is the key bx-ai's gateway registry holds it under. A project then uses it like any other: // gateways/chat.bx class { function configure() { return { type : "matrix", homeserver : "https://matrix.example.org", tokenEnvVar : "MATRIX_TOKEN" }; } } Every option named EnvVar is the name of an environment variable: the gateway receives its value as (here token ), and it is read when the app starts, so a secret is never a literal in the build. The app builds the gateway from the extension's own class file and registers it when it starts. All the types come from one registry, GatewayTypes : the built-in ones, and whatever extensions bring. A built-in type cannot be replaced (an extension cannot take over telegram ). Two extensions on one type is a warning and the later one wins. A file name that is not a usable type name (a letter, then letters, digits and - ) is refused. extensions.disable takes extension:Matrix for one type or the extension's name for all of them. The gateway classes are read from the project's extensions only. Command line verbs @Verb( { name : "greet", valueOptions : [ "name" ] } ) @Hint( "say hello from the command line: bxAgents greet --name=Ada" ) function greet( options ) { return "Hello, #options.name ?: 'there'#!" } bxAgents greet --name=Ada finds the verb in the extensions (modules, the person's own and the project's, loaded as in the chat) when it is not one of the module's own. The method is called with the flags as a struct, as a built-in verb gets them ( --projectRoot is always there). It returns an exit code, a message to print, { exitCode, message } , or nothing. A flag that must have a value is listed in valueOptions , so --name alone is refused as it is for a built-in verb. A method that throws is an error with exit code 1 that names the extension. A built-in verb cannot be replaced, and two extensions on one verb is a warning with the later one winning. bxAgents help lists the verbs extensions add. They are not in the generated shell completions, which stay as they are. registry.verb( "greet", ( options ) => ..., { hint, valueOptions } ) is the call form, and extensions.disable takes extension:method . Where extensions come from Layer Folder Runs in modules extensions/ of an installed BoxLang module everywhere the module is installed user ~/.bxagents/extensions/ the terminal chat on that machine only project /extensions/ the terminal chat, the web page, chat platforms, the server A later layer wins. An extension with the same name replaces the earlier one, and a command replaces an earlier command of the same name or alias, a built-in included. Both are shown in /extensions ; nothing is replaced silently. The build copies the project's extensions/ into the app; a served agent never reads a developer's home folder. Starting one bxAgents add extension standup # asks what it should bring bxAgents add extension standup --with=command,key # or say so, for a pipe or CI bxAgents add extension standup --with=command,tool --description="Daily standup" add extension writes extensions/.bx , or extensions// with an Extension.bx when something needs a file of its own, with working stubs and a TODO where you fill in. --with takes any of command , key , status , prefix , source , slot , verb , listener (methods of the one class) and scheduler , gateway , tool , skill , web (files, so the extension is a folder). --layout=file|folder picks the shape when it can be either. Nothing is overwritten without --force , and --dry-run shows the files. It is yours: commit it with the project. Try it with bxAgents chat and /reload . Installing extensions bxAgents extensions install puts an extension into the project from a folder, a zip, GitHub or ForgeBox. bxAgents extensions install ./my-ext # a folder bxAgents extensions install ./my-ext.zip # a zip file bxAgents extensions install ./greet.bx # a one-class extension bxAgents extensions install acme/tools # GitHub: owner/repo, or owner/repo#ref bxAgents extensions install https://github.com/acme/tools bxAgents extensions install https://example.org/ext.zip # a zip by address bxAgents extensions install acme-tools@1.2.0 # a ForgeBox slug, optionally with a version bxAgents extensions install ./my-ext --system # for you, in ~/.bxagents/extensions A folder that exists wins over owner/repo . To say which you mean, start with path: , github: , forgebox: or url: . An extension is code that runs when the chat or the app starts, so install fetches it into a temporary folder, looks at it without running anything, and shows you what it adds (commands, keys, prefixes, listeners, gateways, tools, skills, web files, verbs) and what its code mentions (files, network, processes, java). It then asks for a yes. --yes skips the question and is required when there is no terminal. Nothing is placed until you agree. Command Does install fetch, preview, ask, place. --name= renames it, --force replaces one that is there, --system installs for you instead of the project install with no source, brings back everything extensions.lock.json lists list --installed what was installed, where from, and whether it is intact , changed or missing update [name...] fetches again, shows the change and asks. A source pinned to a version or ref ( #v1 , @1.2.0 ) is left alone remove deletes it and its lock entry. A folder you edited needs --force The project keeps extensions.lock.json ( ~/.bxagents/extensions.lock.json with --system ): the name, the source, the version or ref fetched, and a checksum of the files. Commit the lock. bxAgents build brings back anything in it that is missing, and refuses a package whose files no longer match their checksum. Installed extensions are not committed (see below), and the build restores them from the lock. An installed extension is kept out of source control with one line per extension in the project's .gitignore ( /extensions/acme-tools/ , or /extensions/acme.bx ), added on install and taken out on remove , only when the project has a .gitignore . An extension you wrote yourself in the same folder is still committed. Commit extensions.lock.json : it is what brings the rest back. What install refuses: a zip entry with an absolute path, a .. part or a backslash, more than 5000 files or 50 MB, a name that is not safe as a folder name, a name already there that this command did not install (unless --force ), a BoxLang module ( ModuleConfig.bx ), and anything that is not an extension. Symbolic links and .git are left out. The preview is a quick read of the text, not a security review: install what you trust. Working on one: link it bxAgents extensions link ./my-ext # ~/.bxagents/extensions/my-ext -> ./my-ext bxAgents extensions link ./greet.bx --name=hi # a one-class extension, under another name bxAgents extensions unlink my-ext # takes the link away, never the folder link makes a symbolic link in your own extensions folder, so the terminal chat on this machine loads the extension from where you are editing it, and /reload picks up a change with nothing to install again. There is no preview and no lock: the code is yours, and a link is a path on this machine, so it is not brought back on another one. A real folder or file in that place is never replaced, a name installed with install --system has to be removed first, and --force only points an existing link somewhere else. list --installed --system shows links beside installs, as linked or broken (the target went away). Because a link is for you, it is not part of a project and does not travel into a built app: put the extension in the project's extensions/ (or install it) for that. Turning things off extensions: disable: [ roll, "deploy:deploy", "acme-*" ] A plain name turns off the extension of that name (and any command called that); extension:item turns off one command; * matches any run of characters. Both Agent.yaml and ~/.bxagents/bxAgents.yml accept it. Looking at them /extensions in the chat, or from the shell: bxAgents extensions # the list, where each came from and what it added bxAgents extensions --json What stays in the project Tools, skills, gateway types and web/ files are read from the project's own extensions/ folder, which the build copies into the app as it is. An extension in an installed module or in your own ~/.bxagents/extensions still adds commands, keys, prefixes, listeners and verbs to the chat and the command line, but it does not travel into a built app: a server never reads a developer's home folder.

Release them | `this.title`, `this.author`, `this.webURL`, `this.description`, `this.version` and `this.enabled` are read as in a module config, and `this.dependencies = [ "other-extension" ]` loads that extension first. An extension that throws while it loads is shown as failed in `/extensions` with the reason; the others still load. ## Injection Every class of an extension has ``$inject( name, object )`. It puts the object in both the `this` and the `variables` scopes. For private only: `$inject( name, object, "variables" )``. `$read( name )` reads a `variables` entry from outside. BxAgents injects two things before `onLoad()`: `settings` and `log` (`log.info( "..." )`, `.warn()`, `.error()`; what an extension logs is also in `/extensions`). To share an object between the files of an extension, create it in `onLoad()` and `$inject` it where it is needed. The same call is how a test hands an extension a fake. ## A folder extension A folder has the same shape as an agent project: extensions/standup/ Extension.bx required: it is what makes the folder an extension (the module config: properties, configure(), onLoad(), onUnload()) commands/ one class per command, like the built-in ones schedulers/ BoxLang scheduler classes, started when the agent is served A class in `commands/` extends `models.chat.commands.BaseCommand@bxagents` and says its `name()`, `hint()`, `transports()` and `run( context, args )`. `settings` and `log` are injected into it. ## Schedulers A class in `schedulers/` is a **BoxLang scheduler** : a class with a `configure()` that defines tasks through the `scheduler` property BoxLang gives it, like any other BoxLang scheduler. When the agent is served (`bxAgents serve`, a `.bxa`, a deployed server) it starts in the runtime's scheduler service. Like every class of an extension it is given `settings` (the defaults with the values from `Agent.yaml`) and `log` before `configure()` runs: class { function configure() { scheduler.task( "standup-reminder" ) .call( () => log.info( "Standup time for #settings.channel#" ) ) .everyDayAt( settings.at ) .withNoOverlaps() } } The BoxLang scheduler lifecycle methods (`onStartup()`, `onShutdown()`, `onAnyTaskError()` and the rest) work as usual. Each scheduler is registered as `extension--`, and a scheduler that fails to start is reported on its extension in `/extensions` while the others still run. The terminal chat does not start schedulers: they belong to the served agent. ## Listening to events An extension is also an interceptor. A method named after an event listens to it, exactly like a BoxLang or ColdBox interceptor: class { function onChatInput( data ) { if ( data.text contains "password" ) { data.cancel( "That looks like a password, so it was not sent." ) } } function onAIError( data ) { log.warn( "the model failed" ) } } Two things can be listened to: * **bx-ai events** (`beforeAIAgentRun`, `afterAIModelInvoke`, `onAIError`, `beforeAIToolExecute` and the rest). They fire wherever the agent runs. * **Chat events**, announced by BxAgents: | Event | When | `data` has | A listener can | |-------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------| | `onChatSessionStart` / `onChatSessionEnd` | the terminal chat opens or closes | `agent`, `transport` | | | `onChatInput` | before a message is sent | `text`, `transport` | `cancel( reason )`, or `replace( newText )` | | `onChatTurnStart` / `onChatTurnEnd` | around one turn of the agent | `text`, `transport` (`reply`, `status` at the end) | | | `onChatConversationChange` | `/new`, `/resume`, `/clear`, `/fork` or `/compact` changed the conversation | `line`, `transport` | | | `onChatCommandBefore` | before any command, on every transport | `line`, `name`, `arguments`, `transport` | `cancel( reason )` | | `onChatCommandAfter` | after any command, on every transport | `line`, `name`, `reply`, `transport` | `replace( newReply )` | The session, input, turn and conversation events are the terminal chat's; the two command events fire in the terminal, the web page and on chat platforms alike. A listener that throws is caught: it can never stop a turn, the listeners after it still run, and the error is shown in `/extensions`. `@On` binds a method with another name, or many events at once, and takes the four forms an annotation takes: @On( [ "beforeAIToolExecute", "afterAIToolExecute" ] ) function toolCalled( data ) { log.info( "a tool ran" ) } `@On` naming an event the runtime does not know is reported in `/extensions`, not ignored. ### `interceptors` and `customInterceptionPoints` As in a module config, `configure()` can name classes from the extension's folder to register, each with its own properties, and points of its own to announce: function configure() { variables.interceptors = [ { class : "interceptors.Audit", properties : { level : "info" } } ] variables.customInterceptionPoints = [ "onAuditRecorded" ] } `interceptors/Audit.bx` listens with methods named after events and has `settings`, `log` and `properties` injected. Any extension can then listen to `onAuditRecorded`, and the one that owns it announces it with `BoxAnnounce( "onAuditRecorded", { ... } )`. `extensions.disable` takes `extension:method` to turn one listener off. ColdBox events (`preProcess`, `postProcess` and the rest) are not part of the terminal chat; they fire only in a served agent. ## Keys and status `@Key` binds keys in the terminal chat to a method. On a command method it runs that command, with the same rules and events as typing it; on any other method it calls the method with the `agentContext` and an empty text and shows what it returns. `@Hint` (or `hint` in the struct form) says what it does. ```js @Command @Hint( "count a pulse" ) @Key( "ctrl+g" ) function pulse( agentContext, commandArguments ) { ... } @Key( { keys : [ "ctrl+y", "alt+y" ], hint : "reset the count" } ) function resetPulse( agentContext, commandArguments ) { ... } ``` A key is named `extension:method` (`pulse:pulse`). `/keys` lists it with the built-in ones, and a person can give it other keys under `chat: keys:` in `~/.bxagents/bxAgents.yml`. A key a built-in action already uses, or an earlier extension holds, is refused with a sentence that says so. A typed draft stays in the box while a key runs. Keys are for the terminal chat; the web page and chat platforms have commands. `@Status` is a piece of status next to the size of the context: a method that returns a short text, asked each time the box is drawn in the terminal and after each change to the conversation on the web page (small chips in the header). Return an empty string to show nothing. It must be quick; one that throws is left out and the reason is put on its extension once. ```js @Status function beats( agentContext ) { return variables.beats > 0 ? "beat #variables.beats#" : "" } ``` `extensions.disable` takes `extension:method` for a key or a status item too. ## `register( registry )` What annotations cannot say, because it is worked out in code, is said as calls. If the class has a `register( registry )` method it is called once, right after `configure()`: ```js function register( registry ) { registry.command( "deploy", { run : ( agentContext, commandArguments ) => ..., hint : "ship it", admin : true, aliases : [ "ship" ] } ) registry.key( "ctrl+d", "/deploy", { hint : "ship it" } ) // a key that runs a command line registry.key( "ctrl+o", ( agentContext ) => "opened", { name : "open", hint : "open it" } ) // or any function registry.status( "branch", ( agentContext ) => "main" ) registry.on( "onChatCommandAfter", ( data ) => ... ) // an event, or an array of them } ``` ## Prefixes and `@` sources Both are for the terminal chat only. `@Prefix` claims the start of a line in the message box. The method gets the `agentContext` and the text after the prefix. It answers one of two ways: a `Reply` (or a string) is shown and nothing is sent, and `{ send : "text" }` is sent to the agent as the message, after `onChatInput` has seen it. ```js @Prefix( "%" ) @Hint( "ask for an explanation: % why is the sky blue" ) function explain( agentContext, text ) { return { send : "Explain this in one short paragraph: #text#" } } @Prefix( "=" ) function count( agentContext, text ) { return agentContext.reply().ok( "#text.listToArray( ' ' ).len()# words" ) } ``` `/`, `!`, `#` and `@` are the chat's own, and a lone `?` asks for the keys; a prefix that starts with one of them, is empty or has a space is refused with a sentence. The longest prefix wins. Two extensions on one prefix are a warning and the later layer wins. `@Source( "ticket" )` brings content along with a message the way `@path` brings a file. Write `@ticket:TCK-1` (or `@ticket:"two words"`) and the method is called with the `agentContext` and the query. It returns `{ name, content }`, an array of them or a string; the content goes with the message and the mention stays in it. `@Suggest( "ticket" )` on another method is optional: it returns the values the menu offers as the person types after the colon. It is asked on keystrokes, so it must be quick; one that throws gives no suggestions and the reason is put on its extension once. A source name can be anything that starts with a letter, since files are plain `@path`. ```js @Source( "ticket" ) function ticket( agentContext, query ) { return { name : "ticket #query#", content : tickets[ query ] } } @Suggest( "ticket" ) function ticketNames( agentContext, query ) { return tickets.keyArray() } ``` Written as calls: `registry.prefix( "%", ( agentContext, text ) => ..., { hint : "..." } )` and `registry.source( "ticket", ( agentContext, query ) => ..., { hint : "...", suggest : ( agentContext, query ) => [ ... ] } )`. The person chooses the prefix or the name, by the id `extension:method`, in `~/.bxagents/bxAgents.yml`: ```yaml chat: prefixes: desk:explain: "?%" sources: desk:ticket: issue ``` A choice that cannot be used is reported and the extension's own is kept. `extensions.disable` takes `extension:method` for these too. ## Asking the person A command, key or prefix can put a question to the person while it runs: ```js var title = agentContext.ask( "Title of the ticket?", { default : commandArguments, help : "A short sentence." } ) var priority = agentContext.choose( "Priority?", [ "low", "normal", { value : "high", label : "high", hint : "someone is blocked" } ] ) if ( agentContext.confirm( "Make the #priority# ticket?" ) ) { ... } ``` `ask()` returns the text, `choose()` returns the value picked, and `confirm()` is true only for a yes. Esc gives `null` (`false` for `confirm()`). Questions work in the terminal chat only. Where nobody can answer (the web page, chat platforms, a server) they answer at once with `null` (`false`) instead of waiting, and `agentContext.canAsk()` tells you beforehand so a command can say so. ## Reloading `/reload` loads the extensions again without leaving the chat: it runs `onUnload()` of what was loaded, reads `~/.bxagents/bxAgents.yml` and the `extensions:` settings of `Agent.yaml` anew, and loads what is found, with its commands, keys, status items, prefixes, sources and listeners. An extension that fails to load is reported and left out; the others load. It is for admins and works in the terminal chat only: a served app registers schedulers and ColdBox listeners when it starts, so restart it instead. ## The web page: slots and `web/` Two ways to add to the web page. Both are served with the page; the terminal chat has no page, so they are ignored there. **Slots** put a string in a named place of the page: `header` (a chip next to the context size), `sidebar` (a panel under the list of conversations) or `composer` (next to the Attach button). The method is called with the `agentContext` and returns the string: ```js @Slot( "header" ) function badge( agentContext ) { return variables.pings > 0 ? "#variables.pings# pings" : "" } @Slot( { place : "sidebar", html : true } ) function about( agentContext ) { return "Panel
Use the Ping button." } ``` The string is shown as text. Only a slot that says `html : true` has its string put into the page as markup; that is the author saying it is their own markup, so it must never carry what a visitor typed (use `encodeForHTML()`). An empty string shows nothing. The page asks for every slot in one request, `GET /__bxagents/slots?conversationId=` (the agent API's own path, which `agentApi.path` can move), behind the same sign-in or token as the rest of the API, each time it refreshes the context size. A slot that throws is left out and the reason is put on its extension once. Written as a call: `registry.slot( "header", ( agentContext ) => "...", { html : false, name : "badge" } )`. `extensions.disable` takes `extension:method` for a slot. **`web/`** is a folder inside a folder extension. The page serves every file in it (images too) at `/ext//`, read from the extension itself in the built app; nothing is copied next to the page. The `*.css` and `*.js` files that sit directly in `web/` are linked into the page, in file name order: styles in the head and scripts at the end of the body. An extension turned off by name in `extensions.disable` brings nothing. extensions/panel/ Extension.bx web/ panel.css panel.js logo.png served at /ext/panel/logo.png The page gives scripts one small object, `bxagents`: | | | |----------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `bxagents.slot( place )` | a box of your own in `header`, `sidebar` or `composer`, to draw into | | `bxagents.runCommand( "/ping" )` | runs a slash command as if it were typed | | `bxagents.onRefresh( fn )` | called after each change to the conversation, once the slots are drawn | | `bxagents.refresh()` | asks the page to refresh now | | `bxagents.conversationId()` | the conversation in view | | `bxagents.apiBase` | the page's API path, for your own `fetch` calls | | `bxagents.icon( "robot" )` | markup for one of the page's [Phosphor icons](https://phosphoricons.com), sized by the text around it. The names are in `tools/webui-vendor/icons.json` | Your CSS can use the page's variables so it follows light, dark and the accent: `--bg`, `--surface`, `--fg`, `--muted`, `--border`, `--accent`, `--accent-fg`, `--accent-soft` (a light tint of the accent), `--accent-ink` (the accent as text or an icon), `--ring` (a focus glow), `--radius` and `--font`. ## Tools and skills A folder extension can carry its own tools and skills: extensions/helpdesk/ Extension.bx tools/Tickets.bx a normal bx-ai tool class skills/triage/SKILL.md a normal skill folder The extension stays as it is. The app reads the folders where they are (`extensions/helpdesk/tools/` in the built app) and gives the tools to the root agent as if they were in the project's own `tools/`, and adds the skills to the global skills every agent gets. Nothing is copied or merged into the project's `tools/` or `skills/`. A tool or skill of the project's own wins over an extension's of the same name, and a later extension wins over an earlier one. `extensions.disable` takes `extension:Tickets` (the tool's file name) or `extension:ticket-triage` (the skill's name) for one, or the extension's name for all of them. ## Gateway types A class in an extension's `gateways/` folder is a gateway type, named after its file in lower case: `extensions/matrix/gateways/Matrix.bx` is the type `matrix`. It is an ordinary bx-ai gateway (see the built-in ones, which extend `ScheduledGatewayBase`); its `getName()` must be the same as its file, lower case, because that is the key bx-ai's gateway registry holds it under. A project then uses it like any other: ```js // gateways/chat.bx class { function configure() { return { type : "matrix", homeserver : "https://matrix.example.org", tokenEnvVar : "MATRIX_TOKEN" }; } } ``` Every option named `EnvVar` is the name of an environment variable: the gateway receives its value as `` (here `token`), and it is read when the app starts, so a secret is never a literal in the build. The app builds the gateway from the extension's own class file and registers it when it starts. All the types come from one registry, `GatewayTypes`: the built-in ones, and whatever extensions bring. A built-in type cannot be replaced (an extension cannot take over `telegram`). Two extensions on one type is a warning and the later one wins. A file name that is not a usable type name (a letter, then letters, digits and `-`) is refused. `extensions.disable` takes `extension:Matrix` for one type or the extension's name for all of them. The gateway classes are read from the project's extensions only. ## Command line verbs ```js @Verb( { name : "greet", valueOptions : [ "name" ] } ) @Hint( "say hello from the command line: bxAgents greet --name=Ada" ) function greet( options ) { return "Hello, #options.name ?: 'there'#!" } ``` `bxAgents greet --name=Ada` finds the verb in the extensions (modules, the person's own and the project's, loaded as in the chat) when it is not one of the module's own. The method is called with the flags as a struct, as a built-in verb gets them (`--projectRoot` is always there). It returns an exit code, a message to print, `{ exitCode, message }`, or nothing. A flag that must have a value is listed in `valueOptions`, so `--name` alone is refused as it is for a built-in verb. A method that throws is an error with exit code 1 that names the extension. A built-in verb cannot be replaced, and two extensions on one verb is a warning with the later one winning. `bxAgents help` lists the verbs extensions add. They are not in the generated shell completions, which stay as they are. `registry.verb( "greet", ( options ) => ..., { hint, valueOptions } )` is the call form, and `extensions.disable` takes `extension:method`. ## Where extensions come from | Layer | Folder | Runs in | |---------|----------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------| | modules | `extensions/` of an installed BoxLang module | everywhere the module is installed | | user | `~/.bxagents/extensions/` | the terminal chat on that machine only | | project | `/extensions/` | the terminal chat, the web page, chat platforms, the server | A later layer wins. An extension with the same name replaces the earlier one, and a command replaces an earlier command of the same name or alias, a built-in included. Both are shown in `/extensions`; nothing is replaced silently. The build copies the project's `extensions/` into the app; a served agent never reads a developer's home folder. ## Starting one ```bash bxAgents add extension standup # asks what it should bring bxAgents add extension standup --with=command,key # or say so, for a pipe or CI bxAgents add extension standup --with=command,tool --description="Daily standup" ``` `add extension` writes `extensions/.bx`, or `extensions//` with an `Extension.bx` when something needs a file of its own, with working stubs and a `TODO` where you fill in. `--with` takes any of `command`, `key`, `status`, `prefix`, `source`, `slot`, `verb`, `listener` (methods of the one class) and `scheduler`, `gateway`, `tool`, `skill`, `web` (files, so the extension is a folder). `--layout=file|folder` picks the shape when it can be either. Nothing is overwritten without `--force`, and `--dry-run` shows the files. It is yours: commit it with the project. Try it with `bxAgents chat` and `/reload`. ## Installing extensions `bxAgents extensions install` puts an extension into the project from a folder, a zip, GitHub or ForgeBox. ```bash bxAgents extensions install ./my-ext # a folder bxAgents extensions install ./my-ext.zip # a zip file bxAgents extensions install ./greet.bx # a one-class extension bxAgents extensions install acme/tools # GitHub: owner/repo, or owner/repo#ref bxAgents extensions install https://github.com/acme/tools bxAgents extensions install https://example.org/ext.zip # a zip by address bxAgents extensions install acme-tools@1.2.0 # a ForgeBox slug, optionally with a version bxAgents extensions install ./my-ext --system # for you, in ~/.bxagents/extensions ``` A folder that exists wins over `owner/repo`. To say which you mean, start with `path:`, `github:`, `forgebox:` or `url:`. An extension is code that runs when the chat or the app starts, so `install` fetches it into a temporary folder, looks at it without running anything, and shows you what it adds (commands, keys, prefixes, listeners, gateways, tools, skills, web files, verbs) and what its code mentions (files, network, processes, java). It then asks for a yes. `--yes` skips the question and is required when there is no terminal. Nothing is placed until you agree. | Command | Does | |--------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `install ` | fetch, preview, ask, place. `--name=` renames it, `--force` replaces one that is there, `--system` installs for you instead of the project | | `install` | with no source, brings back everything `extensions.lock.json` lists | | `list --installed` | what was installed, where from, and whether it is `intact`, `changed` or `missing` | | `update [name...]` | fetches again, shows the change and asks. A source pinned to a version or ref (`#v1`, `@1.2.0`) is left alone | | `remove ` | deletes it and its lock entry. A folder you edited needs `--force` | The project keeps `extensions.lock.json` (`~/.bxagents/extensions.lock.json` with `--system`): the name, the source, the version or ref fetched, and a checksum of the files. **Commit the lock.** `bxAgents build` brings back anything in it that is missing, and refuses a package whose files no longer match their checksum. Installed extensions are not committed (see below), and the build restores them from the lock. An installed extension is kept out of source control with one line per extension in the project's `.gitignore` (`/extensions/acme-tools/`, or `/extensions/acme.bx`), added on `install` and taken out on `remove`, only when the project has a `.gitignore`. An extension you wrote yourself in the same folder is still committed. Commit `extensions.lock.json`: it is what brings the rest back. What `install` refuses: a zip entry with an absolute path, a `..` part or a backslash, more than 5000 files or 50 MB, a name that is not safe as a folder name, a name already there that this command did not install (unless `--force`), a BoxLang module (`ModuleConfig.bx`), and anything that is not an extension. Symbolic links and `.git` are left out. The preview is a quick read of the text, not a security review: install what you trust. ## Working on one: link it ```bash bxAgents extensions link ./my-ext # ~/.bxagents/extensions/my-ext -> ./my-ext bxAgents extensions link ./greet.bx --name=hi # a one-class extension, under another name bxAgents extensions unlink my-ext # takes the link away, never the folder ``` `link` makes a symbolic link in your own extensions folder, so the terminal chat on this machine loads the extension from where you are editing it, and `/reload` picks up a change with nothing to install again. There is no preview and no lock: the code is yours, and a link is a path on this machine, so it is not brought back on another one. A real folder or file in that place is never replaced, a name installed with `install --system` has to be removed first, and `--force` only points an existing link somewhere else. `list --installed --system` shows links beside installs, as `linked` or `broken` (the target went away). Because a link is for you, it is not part of a project and does not travel into a built app: put the extension in the project's `extensions/` (or `install` it) for that. ## Turning things off ```yaml extensions: disable: [ roll, "deploy:deploy", "acme-*" ] ``` A plain name turns off the extension of that name (and any command called that); `extension:item` turns off one command; `*` matches any run of characters. Both `Agent.yaml` and `~/.bxagents/bxAgents.yml` accept it. ## Looking at them `/extensions` in the chat, or from the shell: ```bash bxAgents extensions # the list, where each came from and what it added bxAgents extensions --json ``` ## What stays in the project Tools, skills, gateway types and `web/` files are read from the project's own `extensions/` folder, which the build copies into the app as it is. An extension in an installed module or in your own `~/.bxagents/extensions` still adds commands, keys, prefixes, listeners and verbs to the chat and the command line, but it does not travel into a built app: a server never reads a developer's home folder.
