# Twilio SMS

Part of the push-style [gateways/](/conventions/gateways/index.html) family - see there for the shared "secrets stay external" rule, `GatewaySession`, and the scheduler these gateways run under. This page covers Twilio SMS's own config shape and (where BxAgents does anything platform-specific) how it talks to Twilio SMS.

```javascript
// gateways/twilioChannel.bx
class {
	function configure() {
		return {
			type            : "twilio",
			accountSidEnvVar: "TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID",
			authTokenEnvVar : "TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN",   // also the X-Twilio-Signature HMAC key
			fromEnvVar      : "TWILIO_FROM_NUMBER"   // the Twilio phone number outbound sends go through, E.164
			// messagingServiceSid: "MG..."   // optional - if set, used instead of `from` on outbound sends
			// publicUrl: "https://your-real-public-host/webhooks/twilio"   // optional override for reverse-proxy/tunnel deployments - see the Twilio subsection below
		};
	}
}
```

**Validation:** `type: "twilio"` requires `accountSidEnvVar`, `authTokenEnvVar`, and `fromEnvVar`. Checked the same way a channel-adapter `http` entry's `secretEnvVar` is.

Generated registration statement:

```javascript
aiGatewayRegistry().register( aiGateway( "bxModules.bxagents.models.gateways.TwilioGateway", { "accountSid" : getSystemSetting( "TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID", "" ), "authToken" : getSystemSetting( "TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN", "" ), "from" : getSystemSetting( "TWILIO_FROM_NUMBER", "" ) } ) )
```

## Twilio SMS - a genuinely different signature scheme, and a dual-path response model

`TwilioGateway` is webhook-driven the same way `WhatsAppCloudGateway`/`TeamsGateway` are:

```javascript
post( "/webhooks/twilio" ).toHandler( "Twilio.process" )
```

Three things make Twilio's own webhook contract meaningfully different from every other gateway in this project, both ported faithfully from Vercel Eve's real Twilio channel (`packages/eve/src/public/channels/twilio/`, MIT licensed):

* **The inbound body is form-urlencoded** (`Body`, `From`, `To`, `MessageSid`, `AccountSid`), not JSON - `TwilioGateway` parses it itself (`java.net.URLDecoder`), no JSON deserialization involved.
* **Signature verification is `X-Twilio-Signature`: HMAC-SHA1, base64-encoded** (every other webhook gateway in this project uses HMAC-SHA256, hex-encoded) - the signing base is the exact request URL followed by every POST param's own `key & value` concatenated directly (no separators), sorted alphabetically by key. Because the URL itself is part of what's signed, a project running behind a reverse proxy or tunnel (where the URL ColdBox sees via `event.getUrl()` doesn't match what Twilio actually POSTed to) needs the optional `publicUrl` config override - the same class of gotcha Eve's own docs flag for its `webhookUrl` option.
* **The synchronous webhook response is always an empty TwiML `<Response></Response>`** - Twilio's own classic dual-path model. The real agent reply is sent later, out-of-band, via a separate `deliver()` REST call to the Messages API once GatewaySession's async turn completes - matching Eve's own `emptyTwilioResponse()` exactly (Eve never uses a synchronous TwiML `<Message>` to answer inline).

Outbound sends are Basic-Auth REST calls to `POST /2010-04-01/Accounts/{AccountSid}/Messages.json`, form-encoded body (`To`, `Body`, and either `From` or `MessagingServiceSid` if configured). v1 is SMS text (plus incoming MMS media, see [Pictures and files](/conventions/gateways/index.html#pictures-and-files)) only - Eve's own Twilio channel is a combined SMS+voice channel (`/voice` routes, `<Gather>`/`<Say>` TwiML, call transcription); none of the voice-specific pieces were ported.
> **Warning**
>
> SMS has **no native button/card affordance at all** (confirmed via Eve's own docs), so human-in-the-loop is degraded the same way Email's is - `getDeclaredCapabilities()` omits `"interactiveActions"` (and `"threads"`, since Twilio's classic Messages API has no native reply/quote concept either). `requestHumanInteraction()` sends a plain-text SMS listing the allowed decisions; unlike Email (which embeds a `[bxagents:<requestID>]` tag in the Subject line to correlate the eventual reply), SMS has no subject line to tag - so the pending request is keyed by the sender's own phone number (conversationID) instead, a v1 simplification that assumes at most one open HITL request per phone number at a time.
> **Info**
>
> Unlike Eve (which has no length-limiting logic at all - confirmed absent by grepping its source - and relies entirely on Twilio's own server-side segmentation), `TwilioGateway` still applies `MessageChunker` at 1600 chars (Twilio's own documented single-message concatenation ceiling) for consistency with every other gateway's chunking behavior. The HMAC-SHA1 signature scheme was cross-verified this session against an independently computed Python `hmac`/`hashlib` reference value before trusting the BoxLang implementation, the same discipline used for WhatsApp Cloud's own HMAC-SHA256 scheme.

Checked the same way a channel-adapter http entry's secretEnvVar is. Generated registration statement: aiGatewayRegistry().register( aiGateway( "bxModules.bxagents.models.gateways.whatsapp.WhatsAppCloudGateway", { "accessToken" : getSystemSetting( "WHATSAPP_ACCESS_TOKEN", "" ), "phoneNumberId" : getSystemSetting( "WHATSAPP_PHONE_NUMBER_ID", "" ), "appSecret" : getSystemSetting( "WHATSAPP_APP_SECRET", "" ), "verifyToken" : getSystemSetting( "WHATSAPP_VERIFY_TOKEN", "" ) } ) ) WhatsApp Business Cloud API - webhook-driven, not connection-driven WhatsAppCloudGateway is shaped differently from every other push-style gateway: Meta calls us , over a public webhook, rather than this gateway holding its own outbound connection (a poll task or a websocket). It extends bx-ai's BaseGateway directly, not ScheduledGatewayBase - there's no scheduler task or socket to manage, only a generated handlers/WhatsAppCloud.bx (written whenever a whatsapp-cloud gateway entry exists) wired to two fixed routes: get( "/webhooks/whatsapp-cloud" ).toHandler( "WhatsAppCloud.verify" ) post( "/webhooks/whatsapp-cloud" ).toHandler( "WhatsAppCloud.process" ) Both actions are thin passthroughs into the gateway's own handleVerify() / handleWebhook() - verify answers Meta's subscription handshake ( GET ?hub.mode=subscribe&hub.verify_token=...&hub.challenge=... , echoing the challenge back as plain text only when the mode and token match, constant-time compared); process verifies Meta's own X-Hub-Signature-256 header (HMAC-SHA256 over the exact raw POST body - event.getHTTPContent() , never re-parsed/re-serialized JSON, which would change the bytes and break the signature) before parsing or dispatching anything. This is a genuinely different scheme from bx-ai's own HttpGateway / GatewaySecurity (different header names, different HMAC construction), so it isn't reused here - see the class's own docblock. Ported directly from Hermes Agent's own real, production WhatsApp Cloud adapter ( gateway/platforms/whatsapp_cloud.py , MIT licensed) - the verify handshake, signature scheme, webhook payload walk ( entry[].changes[].value.{messages,contacts} ), outbound message/interactive-button shapes (≤3 allowed decisions render as native buttons, 4+ as a tap-to-open list, matching WhatsApp's own documented limits), and length limits (4096-char messages, 20-char button labels, 1024-char interactive body text) were all read directly from that source this session, not reimplemented from scratch. Inbound messages are deduplicated by their own wamid (Meta retries webhook delivery on any non-200 response for up to 7 days) via a bounded FIFO cache, mirroring Hermes's own _dedup_wamid . Warning v1 scope, matching Hermes's own documented limitation: Cloud API DMs have no separate "chat" entity - chat_id IS the sender's wa_id - and group messages (which carry their own chat field identifying the group JID) are out of scope; a picture or document is read (the media link is fetched with the access token, see Pictures and files ), but video, audio and stickers aren't downloaded, only a caption if present. Every other push-style gateway shares the same one-instance-per-type registry ceiling documented above - whatsapp-cloud is no exception. Info The generated handlers/WhatsAppCloud.bx 's own ColdBox request-context calls ( event.getHTTPContent() / event.getHTTPHeader() / event.renderData() , rc 's URL-scope-merged query params for the GET handshake) are the documented, standard ColdBox REST-handler idioms - but unlike the gateway's own signature/dispatch logic (thoroughly unit-tested and empirically verified against real HMAC/JSON behavior this session), this specific generated-route wiring has NOT been exercised against a real ColdBox boot. There is no "whatsapp-personal" type. The unofficial personal-account bridge (WhatsApp's multi-device Web protocol, the kind Hermes Agent reaches via a Node.js/Baileys subprocess) was researched but deliberately not built - the one MIT-licensed native-Java option (Cobalt, com.github.auties00:cobalt ) turned out to pull in a commercial/proprietary dependency ( com.aspose:aspose-words ) at the version actually published to Maven Central, and a subprocess-bridge port was set aside in favor of a native-JVM approach. Declaring type: "whatsapp-personal" in a gateways/* entry fails validation with an "unknown type" error, same as any other unsupported type.

# WhatsApp Business Cloud

Part of the push-style [gateways/](/conventions/gateways/index.html) family - see there for the shared "secrets stay external" rule, `GatewaySession`, and the scheduler these gateways run under. This page covers WhatsApp Business Cloud's own config shape and (where BxAgents does anything platform-specific) how it talks to WhatsApp Business Cloud.

```javascript
// gateways/whatsappCloud.bx
class {
	function configure() {
		return {
			type               : "whatsapp-cloud",
			accessTokenEnvVar  : "WHATSAPP_ACCESS_TOKEN",     // Graph API access token
			phoneNumberIdEnvVar: "WHATSAPP_PHONE_NUMBER_ID",  // the WhatsApp Business phone number ID sends go through
			appSecretEnvVar    : "WHATSAPP_APP_SECRET",       // HMAC key verifying X-Hub-Signature-256 on inbound webhooks
			verifyTokenEnvVar  : "WHATSAPP_VERIFY_TOKEN"      // shared secret Meta's GET verify handshake must echo back
			// apiVersion: "v21.0"   // optional override - defaults to "v21.0"
		};
	}
}
```

**Validation:** `type: "whatsapp-cloud"` requires `accessTokenEnvVar`, `phoneNumberIdEnvVar`, `appSecretEnvVar`, and `verifyTokenEnvVar`. Checked the same way a channel-adapter `http` entry's `secretEnvVar` is.

Generated registration statement:

```javascript
aiGatewayRegistry().register( aiGateway( "bxModules.bxagents.models.gateways.whatsapp.WhatsAppCloudGateway", { "accessToken" : getSystemSetting( "WHATSAPP_ACCESS_TOKEN", "" ), "phoneNumberId" : getSystemSetting( "WHATSAPP_PHONE_NUMBER_ID", "" ), "appSecret" : getSystemSetting( "WHATSAPP_APP_SECRET", "" ), "verifyToken" : getSystemSetting( "WHATSAPP_VERIFY_TOKEN", "" ) } ) )
```

## WhatsApp Business Cloud API - webhook-driven, not connection-driven

`WhatsAppCloudGateway` is shaped differently from every other push-style gateway: Meta calls **us** , over a public webhook, rather than this gateway holding its own outbound connection (a poll task or a websocket). It extends bx-ai's `BaseGateway` directly, not `ScheduledGatewayBase` - there's no scheduler task or socket to manage, only a generated `handlers/WhatsAppCloud.bx` (written whenever a `whatsapp-cloud` gateway entry exists) wired to two fixed routes:

```javascript
get( "/webhooks/whatsapp-cloud" ).toHandler( "WhatsAppCloud.verify" )
post( "/webhooks/whatsapp-cloud" ).toHandler( "WhatsAppCloud.process" )
```

Both actions are thin passthroughs into the gateway's own `handleVerify()`/`handleWebhook()` - `verify` answers Meta's subscription handshake (`GET ?hub.mode=subscribe&hub.verify_token=...&hub.challenge=...`, echoing the challenge back as plain text only when the mode and token match, constant-time compared); `process` verifies Meta's own `X-Hub-Signature-256` header (HMAC-SHA256 over the **exact raw POST body** - `event.getHTTPContent()`, never re-parsed/re-serialized JSON, which would change the bytes and break the signature) before parsing or dispatching anything. This is a genuinely different scheme from bx-ai's own `HttpGateway`/`GatewaySecurity` (different header names, different HMAC construction), so it isn't reused here - see the class's own docblock.

Ported directly from [Hermes Agent's](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent) own real, production WhatsApp Cloud adapter (`gateway/platforms/whatsapp_cloud.py`, MIT licensed) - the verify handshake, signature scheme, webhook payload walk (`entry[].changes[].value.{messages,contacts}`), outbound message/interactive-button shapes (≤3 allowed decisions render as native buttons, 4+ as a tap-to-open list, matching WhatsApp's own documented limits), and length limits (4096-char messages, 20-char button labels, 1024-char interactive body text) were all read directly from that source this session, not reimplemented from scratch. Inbound messages are deduplicated by their own `wamid` (Meta retries webhook delivery on any non-200 response for up to 7 days) via a bounded FIFO cache, mirroring Hermes's own `_dedup_wamid`.
> **Warning**
>
> v1 scope, matching Hermes's own documented limitation: Cloud API DMs have no separate "chat" entity - `chat_id` IS the sender's `wa_id` - and group messages (which carry their own `chat` field identifying the group JID) are out of scope; a picture or document is read (the media link is fetched with the access token, see [Pictures and files](/conventions/gateways/index.html#pictures-and-files)), but video, audio and stickers aren't downloaded, only a caption if present. Every other push-style gateway shares the same one-instance-per-type registry ceiling documented above - `whatsapp-cloud` is no exception.
> **Info**
>
> The generated `handlers/WhatsAppCloud.bx`'s own ColdBox request-context calls (`event.getHTTPContent()`/`event.getHTTPHeader()`/`event.renderData()`, `rc`'s URL-scope-merged query params for the GET handshake) are the documented, standard ColdBox REST-handler idioms - but unlike the gateway's own signature/dispatch logic (thoroughly unit-tested and empirically verified against real HMAC/JSON behavior this session), this specific generated-route wiring has NOT been exercised against a real ColdBox boot.

**There is no `"whatsapp-personal"` type.** The unofficial personal-account bridge (WhatsApp's multi-device Web protocol, the kind Hermes Agent reaches via a Node.js/Baileys subprocess) was researched but deliberately not built - the one MIT-licensed native-Java option (Cobalt, `com.github.auties00:cobalt`) turned out to pull in a commercial/proprietary dependency (`com.aspose:aspose-words`) at the version actually published to Maven Central, and a subprocess-bridge port was set aside in favor of a native-JVM approach. Declaring `type: "whatsapp-personal"` in a `gateways/*` entry fails validation with an "unknown type" error, same as any other unsupported type.

# Guide: Write Your First Extension

An [extension](/conventions/extensions/index.html) adds to the chat and the app without touching the framework: a command, a key, a status item, a tool, a web page slot. This guide takes one from nothing to something you can share. It needs a project (`bxAgents new` makes one).

## 1. Start it

```bash
bxAgents add extension standup --with=command,key --layout=file --description="Daily standup"
```

That writes `extensions/standup.bx`: one class with a `/standup` command and a key, each with a `TODO` to fill in. Leave `--with` or `--layout` out at a terminal and it asks (what to bring, and one file or a folder). If you tick a scheduler, gateway, tool, skill or web files, it makes a folder (`extensions/standup/Extension.bx` plus those files) instead.

## 2. Try it

```bash
bxAgents chat
```

Type `/extensions` to see it loaded, then `/standup`. A problem in the file shows up there with its reason, so a typo is never silent. From a shell, `bxAgents extensions` prints the same list.

## 3. Change it live

Edit the command in `extensions/standup.bx`, then type `/reload` in the same chat. The change is in, with no restart. `/reload` is for admins; in your own terminal chat you are one. A setting goes in `configure()`:

```boxlang
function configure() {
	variables.settings = { greeting : "Good morning" }
}
```

Read it in the command as `settings.greeting`. `Agent.yaml` (or your own `~/.bxagents/bxAgents.yml`) can change it without touching the code:

```yaml
extensions:
  standup:
    greeting: "Hello team"
```

## 4. Use it in every project

An extension in the project's `extensions/` belongs to that project and goes into its built app. To have one in your own terminal chat everywhere, link it:

```bash
bxAgents extensions link ./extensions/standup.bx
```

It now loads from where you edit it, in every chat on this machine, and `/reload` picks up a change.

## 5. Share it

An extension is a folder or a file, so sharing is giving someone that:

* zip the folder, or push it to a GitHub repository;
* they run `bxAgents extensions install ./standup.zip`, or `bxAgents extensions install you/standup`.

They see what it adds and what its code mentions, and say yes before anything is placed. The install is recorded in `extensions.lock.json`, which they commit; the extension itself is restored from it at build time.

## Where next

* [Extensions](/conventions/extensions/index.html) lists everything an extension can bring, with the exact shape of each.
* [`examples/extensions-agent`](https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/bx-agents/tree/development/examples/extensions-agent) has a working extension of each kind.

# Installation

BxAgents is a BoxLang module. It needs two things on the machine that runs it:

1. A [BoxLang](https://www.boxlang.io) runtime.
2. BxAgents itself. It bundles everything else it needs: `bx-ai`, `bx-sqlite`, `bx-ftp`, `bx-mail`, `bx-yaml` and `bx-markdown` as nested BoxLang modules, plus ColdBox, `qb`, `cbsecurity`, `cbauth` and `cbmailservices` for the apps it generates. There is nothing else to install.

> **Info**
>
> BxAgents needs BoxLang **1.18.0 or later**, which supports the nested modules it bundles.
> **Info**
>
> `serve`, `chat --server` and `invoke --server` additionally need the standalone [`boxlang-miniserver`](https://boxlang.ortusbooks.com/getting-started/running-boxlang/miniserver) binary on `PATH`. Every other verb (`build`, plain `chat` and `invoke`, `package`, `inspect`, `clean`, `new`, ...) doesn't.

1

Install BoxLang

Follow the [official BoxLang installation guide](https://boxlang.ortusbooks.com/getting-started/installation). The quick installer also sets up `~/.boxlang/bin` on your `PATH`, which is where module-provided executables (like BxAgents' own `bxAgents` command, below) land.

2

Install BxAgents

```bash
install-bx-module bx-agents
```

This fetches the module, with its bundled dependencies, into your BoxLang modules directory (`~/.boxlang/modules` by default, or `boxlang_modules/` with `--local`).

3

Verify it worked

```bash
bxAgents --version
bxAgents --help
```

`--help` lists all 20 verbs (`new`, `add`, `build`, `test`, `serve`, `chat`, `invoke`, `package`, `deploy`, `inspect`, `clean`, `hash-password`, `token`, `notes`, `models`, `sessions`, `stats`, `doctor`, `skills`, `extensions`) with a one-line summary of each.

## The `bxAgents` command

BxAgents declares a native executable in its `box.json`:

```json
"boxlang": { "moduleName": "bxagents", "executable": "bxAgents" }
```

The installer turns that into a `bxAgents` wrapper script on your `PATH`, so you can run:

```bash
bxAgents new my-agent --model=openai/gpt-5
```

instead of the longer form:

```bash
boxlang module:bxagents new my-agent --model=openai/gpt-5
```

Both are equivalent - every verb dispatches through the same `ModuleConfig.bx main(args)` entry point either way. This doc uses the short `bxAgents <verb>` form throughout.

## What is bundled

The module zip carries its own dependencies, pinned to the stable releases it was built with. A bug fix in one of them ships as a BxAgents patch release, so nobody installs or updates them by hand.

|                Where                |                                                       What                                                        |                                                                       Used for                                                                       |
|-------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `modules/` (nested BoxLang modules) | `bx-ai` 3.7.0-snapshot, `bx-sqlite` 1.3.0, `bx-ftp` 1.9.0, `bx-mail` 1.4.15, `bx-yaml` 1.1.0, `bx-markdown` 1.1.0 | The agent runtime, the web UI's SQLite store, the `ftp`/`sftp` deploy targets, the email gateway, `Agent.yaml`, the HTML of an exported conversation |
| `lib/` (ColdBox runtime)            | ColdBox, `qb`, `cbsecurity`, `cbauth`, `cbmailservices`                                                           | Copied into every app `build` generates                                                                                                              |

`serve` points the served app at the same bundled modules. The versions above are the ones pinned in the repository's `gradle.properties` for this release.

### Adding your own libraries

Put extra ColdBox libraries in a `lib/` folder in your project, using the same layout as the bundled one:

```text
my-agent/
  lib/
    coldbox/          # replaces the bundled ColdBox
    modules/
      cbvalidation/   # added next to the bundled modules
      qb/             # replaces the bundled qb
```

`build` copies the bundled set first and your `lib/` second, so yours wins.

## Tab completion

The module ships tab completion for `bxAgents` (and `bxagents`) in three shells. It completes verbs, flags, the `--template` and `--target` values, and project folders.

|   Shell    |                                                                                                     Setup                                                                                                     |
|------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| bash, zsh  | Automatic. `install-bx-module` copies `completions/bxAgents.bash` to `~/.boxlang/completions/` and BVM sources it in new sessions. Without the installer: `source <module folder>/completions/bxAgents.bash`. |
| fish       | `cp <module folder>/completions/bxAgents.fish ~/.config/fish/completions/`                                                                                                                                    |
| PowerShell | Add `. "<module folder>\completions\bxAgents.ps1"` to your `$PROFILE`.                                                                                                                                        |

The scripts in `completions/` are generated from the CLI's own verb tables, so they cannot drift from the verbs. After changing a verb or a flag in `ModuleConfig.bx`, regenerate them with `tools/generate-completions.bxs` (add `--check` to only verify); the spec suite fails if they are stale.

See [Quick Start](/getting-started/quick-start/index.html) to scaffold your first agent.

# interceptors/

`interceptors/*.bx` are ColdBox interceptors (lifecycle hook classes - `preProcess`, `postProcess`, etc.), scoped via an `@scope` annotation on the class itself:

```javascript
// interceptors/AuditLogger.bx
/**
 * @scope agent
 */
class {

	function preProcess( event, interceptData ) {
		// ...
	}

}
```

> **Tip**
>
> `bxAgents add interceptor` scaffolds one: pick the scope and the interception points and it writes `interceptors/<Name>.bx` with a method for each. See [`add`](/cli-reference/index.html#add-interceptor).

## `agent` vs `runtime` scope

|       Scope       |                                                                                                      Effect                                                                                                       |
|-------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `agent` (default) | Copied into the generated app's own `interceptors/` folder and registered with ColdBox when the app starts - affects only this app.                                                                               |
| `runtime`         | Copied separately to `.build/runtime-interceptors` (not into the generated app), for the way a BoxLang module registers its own interceptors. BxAgents does not register them for you: loading them is up to you. |

An interceptor with **no** `@scope` annotation at all defaults to `agent` - the narrower, safer default, since `runtime` scope has effects beyond this one app.

An `@scope` value that isn't `agent` or `runtime` (case-insensitive) fails the build with a clear error - there's no silent fallback for a typo'd scope.

## Generated wiring

For each `agent`-scope interceptor, the generated base `Application` ([`bxagents/Application.bx`](/conventions/application-bx/index.html)) registers an instance with ColdBox's interceptor service from `onApplicationStart()`:

```javascript
application.cbController.getInterceptorService().register(
	target: application.cbController.getWireBox().getInstance( "interceptors.AuditLogger" ),
	name: "AuditLogger"
)
```

Every agent-scope interceptor is registered exactly once. The generated `config/ColdBox.bx` has no `interceptors` array: a declarative array there never reaches ColdBox's interceptor service on the stack BxAgents generates for, so the registration happens at startup instead.

title: Introduction to BxAgents
body: Introduction to BxAgents Twenty lessons, start to finish: install the CLI, scaffold a project, understand Agent.yaml , wire up tools, skills and subagents, expose your agent over HTTP and to chat platforms, ship the generated web UI, schedule background work, test it for real, and package + deploy it. # Packaging Skills

Where `tools/` gives your agent a single callable function, `skills/` gives it a
packaged, freeform capability - instructions the agent loads on demand rather than a
function it calls directly.

Each immediate subfolder of `skills/` that contains a `SKILL.md` file is one skill,
following the [Claude Agent Skills](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/claude-skills)
convention: YAML frontmatter (`name`, `description`) followed by a body of freeform
instructions.

    skills/
    └── greeting/
        └── SKILL.md

```markdown
---
name: greeting
description: How to greet people warmly.
---

Always greet the user warmly and use their name if known.
```

## Naming

The skill's name is its frontmatter `name:` if present; otherwise it falls back to the
folder name. An explicit `name:` always wins even if it differs from the folder. Two
skills resolving to the same name fail validation with a duplicate-name error.

A folder without a `SKILL.md` inside it isn't discovered as a skill at all - it's
simply ignored, which is handy for scratch subfolders or assets kept alongside a skill
under a different structure.

## Starting one, and installing one

`bxAgents add skill code-review` writes `skills/code-review/SKILL.md` with the frontmatter and
a body to fill in. Skills other people published are installed from skills.boxlang.io:

```bash
bxAgents skills find review
bxAgents skills install <owner/repo/skill>
bxAgents skills list
```

Installed skills go into `.agents/skills/` (kept out of source control) and are recorded in
`.agents/skills.lock.json`, which you commit; `build` restores whatever the lock lists and the
disk lacks. Skills in `skills/` and installed ones both go into the build, and one of your own
with the same name wins. `skills update` and `skills remove` do what they say.

## How it's wired at runtime

`skills/` is copied verbatim into the generated app, the same wipe-then-write,
dotfile-excluding copy as `tools/`. The generated `config/ColdBox.bx` always points
bx-ai's own `skillsDirectory` module setting at `/skills` - you never need to set this
yourself, even though bx-ai's own default is a different path (`/.agents/skills`).

## Tools vs. skills - when to reach for which

Use a **tool** when the agent needs to call a specific function with specific
arguments and get a specific return value back (get the weather, look up an order).
Use a **skill** when you want to hand the agent a body of know-how it applies
judgment to (how to write a professional email, how your team formats commit
messages, how to review a pull request against your team's checklist).

## Try it

    skills/
    └── code-review/
        └── SKILL.md

```markdown
---
name: code-review
description: How to review a code change for this project.
---

When asked to review code, check for: unhandled errors, missing tests for new
behavior, and inconsistent naming with the surrounding file. Be specific - point to
the exact line and explain the risk, don't just say "looks fine" or "consider
improving this."
```

Rebuild and try asking your agent to review a snippet of code. (Or scaffold the file with
`bxAgents add skill code-review`.)

Full reference: [skills/](/conventions/skills/index.html).

Next: [Lesson 11 - Composing Subagents](/course/11-composing-subagents/index.html)
headings: Tools vs. skills - when to reach for which

title: Lesson 11: Composing Subagents
body:
Composing Subagents subagents/ holds nested agents - each an ordinary BxAgents project of its own, with its own Agent.yaml + instructions.md , and optionally its own tools/ , skills/ , etc. my-agent/ ├── Agent.yaml # subAgents: [ researcher ] ├── instructions.md └── subagents/ └── researcher/ ├── Agent.yaml └── instructions.md A subagent is wired to its parent by name, declared in the parent's Agent.yaml this is the subagents/ folder name : subAgents: [ researcher ] At build time, bx-ai's addSubAgent() wraps each built subagent instance as a callable tool on the parent automatically - there's no separate tool-wrapping step to write yourself. Flat on disk, a graph in config Every subagent - no matter how deeply another subagent's own config references it - lives directly under the root project's subagents/ folder. A subagent's own declared subAgents names reference sibling entries in that same root-level folder, never a folder nested under itself. flowchart LR subgraph disk["ON DISK - always flat"] direction TB R1["subagents/A/"] R2["subagents/B/"] R3["subagents/C/"] end subgraph declared["DECLARED - each agent definition's own subAgents list"] direction TB GA["A"] --> GB["B"] --> GC["C"] end subgraph built["BUILT - leaf-first"] direction TB O1["1. build C"] --> O2["2. build B
with the built C"] --> O3["3. build A
with the built B"] end disk -.-> declared declared -.-> built A cycle in the declared graph ( A -> B -> A ) is rejected at validation, before anything is generated. A diamond (two parents sharing one descendant) is fine. Two different names, two different jobs The folder name under subagents/ is what subAgents: [ "..." ] references - purely a build-time wiring concern. The subagent's own declared name (its definition's name field) is what you retrieve it by at runtime - every agent in the tree is registered in config/WireBox.bx under this name, so a schedules/ scheduler (or anything else WireBox-aware) reaches it with getInstance( "TheAgentName" ) . These two names can differ, and often will. Because name is now also a WireBox binding key, it must be unique across the whole project - build fails validation if two agents share one. Try it Scaffold a subagents/researcher/ folder as its own small BxAgents project (its own Agent.yaml + instructions.md ), then wire it into your root Agent.yaml 's subAgents list. Rebuild and ask your root agent something that would naturally delegate to the researcher subagent - it's callable exactly like any other tool. Full reference: subagents/ . Next: Lesson 12 - Models and Profiles

# Models and Profiles

You already pick a model with a slug, `model: openai/gpt-5` ([Lesson 5](/course/05-agent-bx/index.html)). When you want more than one model in the same project, you name them: a **profile** is a provider, a model and a few settings under a name such as `fast` or `planner`. Everything lives in `Agent.yaml`; you never write a `boxlang.json`.

```yaml
provider: openai
model: gpt-5
params: { temperature: 0.2 }

profiles:
  fast:    { description: Cheap and quick, provider: openai, model: gpt-5-mini, params: { temperature: 0 } }
  planner: { description: Careful planning, provider: claude, model: claude-opus-4, apiKeyEnv: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }
```

A subagent picks one with `profile:`; an agent that says nothing uses the default. A profile cannot be named `default` or like a provider, and a key is never written in the file: `apiKeyEnv` names the environment variable that holds it.

`defaultProfile: fast` makes a profile the default model (when a top-level `model` is written beside it, the profile wins and `build` and `doctor` warn that the model is ignored). `bxAgents add profile` and `add provider` write these blocks for you, with an empty key stub in `.env`.

## What the project can say about a model

`contextWindow` and `vision` on the default model and on each profile say what the model can hold and whether it can see images. Both are optional and nothing is guessed. `/info`, `/model` and the context size in the chat show them, and a picture sent to a profile with `vision: false` is refused with that reason.

## Using and testing profiles

* In the terminal chat, `/model` shows the model, `/profile` picks a profile from a list (or `/profile fast`) and `/default` goes back. The conversation, memory and tools stay.
* A web chat entry or an agent API that lists `profiles` offers them as a picker. Only the listed ones can be chosen, and the page never sees a key.
* `bxAgents models list` shows what the project can talk to, and `bxAgents models test --all` sends each model one tiny question and says whether it answered and how long it took. In the chat, `/ping` does the same.
* Set `usage: true` in `Agent.yaml` and `bxAgents stats` (or `/stats`) shows what the model calls used, by model, provider, day or user. It keeps counts only.

## Why bother

A slug is enough for most agents. Reach for profiles when several agents share a configuration (a cheaper model your routing subagents use), or when a model needs settings you do not want to repeat.

## Try it

Add a `fast` profile that points at a smaller model than your root agent's default, then give a subagent `profile: fast`, a natural fit for the researcher from [Lesson 11](/course/11-composing-subagents/index.html). Run `bxAgents inspect --section=ai` to see the default, the providers and the profiles, and which variable each key comes from.

Full reference: [Models and profiles](/conventions/models/index.html).

Next: [Lesson 13 - Exposing Your Agent over HTTP and MCP](/course/13-exposing-http-and-mcp/index.html)
headings: What the project can say about a model

title: Lesson 13: Exposing Your Agent over HTTP and MCP
body:
Exposing Your Agent over HTTP and MCP gateways/*.bx files cover two distinct, unrelated things - which kind an entry is depends entirely on whether its configure() struct has an exposes key. This lesson covers exposure ( exposes: "agent" | "mcp" | "webui" ); the next lesson covers the other kind, channel adapters that connect to chat platforms. flowchart TD F["a file under gateways/"] --> Q{"does configure() return
an 'exposes' key?"} Q -->|"yes"| E["EXPOSURE
a route into your agent"] Q -->|"no - it has 'type' instead"| C["CHANNEL ADAPTER
Lesson 14"] style E fill:#d4edda,stroke:#155724 Exposing the agent itself // gateways/expose.bx class { function configure() { return { exposes : "agent", path : "/api/chat" }; } } Generates, in config/Router.bx , four routes served by the agent API's handler: POST /api/chat/invoke , POST /api/chat/stream (SSE), POST /api/chat/batch , GET /api/chat/info . The bare /api/chat path itself is not routable. This is a plain entry point under a path of your choosing; with agentApi.access: token it needs a token like the rest of the agent API. Exposing a local MCP server class { function configure() { return { exposes : "mcp", path : "/mcp/tools", target : "local-server" // must match an mcp/*.bx entry's file name }; } } You'll write that mcp/*.bx entry in Lesson 17 . Exposing the web chat UI // gateways/chat.bx class { function configure() { return { exposes : "webui", path : "/chat" }; } } This one is big enough to earn its own lesson - see Lesson 15 . The agent API that is always there Every built agent also serves one HTTP API at /__bxagents , with no gateways/ entry at all. The web page, the terminal chat ( chat --server and --connect ) and the chat platforms use it too, so anything they do, your program can do: run a turn ( invoke , stream , events ), stop or steer a run, answer an approval, list and fork conversations, keep notes, run slash commands. It describes itself: GET /__bxagents/openapi returns an OpenAPI document of the routes your server really has. A BoxLang client, bxModules.bxagents.models.api.AgentApiClient , has one method per route. The tour, with curl and BoxLang examples, is in Call your agent from code . Who may call it is set under agentApi in Agent.yaml : Open (the default): anyone who can reach the port, all as one user, local . Fine on your own machine. bxAgents serve listens on 127.0.0.1 by default and warns if an open API listens on an address other machines can reach. Behind tokens : callers send an x-bxagents-token header. tokenEnvVar: MY_SECRET names an environment variable holding one shared secret (it acts as an admin). tokens: true also accepts tokens made per person or program with bxAgents token create --name=laptop ( --scope=chat or admin , --expires=90d ). A token is shown once and only a hash is kept, so token revoke works at once on a running server. Guards : allowedIPs lets only listed addresses and networks in at all, and rateLimit: { requests, perSeconds } caps calls per address. Both work open or closed. Managing tokens over the API : manageTokens: true (with tokens: true ) lets an admin make and revoke tokens remotely, and shows a Tokens panel in the web page. Moving it : path: /agent-api serves the whole API somewhere else. agentApi: tokenEnvVar: AGENT_ADMIN_TOKEN # the NAME of an environment variable tokens: true allowedIPs: [ "10.0.0.0/8" ] rateLimit: { requests: 60, perSeconds: 60 } bxAgents token create --name=laptop --expires=90d bxAgents chat --connect=https://agent.example.com --token= Full list of settings: Agent.bx . Validation exposes must be agent , mcp , or webui ; path is required and must be unique across every exposure entry; an mcp exposure's target must match a real mcp/* entry's file name. Try it bxAgents build bxAgents serve --port=8080 curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/chat/invoke \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"input":"Hi there"}' (Or skip serve entirely and reach for bxAgents invoke --message="Hi there" --server from Lesson 8 , which exercises this exact route without you having to manage the server process yourself.) Full reference: gateways/ . Next: Lesson 14 - Connecting Chat Platforms

# Exposing Your Agent over HTTP and MCP `gateways/*.bx` files cover two distinct, unrelated things - which kind an entry is depends entirely on whether its `configure()` struct has an `exposes` key. This lesson covers **exposure** (`exposes: "agent" | "mcp" | "webui"`); the next lesson covers the other kind, channel adapters that connect to chat platforms. ```mermaid flowchart TD F["a file under gateways/"] --> Q{"does configure() return
an 'exposes' key?"} Q -->|"yes"| E["EXPOSURE
a route into your agent"] Q -->|"no - it has 'type' instead"| C["CHANNEL ADAPTER
Lesson 14"] style E fill:#d4edda,stroke:#155724 ``` ## Exposing the agent itself ```javascript // gateways/expose.bx class { function configure() { return { exposes : "agent", path : "/api/chat" }; } } ``` Generates, in `config/Router.bx`, four routes served by the agent API's handler: `POST /api/chat/invoke`, `POST /api/chat/stream` (SSE), `POST /api/chat/batch`, `GET /api/chat/info`. The bare `/api/chat` path itself is not routable. This is a plain entry point under a path of your choosing; with `agentApi.access: token` it needs a token like the rest of the agent API. ## Exposing a local MCP server ```javascript class { function configure() { return { exposes : "mcp", path : "/mcp/tools", target : "local-server" // must match an mcp/*.bx entry's file name }; } } ``` You'll write that `mcp/*.bx` entry in [Lesson 17](/course/17-hosting-mcp-servers/index.html). ## Exposing the web chat UI ```javascript // gateways/chat.bx class { function configure() { return { exposes : "webui", path : "/chat" }; } } ``` This one is big enough to earn its own lesson - see [Lesson 15](/course/15-the-generated-web-chat-ui/index.html). ## The agent API that is always there Every built agent also serves one HTTP API at `/__bxagents`, with no `gateways/` entry at all. The web page, the terminal chat (`chat --server` and `--connect`) and the chat platforms use it too, so anything they do, your program can do: run a turn (`invoke`, `stream`, `events`), stop or steer a run, answer an approval, list and fork conversations, keep notes, run slash commands. It describes itself: `GET /__bxagents/openapi` returns an OpenAPI document of the routes your server really has. A BoxLang client, `bxModules.bxagents.models.api.AgentApiClient`, has one method per route. The tour, with curl and BoxLang examples, is in [Call your agent from code](/guides/agent-api/index.html). Who may call it is set under `agentApi` in `Agent.yaml`: * **Open** (the default): anyone who can reach the port, all as one user, `local`. Fine on your own machine. `bxAgents serve` listens on `127.0.0.1` by default and warns if an open API listens on an address other machines can reach. * **Behind tokens** : callers send an `x-bxagents-token` header. `tokenEnvVar: MY_SECRET` names an environment variable holding one shared secret (it acts as an admin). `tokens: true` also accepts tokens made per person or program with `bxAgents token create --name=laptop` (`--scope=chat` or `admin`, `--expires=90d`). A token is shown once and only a hash is kept, so `token revoke` works at once on a running server. * **Guards** : `allowedIPs` lets only listed addresses and networks in at all, and `rateLimit: { requests, perSeconds }` caps calls per address. Both work open or closed. * **Managing tokens over the API** : `manageTokens: true` (with `tokens: true`) lets an admin make and revoke tokens remotely, and shows a **Tokens** panel in the web page. * **Moving it** : `path: /agent-api` serves the whole API somewhere else. ```yaml agentApi: tokenEnvVar: AGENT_ADMIN_TOKEN # the NAME of an environment variable tokens: true allowedIPs: [ "10.0.0.0/8" ] rateLimit: { requests: 60, perSeconds: 60 } ``` ```bash bxAgents token create --name=laptop --expires=90d bxAgents chat --connect=https://agent.example.com --token= ``` Full list of settings: [Agent.bx](/conventions/agent-bx/index.html#the-always-on-agent-route). ## Validation `exposes` must be `agent`, `mcp`, or `webui`; `path` is required and must be unique across every exposure entry; an `mcp` exposure's `target` must match a real `mcp/*` entry's file name. ## Try it ```bash bxAgents build bxAgents serve --port=8080 curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/chat/invoke \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"input":"Hi there"}' ``` (Or skip `serve` entirely and reach for `bxAgents invoke --message="Hi there" --server` from [Lesson 8](/course/08-talking-to-your-agent/index.html), which exercises this exact route without you having to manage the server process yourself.) Full reference: [gateways/](/conventions/gateways/index.html). Next: [Lesson 14 - Connecting Chat Platforms](/course/14-connecting-chat-platforms/index.html)

body:
Connecting Chat Platforms The other kind of gateways/* entry - one with a type key instead of exposes - registers a bx-ai IGateway , a channel adapter for external delivery or human-in-the-loop approval. This is a real "chat bot" connection, distinct from the REST exposure you built in Lesson 13 . Two request-driven types: mock and cli mock is test-only. cli is bx-ai's own built-in human-in-the-loop approval channel - a blocking stdin/stdout prompt, and what HumanInTheLoopMiddleware attaches by default when no gateway is specified. http - your own webhook endpoint // gateways/slack.bx class { function configure() { return { type : "http", secretEnvVar : "SLACK_WEBHOOK_SECRET" }; } } secretEnvVar names an environment variable holding the signing secret - never the secret value itself . It's resolved live at server startup, so it's never present in generated source or a packaged .bxa either. This gets real routes, from a single route( "/gateways" ).toAiGateway() in the generated router: POST /gateways/:gateway/events , GET /gateways/:gateway/events (the platform's URL verification handshake), GET /gateways/interactions/:requestID , and POST /gateways/interactions/:requestID/decisions . Nine push-style platforms Telegram, Slack, Discord, Email, WhatsApp Business Cloud, Microsoft Teams, Twilio SMS, GitHub, and Signal each hold their own connection (long-poll, websocket, webhook, or SSE) and push inbound messages to your agent as they arrive: // gateways/telegramChannel.bx class { function configure() { return { type : "telegram", botTokenEnvVar: "TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN" }; } } Every platform follows the same secrets stay external rule - every *EnvVar key names an environment variable, resolved live, never a literal in generated code. One GatewaySession ties them together Any project with at least one push-style gateway gets a generated start-up statement in the generated base Application that builds a single bx-ai GatewaySession bundling every push-style gateway, bound to your project's root agent: flowchart TD M["a message arrives on thread T"] --> B{"is a run already
in flight on T?"} B -->|"no"| D["dispatch a new turn"] B -->|"yes"| P{"policy"} P -->|"reject"| R["Immediate 'busy' reply"] P -->|"queue (default)"| Q["Enqueue, runs after the current turn"] P -->|"steer"| ST["Spliced into the SAME run"] P -->|"interrupt"| I["Cancel current turn, then run this one"] style D fill:#d4edda,stroke:#155724 style R fill:#f8d7da,stroke:#721c24 Control the policy from Agent.yaml : gatewaySession: policy: queue # both optional, these are the defaults maxQueueDepth: 50 Warning v1 limitation: exactly one GatewaySession , always bound to the project's root agent - a project with subagents can't yet route different gateways to different subagents. Every person has their own conversation The agent is told who is writing (the platform and their id there, such as slack:U123 ) and which conversation it is: the chat, plus its thread when the platform has them (a Telegram forum topic, a Slack thread). So memory, /notes , /remember and the conversation list are kept apart per person and per thread. Two people in one channel do not share a memory, and neither do two chats on two platforms. The list is stored in the same data/chat.db the web page uses, marked with the platform it started on; an admin can see it with GET /__bxagents/sessions?all=1 . Commands in a chat A message that is a slash command is answered by BxAgents and never reaches the model. A safe set is on by default: /help , /tools , /model , /info , /ping , /remember , /notes and /connect . The conversation commands ( /new , /clear , /compact , /sessions , /resume ) are off, because most chats are one long conversation; turn them on with conversation: true . Each platform shows the commands its own way (Telegram's / menu, Discord application commands, Slack slash commands, buttons on WhatsApp, a numbered list on SMS). gatewaySession: commands: conversation: true # also /new, /clear, /compact, /sessions, /resume prefixes: { slack: "!" } # a different one-character prefix for one gateway Pictures and text files sent on Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp and Twilio MMS reach the agent with the message ( gatewaySession.attachments: false switches that off). Adding a platform, or your own bxAgents add gateway adds a platform the way the new wizard does: it writes the gateways/ file, an empty .env line for each credential and the setup steps that happen outside the project (a bot token, a public address). bxAgents doctor reports credentials that are still not set. If a platform is not in the list, an extension can bring a new gateway type. Try it If you have a disposable Telegram bot token, add a gateways/telegramChannel.bx entry, export TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN , and bxAgents serve - message your bot and watch it reply. No token handy? Read through a couple of the platform sections in the full reference below; the shape is consistent across all nine. Full reference: gateways/ . Next: Lesson 15 - The Generated Web Chat UI

# The Generated Web Chat UI

A `gateways/*.bx` entry with `exposes: "webui"` ships a complete browser chat client
for your agent - a conversation sidebar, streaming with reasoning and tool calls,
human-in-the-loop approvals, per-visitor theming, and a real SQLite store behind it.

```javascript
// gateways/chat.bx
class {
	function configure() {
		return {
			exposes     : "webui",
			path        : "/chat",
			apiKeyEnvVar: "CHAT_UI_API_KEY"   // optional - see "Securing it" below
		};
	}
}
```

This generates a static `<path>/index.html` (served directly, no route needed) that calls the agent API
at `/__bxagents`. The page is dependency-free vanilla HTML/CSS/JS,
pre-built and vendored inside BxAgents itself - `bxAgents build` never runs `npm install`, and a generated project never needs Node installed at all.

![The generated web chat UI, branded and populated with an example conversation](/assets/webui-chat-light.png)

That's the real, unmodified generated page - this one branded with
[`examples/webui-agent`](https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/bx-agents/tree/development/examples/webui-agent)'s
`theme`/`title`/`icon` config from [Lesson 13](/course/13-exposing-http-and-mcp/index.html)'s exposure
concept, taken further. `bxAgents build && bxAgents serve` in that example gets you the
same page for real.

## What the page can do

* **Conversation sidebar** - switch, rename, delete, or start a new conversation.
* **Steer while streaming** - the composer stays live during a turn; **Send** becomes **Steer**, splicing your message into the run already in flight.
* **Stop** - posts `/cancel` before aborting, so the server actually stops spending tokens rather than just abandoning the browser connection.
* **Reasoning + tool calls** - collapsed disclosures fed straight off the streamed response.
* **Approvals** - a human-in-the-loop pause renders an Approve/Reject card.
* **Rendered answers** - full Markdown, with code blocks that show their language and have a **Copy** button, and tool cards with a status chip and a one-line preview of the arguments.
* **Slash commands** - type `/` for a menu (or press the lightning button): `/new`, `/sessions`, `/fork`, `/export`, `/context` and more, the same ones as in the terminal. Commands an [extension](/course/18-interceptors-and-modules/index.html) adds show the extension's name as a badge.
* **Suggestions** - set up to four `suggestions` on the entry and the empty conversation shows them as buttons that send on one click.
* **Pictures** - an Attach button, paste and drop send pictures with a message (refused when the model's profile says `vision: false`).
* **Context ring** - the header shows how much of the model's window is used; click it for the breakdown.
* **Model picker** - when the entry lists `profiles`, visitors can choose one per message.

### The Settings menu

The header keeps only what you use every minute: the **Chats** button, the context ring, the model
picker and a **Settings** gear. The gear opens one menu in three groups. An item the server does
not offer, and a group with nothing in it, is left out.

|    Group     |                                             Items                                              |
|--------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Conversation | Fork this conversation, Export as Markdown, Clear messages, Compact older messages             |
| You          | Notes (what the agent keeps about you and about its own work), Appearance, light or dark theme |
| Server       | Password, Access tokens                                                                        |

**Appearance** lets each visitor pick light, dark or system, an accent color, the text size and the
density, saved in their own browser. It never changes your `theme`, which stays the default.
**Access tokens** lists, creates and revokes tokens for admins, when the server sets
`agentApi.manageTokens: true` ([Lesson 13](/course/13-exposing-http-and-mcp/index.html)).

## Without accounts: one shared workspace

By default the UI has **no accounts and no gate** - every visitor is anonymous, and
every visitor reads and writes the **same** conversations, preferences and agent
memory. This is the zero-ceremony local-dev experience, not a deployment posture.
> **Warning**
>
> An open UI has no privacy between visitors. Declare `users` if the page is
> reachable by more than the people who should see the transcripts.

```javascript
users : [
    { username: "ada", passwordEnvVar: "ACME_ADA_PASSWORD", displayName: "Ada Lovelace" }
]
```

An account names the **environment variable** holding its password, or carries an
already-hashed value - a literal `password` key is a build error, not a warning.
Generate a hash with:

```bash
bxAgents hash-password --password="<your-password>"
```

## Branding it

Every key is optional:

```javascript
theme: {
	accent : "0f766e",
	radius : "10px",
	font   : "Inter, system-ui, sans-serif",
	dark   : { accent : "rgb(45, 212, 191)" }
}
```

> **Info**
>
> Write hex colors bare, with no leading `#` - BoxLang begins string interpolation
> at `#` in both quote styles, so the generator adds it back for you.

`title`, `subtitle`, `icon`, `welcome`, `placeholder`, `footer` and `suggestions` are also
available, plus a `themeFile` for anything the tokens don't cover. `icon` can be an emoji, an
image address or `phosphor:<name>` (a Phosphor icon built into the page).

## Securing it

`apiKeyEnvVar` is the agent API's shared secret - not a full login system. Left unset,
the API is open (fine for local dev). Set it, and every call to `/__bxagents` must carry
a matching `x-bxagents-token` header. The static shell itself is deliberately **not**
gated, since a browser's plain page navigation can't send a custom header: the page asks for the
secret in a **Password** form that opens by itself when the server answers `401`, and says when
the password was not accepted. For several people, use issued tokens or list `users`
([Lesson 13](/course/13-exposing-http-and-mcp/index.html) covers tokens, `allowedIPs` and `rateLimit`).

## Try it

```bash
bxAgents build
bxAgents serve --port=8080
```

Open `http://localhost:8080/chat` in a browser and talk to your agent - the same one
you've been building tools, skills and subagents onto since [Lesson 9](/course/09-giving-your-agent-tools/index.html).

Full reference: [The web chat UI](/conventions/web-ui/index.html).

Next: [Lesson 16 - Scheduling Background Work](/course/16-scheduling-background-work/index.html)

title: Lesson 16: Scheduling Background Work
body: Scheduling Background Work Every schedules/*.bx is a BoxLang scheduler : a plain class whose configure() builds tasks. There is no ColdBox in it and nothing to extend - the build adds the base class that gives it task() , run() and agent() . // schedules/Nightly.bx class { function configure() { task( "nightly" ) .cron( "0 0 * * *" ) .call( () => run( "cleanup" ) ) .withNoOverlaps() } } .cron() takes five fields ( minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week ) or six, with seconds in front. BoxLang's other task methods work too: .every( 15, "minutes" ) , .everyDayAt( "09:00" ) , .onWeekdays( "08:30" ) , .startOn() / .endOn() , .when() , .withNoOverlaps() , lifecycle hooks, timezones. Retrieving your agent run( ... ) sends a message to the default agent , the root agent your Agent.yaml defines. agent( "TheAgentName" ) gets any other agent in the tree by the name its definition declares (see Lesson 11 ): task( "weekly-digest" ) .cron( "0 8 * * MON" ) .call( () => agent( "ResearchBot" ).run( "summarize this week's findings" ) ) Many schedulers Each file is its own scheduler, so group tasks however you like: one file per job, or related tasks together. BoxLang starts them with the app and stops them with it, so they run while the app is served. Validation build checks that each file name is a valid class name ( MyJob.bx , not my-job.bx ), that a scheduler does not extend ColdBox's scheduler any more, and warns about a file in schedules/ that is not a .bx file. The body is real code: a syntax error or a bad agent name surfaces when the app starts ( serve ), not at build . Try it bxAgents add schedule --when="weekdays 08:30" --prompt="Summarize yesterday's findings" bxAgents build --verbose bxAgents inspect --section=schedule add schedule writes schedules/<Name>.bx ; inspect lists each scheduler with its tasks, cron and agent. Full reference: schedules/ . Next: Lesson 17 - Hosting and Consuming MCP Servers
markdown:
# Scheduling Background Work

Every `schedules/*.bx` is a **BoxLang scheduler** : a plain class whose `configure()`
builds tasks. There is no ColdBox in it and nothing to extend - the build adds the
base class that gives it `task()`, `run()` and `agent()`.

```javascript
// schedules/Nightly.bx
class {

	function configure() {
		task( "nightly" )
			.cron( "0 0 * * *" )
			.call( () => run( "cleanup" ) )
			.withNoOverlaps()
	}

}
```

`.cron()` takes five fields (`minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week`) or six, with
seconds in front. BoxLang's other task methods work too: `.every( 15, "minutes" )`,
`.everyDayAt( "09:00" )`, `.onWeekdays( "08:30" )`, `.startOn()`/`.endOn()`, `.when()`,
`.withNoOverlaps()`, lifecycle hooks, timezones.

## Retrieving your agent

`run( ... )` sends a message to the **default agent** , the root agent your
`Agent.yaml` defines. `agent( "TheAgentName" )` gets any other agent in the tree by the
`name` its definition declares (see [Lesson 11](/course/11-composing-subagents/index.html)):

```javascript
task( "weekly-digest" )
	.cron( "0 8 * * MON" )
	.call( () => agent( "ResearchBot" ).run( "summarize this week's findings" ) )
```

## Many schedulers

Each file is its own scheduler, so group tasks however you like: one file per job, or
related tasks together. BoxLang starts them with the app and stops them with it, so they
run while the app is served.

## Validation

`build` checks that each file name is a valid class name (`MyJob.bx`, not `my-job.bx`),
that a scheduler does not extend ColdBox's scheduler any more, and warns about a file in
`schedules/` that is not a `.bx` file. The body is real code: a syntax error or a bad
agent name surfaces when the app starts (`serve`), not at `build`.

## Try it

```bash
bxAgents add schedule --when="weekdays 08:30" --prompt="Summarize yesterday's findings"
bxAgents build --verbose
bxAgents inspect --section=schedule
```

`add schedule` writes `schedules/<Name>.bx`; `inspect` lists each scheduler with its
tasks, cron and agent.

Full reference: [schedules/](/conventions/schedules/index.html).

# Hosting and Consuming MCP Servers

Model Context Protocol (MCP) works in two directions in a BxAgents project, and
nothing links them - an agent consuming remote servers need not host one, and a hosted
server is only reachable if a `gateways/` entry exposes it (see
[Lesson 13](/course/13-exposing-http-and-mcp/index.html)).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph consume["CONSUMING - declared on Agent.yaml"]
        direction LR
        AG["your agent"] -->|"calls out at runtime"| RM["a remote MCP server"]
    end
    subgraph host["HOSTING - one file per server under mcp/"]
        direction LR
        TL["tools/"] -->|"a named SUBSET"| MS["mcpServer('localServer')"]
        MS --> GW["gateways/ entry, exposes: mcp"]
    end
    style consume fill:#e7f1ff,stroke:#004085
    style host fill:#eaf6ec,stroke:#155724
```

## Consuming a remote server

Declared directly in `Agent.yaml` via `mcpServers` - not a file under `mcp/`:

```yaml
mcpServers:
  - https://example.com/mcp
  - url: https://other.com/mcp
    name: other
```

A server can need a sign-in: write it as a ``${env.NAME}` placeholder (`token: "${env.GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN}"``),
never the secret itself. An entry can also start a program on the agent's machine
(`command: [uvx, mcp-server-git]`) instead of a web address, and `toolFilter` limits which tools the
agent gets. `bxAgents add mcp client` writes such an entry for you (a catalog name such as GitHub
or Notion, or `--url`), with an empty stub for the key in `.env`; the [`new` wizard](/guides/new-wizard/index.html)
offers the same catalog. See [mcp/](/conventions/mcp/index.html) for every option.

**No network connection is ever attempted at build time** - reachability is a runtime
concern, so an unreachable server at build time is not a build error. Subagents can
declare their own `mcpServers` independently.

## Hosting a local server

Each `mcp/*.bx` file is a local MCP server your project hosts, exposing a named subset
of your `tools/` (from [Lesson 9](/course/09-giving-your-agent-tools/index.html)) as MCP tools:

```javascript
// mcp/localServer.bx
class {
	function configure() {
		return {
			description : "Internal tools MCP server",
			version     : "1.0.0",
			cors        : "*",             // optional
			tools       : [ "sayHello" ]   // function names of @AITool tools already under tools/
		};
	}
}
```

The entry's discovered name is its **filename** (`localServer.bx` -\> `localServer`),
not any `name` inside `configure()`. At build time the file is copied verbatim, and a
registration statement is emitted at startup.

## Exposing it over HTTP

A local server isn't reachable on its own - pair it with the `gateways/` exposure
entry you saw in [Lesson 13](/course/13-exposing-http-and-mcp/index.html):

```javascript
// gateways/expose-mcp.bx
class {
	function configure() {
		return {
			exposes : "mcp",
			path    : "/mcp/tools",
			target  : "localServer"
		};
	}
}
```

## Try it

Host the `GetTime` tool you wrote in [Lesson 9](/course/09-giving-your-agent-tools/index.html) as its
own MCP server (`tools: [ "currentTime" ]`, the tool's function name), expose it at `/mcp/tools`, build, and `serve` - it's now reachable by
any outside MCP client, independent of your agent's own chat interface.

`bxAgents add mcp server` writes the `mcp/` file and the `gateways/` entry for you. Full
reference: [mcp/](/conventions/mcp/index.html).

Next: [Lesson 18 - Interceptors and Module Dependencies](/course/18-interceptors-and-modules/index.html)

# Interceptors and Module Dependencies

Three smaller, independent conventions round out the picture: lifecycle hooks into the
generated ColdBox app, extensions for the chat and the served agent, and declared BoxLang
module dependencies.

## `interceptors/` - ColdBox lifecycle hooks

`interceptors/*.bx` are ColdBox interceptors (`preProcess`, `postProcess`, and other
lifecycle hook points), scoped via an `@scope` annotation on the class itself:

```javascript
// interceptors/AuditLogger.bx
/**
 * @scope agent
 */
class {

	function preProcess( event, interceptData ) {
		// ...
	}

}
```

|       Scope       |                                                                            Effect                                                                            |
|-------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `agent` (default) | Copied into the generated app's own `interceptors/` folder - affects only this app.                                                                          |
| `runtime`         | Copied to `.build/runtime-interceptors`, outside the app, for the whole BoxLang runtime rather than just this app. BxAgents does not register these for you. |

An interceptor with no `@scope` at all defaults to `agent` - the narrower, safer
choice, since `runtime` scope has effects beyond one app. An `@scope` value that isn't
`agent` or `runtime` fails the build with a clear error.

You've already seen a **generated** interceptor without writing one yourself - when you list
`users` on the web chat ([Lesson 15](/course/15-the-generated-web-chat-ui/index.html)), its sign-in gate is
registered exactly this way, just written by BxAgents instead of by you.

## `extensions/` - add to the chat and the served agent

An interceptor reacts to the ColdBox request. An **extension** adds to BxAgents itself, without
changing it. One `.bx` file is a whole extension: it reads like a ColdBox `ModuleConfig` (a
`configure()`, an `onLoad()`), and annotated methods become chat commands.

```javascript
// extensions/hello.bx
class {

	@Command( "hello" )
	@Hint( "say hello: /hello <name>" )
	function greet( agentContext, commandArguments ) {
		return agentContext.reply().ok( "Hello, #commandArguments#!" )
	}

}
```

Run `bxAgents chat` and type `/hello Ada`; `/extensions` lists what loaded. The same command runs
in the web page and, if allowed, on chat platforms. A folder with an `Extension.bx` can bring more:
keys (`@Key`), status items (`@Status`), `@` sources and message prefixes for the terminal, web
page slots, listeners for chat and bx-ai events, schedulers, tools, skills, a new gateway type or
a `bxAgents` verb. Values for an extension go under `extensions:` in `Agent.yaml`.

Start one with `bxAgents add extension standup`, which asks what to bring and writes working
stubs. Install someone else's with `bxAgents extensions install <folder, zip, owner/repo, address or ForgeBox slug>`: it shows what the extension adds and asks first, and records it in
`extensions.lock.json`, which you commit. `bxAgents extensions link <folder>` links one you are
working on, and `/reload` picks up your edits. See the [`extensions/`](/conventions/extensions/index.html)
reference and the guide [Your first extension](/guides/first-extension/index.html).

## `modules/` - BoxLang module dependencies

`modules/` holds BoxLang module dependencies your agent declares - one immediate
subfolder per module, discovered by folder name (not recursive):

    modules/
    └── my-extra-module/
        ├── module.json
        └── ...

A module folder may include a `module.json` with a `dependsOn` array naming other
`modules/*` entries by folder name:

```json
{
	"dependsOn": [ "some-other-module" ]
}
```

This is BxAgents' own dependency-declaration convention for validation purposes - it's
independent of BoxLang's own module-loading mechanism, and today `build` validates and
records these folders in the manifest without loading them into the generated app. **Circular dependencies** are
rejected the same way subagent cycles are (see [Lesson 11](/course/11-composing-subagents/index.html)):
full cycle path reported, no code generation until the graph is acyclic. A
`module.json` is entirely optional - a module folder with none is assumed to have no
declared dependencies.

## Try it

Try `bxAgents add extension hello --with=command` and `/hello` in the chat. Then add an `interceptors/RequestLogger.bx` with an explicit `@scope agent` annotation that
logs every incoming request via `writeLog()`, rebuild, and check
`.build/app/interceptors/` for the copy plus its registration in
`.build/app/bxagents/Application.bx`.

Full reference: [interceptors/](/conventions/interceptors/index.html), [modules/](/conventions/modules/index.html).

Next: [Lesson 19 - Testing Your Agent](/course/19-testing-your-agent/index.html)

# Testing Your Agent

Every project scaffolded via `bxAgents new` ([Lesson 4](/course/04-scaffolding-your-first-agent/index.html))
already has a root `box.json` (TestBox as a development dependency) and a ready-to-run
`tests/` folder with `tests/specs/AgentSpec.bx`, a spec that passes out of the box.

```bash
cd my-agent
box install       # fetches testbox into lib/testbox - new already ran this for you
bxAgents test
```

## Writing a spec

Extend `bxModules.bxagents.models.testing.BaseAgentSpec` instead of
`testbox.system.BaseSpec` directly:

```javascript
// tests/specs/AgentSpec.bx
class extends="bxModules.bxagents.models.testing.BaseAgentSpec" {

	function run() {
		describe( "my-agent", function() {

			it( "responds to a greeting", function() {
				mockResponses( [ "Hello! How can I help you today?" ] )

				var response = agent.run( "Hi there" )

				expect( response ).toContainText( "Hello" )
			} )

		} )
	}

}
```

`BaseAgentSpec` builds your agent once per spec bundle, against a **throwaway temp
copy** of your project - it never touches your real `.build/app`, so testing never
clobbers a real `build`/`serve`/`package` cycle. The built agent is exposed as `agent`.

## Testing needs no API key

By default, `bxAgents test` builds your agent using an `Agent.yaml` `test` environment
override, scaffolded automatically by `new`:

```yaml
environments:
  test:
    model: mock/mock-model
```

This is the same `mock` provider you met in [Lesson 5](/course/05-agent-bx/index.html) - no network
call, no API key, deterministic CI.

## `mockResponses()`

Scripts the agent's next replies, consumed in order - one per LLM round-trip,
including the intermediate turns of a tool-calling loop:

```javascript
mockResponses( [
	{ toolCalls: [ { name: "getWeather", arguments: { city: "Miami" } } ] },
	"It's sunny in Miami!"
] )

var response = agent.run( "What's the weather in Miami?" )
```

A plain string scripts a final reply. A `{ toolCalls: [...] }` struct scripts a
tool-call turn - the named tool **actually executes for real** against your real
`tools/` implementation (from [Lesson 9](/course/09-giving-your-agent-tools/index.html)); only the
LLM's own reply is scripted, never the tool's behavior.

## Matchers built for agent behavior

|                Matcher                 |                                                                Checks                                                                |
|----------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `toContainText( "substring" )`         | The response contains the given text, case-insensitively.                                                                            |
| `toHaveCalledTool( "toolName" )`       | The agent actually decided to invoke the named tool.                                                                                 |
| `toHaveReceivedMessage( "substring" )` | Some message sent to the provider contained the given text - useful for asserting your `instructions.md` actually reached the model. |

```javascript
expect( agent ).toHaveCalledTool( "getWeather" )
expect( agent ).notToHaveCalledTool( "getStockPrice" )
```

## Try it

Write a spec that scripts a tool call for the `GetTime` tool from
[Lesson 9](/course/09-giving-your-agent-tools/index.html), and assert `toHaveCalledTool( "currentTime" )`.

```bash
bxAgents test
```

Prints pass/fail/error/skipped counts, one line per failure, and exits non-zero on
failure - suitable as a CI gate before you deploy in the next lesson.

Full reference: [tests/](/conventions/testing/index.html).

Next: [Lesson 20 - Packaging, Deploying, and Wrapping Up](/course/20-packaging-deploying-and-wrapping-up/index.html)

# Welcome to BxAgents

Welcome! This is a 20-lesson course on **BxAgents** , a conventions-based AI agent
framework for [BoxLang](https://www.boxlang.io), built on [ColdBox](https://www.coldbox.org)
and [BX AI](https://ai.boxlang.io).

The idea behind BxAgents is simple: you describe an agent with **files and folders** ,
not a framework's API surface, and one command - `bxAgents build` - assembles a real,
runnable ColdBox application out of it.

    my-agent/
    ├── Agent.yaml         # name, model, description
    ├── instructions.md    # the system prompt
    ├── tools/             # @AITool functions
    ├── skills/            # SKILL.md capabilities
    ├── subagents/         # nested agent trees
    ├── gateways/           # HTTP/MCP/chat exposure
    ├── schedules/          # BoxLang schedulers
    ├── mcp/                # MCP servers you host
    ├── interceptors/        # lifecycle hooks
    ├── extensions/         # chat commands, keys and more
    └── modules/            # module dependencies

Every folder above is optional except `Agent.yaml`. Add the ones your agent actually
needs; the rest can stay empty or simply not exist. (`bxAgents new` creates every folder except
`extensions/`, which appears when you run `bxAgents add extension`.)

## How this course is organized

The 20 lessons follow the order you'd naturally build a real project in:

1. **Lessons 1-4** - orientation, install, and your first scaffolded project.
2. **Lessons 5-8** - the required pieces: `Agent.yaml`, instructions, building, and chatting with the agent in the terminal.
3. **Lessons 9-12** - giving your agent abilities: tools, skills, subagents, and models and profiles.
4. **Lessons 13-16** - reaching your agent: the HTTP API and its tokens, MCP exposure, chat platforms, the generated web UI, and scheduled background work.
5. **Lessons 17-18** - hosting your own MCP servers, lifecycle interceptors, extensions and module dependencies.
6. **Lessons 19-20** - testing for real, then packaging and deploying what you built.

## What you need

* A terminal.
* About 30-60 minutes per lesson if you're following along hands-on (most lessons work fine read-only too).
* No prior BoxLang or ColdBox experience required - Lesson 3 installs everything you need.

Every lesson links back to the full [Conventions](/conventions/agent-yaml/index.html) reference
for anything this course only summarizes - the course is the guided path, the
Conventions section is the exhaustive reference you'll come back to later.

Next: [Lesson 2 - What Is BxAgents?](/course/02-what-is-bxagents/index.html)

body:
Packaging, Deploying, and Wrapping Up You've built an agent with tools, skills, subagents, an HTTP route, a chat-platform connection, a web UI, a schedule, and a test suite. This last lesson ships it. The chain, end to end flowchart LR P["your project"] -->|"bxAgents build"| B[".build/app/

title: Lesson 2: What Is BxAgents?
body:
What Is BxAgents? Most agent frameworks wire tools, skills, routes and schedules together at request time , on every boot. BxAgents does the opposite: bxAgents build runs discovery, validation and code generation exactly once , producing a plain ColdBox application under .build/app/ . Starting it afterwards - via bxAgents serve , a real boxlang-miniserver process, or a portable .bxa deployed anywhere BoxLang runs - is then just booting an ordinary app. No convention scanning, no dynamic file walking, no build-time work deferred into the request path. flowchart LR A["your convention tree
Agent.yaml, tools/, skills/, ..."] -->|"bxAgents build"| B[".build/app/
a plain ColdBox application"] B -->|"bxAgents serve / chat / invoke"| C["running agent"] B -->|"bxAgents package"| D["dist/name-version.bxa"] D -->|"bxAgents deploy"| E["a real target"] style B fill:#d4edda,stroke:#155724 Folders are the API Agent.yaml and instructions.md are the only files that matter to get started. Every other convention folder - tools/ , skills/ , subagents/ , gateways/ , schedules/ , mcp/ , interceptors/ , extensions/ , modules/ - is optional and only shapes the generated output if it exists and has content in it . You add conventions as you actually need them, not up front. Agent.yaml defines the agent Agent.yaml is plain settings - a name, a model, and any optional extras - and the build turns it into a real BX AI agent. No code is needed for most agents. You'll write your first one in Lesson 5 . When the definition itself needs code (hooks, dynamic instructions, tools registered in code), there is an advanced option: a class-based Agent.bx that extends BX AI's own AiAgent , which the build instantiates as-is. Lesson 5 ends with when to reach for it. What build actually produces Your convention tree on the left, the plain ColdBox application build turns it into on the right: your-agent/ ├── Application.bx ├── Agent.yaml ├── instructions.md ├── tools/ ├── skills/ ├── subagents/ ├── gateways/ ├── schedules/ ├── mcp/ ├── interceptors/ └── modules/ .build/app/ ├── Application.bx ├── bxagents/ │ ├── Application.bx │ └── Scheduler.bx ├── config/ │ ├── ColdBox.bx │ ├── WireBox.bx │ └── Router.bx ├── schedules/ ├── agent/ │ └── GeneratedAgentFactory.bx ├── tools/ skills/ mcp/ ├── handlers/ interceptors/ └── index.bxm Why this matters Rebuilding an unchanged project produces byte-identical output, down to a hash- stamped manifest recording exactly what went into the build (more on that in Lesson 20 ). That's the whole point of paying the assembly cost once, at build time, rather than deferring any of it into request handling. See BxAgents home and The Build Pipeline for more detail whenever you want it. Next: Lesson 3 - Installing BxAgents
