# Installing BxAgents

BxAgents is a BoxLang module. It needs two things on the machine that runs it:

1. A [BoxLang](https://www.boxlang.io) runtime.
2. BxAgents itself, which bundles everything else it needs (`bx-ai`, `bx-sqlite`, `bx-ftp`, `bx-mail`, `bx-yaml`, `bx-markdown`, and ColdBox with its modules for the apps it generates). BoxLang **1.18.0 or later** is required.

1

Install BoxLang

Follow the [official BoxLang installation guide](https://boxlang.ortusbooks.com/getting-started/installation).
The quick installer also sets up `~/.boxlang/bin` on your `PATH`, which is where
module-provided executables (like BxAgents' own `bxAgents` command) land.

2

Install BxAgents

```bash
install-bx-module bx-agents
```

This fetches the module, with its bundled dependencies, into your BoxLang modules directory (`~/.boxlang/modules`
by default, or `boxlang_modules/` with `--local`).

3

Verify it worked

```bash
bxAgents --version
bxAgents --help
```

`--help` lists all 20 verbs (`new`, `add`, `build`, `test`, `serve`, `chat`, `invoke`,
`package`, `deploy`, `inspect`, `clean`, `hash-password`, `token`, `notes`, `doctor`, `skills`,
`models`, `sessions`, `stats`, `extensions`) with a one-line summary of each. You'll use most of them in this course.

## The `bxAgents` command

BxAgents declares a native executable in its `box.json`:

```json
"boxlang": { "moduleName": "bxagents", "executable": "bxAgents" }
```

The installer turns that into a `bxAgents` wrapper script on your `PATH`. `bxAgents new my-agent --model=openai/gpt-5` is shorthand for the longer, always-equivalent form:

```bash
boxlang module:bxagents new my-agent --model=openai/gpt-5
```

This course uses the short `bxAgents <verb>` form throughout.

## Optional, for later lessons

* **`serve`** , **`chat --server`** and **`invoke --server`** ([Lesson 8](/course/08-talking-to-your-agent/index.html)) additionally need the standalone [`boxlang-miniserver`](https://boxlang.ortusbooks.com/getting-started/running-boxlang/miniserver) binary on `PATH`.

None of them is required to follow along with `build`, plain `chat`, `test`, `package`,
`inspect`, `clean`, `new` or `doctor`. After installing, `bxAgents doctor` inside a project
checks the BoxLang version, whether `bx-ai` is loaded, whether the project validates and
which environment variables it needs are not set.

See [Installation](/getting-started/installation/index.html) for the full reference page.

Next: [Lesson 4 - Scaffolding Your First Agent](/course/04-scaffolding-your-first-agent/index.html)

title: Lesson 4: Scaffolding Your First Agent
body: Scaffolding Your First Agent With BoxLang and BxAgents installed ( Lesson 3 ), scaffold your first project: bxAgents new my-agent --model=openai/gpt-5 --model is a provider/model slug (you'll see exactly how this gets parsed in Lesson 5 ). Pass it for a script-friendly run: without --model , at a terminal, new asks you questions instead (see new wizard ). --name and --description are optional; --name defaults to the target directory's own name. new refuses to run if the target already contains an Agent.yaml or Agent.bx . The wizard At a terminal, bxAgents new my-agent (no --model ) opens a full-screen wizard. It asks what the agent should do: its model, tools, memory, MCP servers, channels (web chat, Slack, Telegram and so on), how people sign in, and where it deploys. Esc goes back one question and Ctrl+C creates nothing. One question picks a template, the shape the project starts from, and your other answers are added on top of it: a template is a preset, not a limit. The last screen prints the one-line command that builds the same project without questions, so a script can repeat it. Pass --model (or --no-wizard ) to skip the questions. See the new wizard for every question and flag. What gets created my-agent/ ├── Agent.yaml ├── box.json ├── instructions.md ├── tools/ ├── skills/ ├── subagents/ ├── gateways/ ├── schedules/ ├── mcp/ ├── interceptors/ ├── modules/ └── tests/ └── specs/ └── AgentSpec.bx Plus a .env declaring BOXLANG_HOME=.build/runtime (matching serve 's own scoped runtime home), a .gitignore (it ignores .build/ , dist/ , .env , lib/ and data/chat.db* , among others) and a few dotfiles ( .boxlang.json , .editorconfig , .bxlint.json , .gitattributes , .markdownlint.json ) - new never overwrites them if they already exist. BoxLang loads the .env from the project root itself, so this is where secrets live: the wizard and add write an empty line for each key your choices need (a provider key, a bot token), and the files that use it hold only the variable's name. Every convention folder is created empty . You add files to the ones your agent actually needs and leave the rest alone - an empty tools/ folder has zero effect on the generated app. Agent.yaml looks like this (Pass --description and new adds a description: line.) # Your agent. Most agents need nothing more than this file and instructions.md. # For code in the definition (hooks, dynamic instructions), scaffold with --class. name: my-agent provider: openai model: gpt-5 environments: # `bxAgents test` builds against this override by default (see # BaseAgentSpec.bx) so a fresh project's tests need no API key or # network access - swap the model to test against a real provider. test: model: mock/mock-model That is the whole agent definition - more on each key in Lesson 5 . If you need code in the definition, pass --class and new scaffolds a class-based Agent.bx instead (also covered at the end of Lesson 5). The test suite runs itself new also runs box install in the scaffolded project root (its box.json lists TestBox, installed into lib/testbox ), so bxAgents test ( Lesson 19 ) works immediately with no separate step. This is best-effort - if box isn't on PATH or the install fails, new still succeeds and just tells you to run it yourself. Pass --skipInstall to opt out entirely. Try it bxAgents new my-agent --model=openai/gpt-5 cd my-agent ls You now have a real, if minimal, BxAgents project. Later you can add to it without editing files by hand: bxAgents add tool , add skill , add subagent , add gateway , add schedule and the other add kinds ask a few questions and write the files for you ( --dry-run shows them first). The next four lessons walk through what's actually required to run it. Next: Lesson 5 - The Agent Definition: Agent.yaml

# Scaffolding Your First Agent

With BoxLang and BxAgents installed ([Lesson 3](/course/03-installing-bxagents/index.html)),
scaffold your first project:

```bash
bxAgents new my-agent --model=openai/gpt-5
```

`--model` is a `provider/model` slug (you'll see exactly how this gets
parsed in [Lesson 5](/course/05-agent-bx/index.html)). Pass it for a script-friendly run: without
`--model`, at a terminal, `new` asks you questions instead (see [`new` wizard](/guides/new-wizard/index.html)).
`--name` and `--description` are optional;
`--name` defaults to the target directory's own name. `new` refuses to run if the
target already contains an `Agent.yaml` or `Agent.bx`.

## The wizard

At a terminal, `bxAgents new my-agent` (no `--model`) opens a full-screen wizard. It asks what
the agent should do: its model, tools, memory, MCP servers, channels (web chat, Slack, Telegram
and so on), how people sign in, and where it deploys. Esc goes back one question and Ctrl+C
creates nothing. One question picks a template, the shape the project starts from, and
your other answers are added on top of it: a template is a preset, not a limit. The last screen
prints the one-line command that builds the same project without questions, so a script can
repeat it. Pass `--model` (or `--no-wizard`) to skip the questions. See the
[`new` wizard](/guides/new-wizard/index.html) for every question and flag.

## What gets created

    my-agent/
    ├── Agent.yaml
    ├── box.json
    ├── instructions.md
    ├── tools/
    ├── skills/
    ├── subagents/
    ├── gateways/
    ├── schedules/
    ├── mcp/
    ├── interceptors/
    ├── modules/
    └── tests/
        └── specs/
            └── AgentSpec.bx

Plus a `.env` declaring `BOXLANG_HOME=.build/runtime` (matching `serve`'s own scoped
runtime home), a `.gitignore` (it ignores `.build/`, `dist/`, `.env`, `lib/` and `data/chat.db*`, among others)
and a few dotfiles (`.boxlang.json`, `.editorconfig`, `.bxlint.json`, `.gitattributes`,
`.markdownlint.json`) - `new` never overwrites them if they already exist. BoxLang loads the `.env` from the project root itself, so
this is where secrets live: the wizard and `add` write an empty line for each key your choices
need (a provider key, a bot token), and the files that use it hold only the variable's name.

Every convention folder is created **empty** . You add files to the ones your agent
actually needs and leave the rest alone - an empty `tools/` folder has zero effect on
the generated app.

## `Agent.yaml` looks like this

(Pass `--description` and `new` adds a `description:` line.)

```yaml
# Your agent. Most agents need nothing more than this file and instructions.md.
# For code in the definition (hooks, dynamic instructions), scaffold with --class.
name: my-agent
provider: openai
model: gpt-5

environments:
  # `bxAgents test` builds against this override by default (see
  # BaseAgentSpec.bx) so a fresh project's tests need no API key or
  # network access - swap the model to test against a real provider.
  test:
    model: mock/mock-model
```

That is the whole agent definition - more on each key in [Lesson 5](/course/05-agent-bx/index.html).
If you need code in the definition, pass `--class` and `new` scaffolds a class-based
`Agent.bx` instead (also covered at the end of Lesson 5).

## The test suite runs itself

`new` also runs `box install` in the scaffolded project root (its `box.json` lists TestBox, installed into `lib/testbox`), so `bxAgents test`
([Lesson 19](/course/19-testing-your-agent/index.html)) works immediately with no separate step. This
is best-effort - if `box` isn't on `PATH` or the install fails, `new` still succeeds
and just tells you to run it yourself. Pass `--skipInstall` to opt out entirely.

## Try it

```bash
bxAgents new my-agent --model=openai/gpt-5
cd my-agent
ls
```

You now have a real, if minimal, BxAgents project. Later you can add to it without editing
files by hand: `bxAgents add tool`, `add skill`, `add subagent`, `add gateway`, `add schedule` and
the other `add` kinds ask a few questions and write the files for you (`--dry-run` shows them
first). The next four lessons walk through what's actually required to run it.

Next: [Lesson 5 - The Agent Definition: Agent.yaml](/course/05-agent-bx/index.html)

markdown:
# The Agent Definition - Agent.yaml

`Agent.yaml` is the **only required file** in a BxAgents project (beside the
instructions it points at). It is plain settings - a name, a model, and any optional
extras - and the build turns it into a real
[BX AI agent](https://ai.ortusbooks.com/main-components/agents/class-based-agents).
No code needed.

```yaml
name: my-agent
description: A helpful assistant
model: openai/gpt-5
instructions: |
  You are a helpful assistant.
```

That is a complete agent. `bxAgents new` scaffolds this shape for you (see
[Lesson 4](/course/04-scaffolding-your-first-agent/index.html)), with the system prompt in an
`instructions.md` beside it (see [Lesson 6](/course/06-instructions-and-system-prompt/index.html)).
> **Info**
>
> A folder holds **one** agent definition. An `Agent.yaml` together with an
> `Agent.bx` (or an `Agent.yml`) in the same folder is an error, and the build names
> both files so you can keep one.

## The keys

|                                                                                                        Key                                                                                                         |                                                                               What it does                                                                               |
|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `name`                                                                                                                                                                                                             | The agent's name. Also its WireBox binding key, so it must be unique across the whole project.                                                                           |
| `model`                                                                                                                                                                                                            | A `provider/model` slug (see below).                                                                                                                                     |
| `description`                                                                                                                                                                                                      | Optional.                                                                                                                                                                |
| `instructions`                                                                                                                                                                                                     | Inline system prompt. An `instructions.md` beside the file wins when both exist.                                                                                         |
| `tools`                                                                                                                                                                                                            | Module tools this agent gets, as `item@module` or `*@module` (see [Lesson 9](/course/09-giving-your-agent-tools/index.html)).                                            |
| `toolOptions`                                                                                                                                                                                                      | Options for a module's tools, keyed by module name.                                                                                                                      |
| `subAgents`                                                                                                                                                                                                        | Names of sibling folders under `subagents/` (see [Lesson 11](/course/11-composing-subagents/index.html)).                                                                |
| `mcpServers`                                                                                                                                                                                                       | Remote MCP servers the agent can call (see [Lesson 17](/course/17-hosting-mcp-servers/index.html)).                                                                      |
| `security`, `memory`, `checkpointer`                                                                                                                                                                               | Guardrails, conversation memory and human-in-the-loop state.                                                                                                             |
| `gatewaySession`                                                                                                                                                                                                   | How chat gateways queue messages, which slash commands they answer and whether they read attachments (see [Lesson 14](/course/14-connecting-chat-platforms/index.html)). |
| `agentApi`                                                                                                                                                                                                         | The always-on agent API: who may call it (tokens, allowed addresses, rate limit) and where it is served (see [Lesson 13](/course/13-exposing-http-and-mcp/index.html)).  |
| `environments`                                                                                                                                                                                                     | Per-environment overrides (see below).                                                                                                                                   |
| `provider`, `params`, `options`, `providers`, `profiles`, `notes` (short notes the agent keeps), `usage` (record token counts for `bxAgents stats`), `tui` (the look of the terminal chat), `extensions`, and more | Further settings, all listed in the [Agent.yaml](/conventions/agent-yaml/index.html) reference.                                                                          |

An **unknown key is an error** that lists the valid ones, so a typo such as `modle:`
can never quietly do nothing. Wrong types and empty values are errors too.
> **Info**
>
> The checkpointer is the one thing the build fills in unasked. An agent reachable
> from a gateway with no checkpointer has silently broken human-in-the-loop, so a
> definition that sets none still gets the `cache` default.

## The model slug

`model` is BxAgents' own convention - bx-ai itself takes `provider` and `model` as two
separate arguments. BxAgents splits the slug **on the first `/` only**:

|          `model` value          |   provider   |        model         |
|---------------------------------|--------------|----------------------|
| `openai/gpt-5`                  | `openai`     | `gpt-5`              |
| `openrouter/anthropic/claude-x` | `openrouter` | `anthropic/claude-x` |
| `mock/mock-model`               | `mock`       | `mock-model`         |

`mock` is a real provider that never makes a network call - useful for tests (see
[Lesson 19](/course/19-testing-your-agent/index.html)) and for following this course with no API key
at all.

## Adding settings

Other settings are just more keys:

```yaml
name: with-mcp-servers-agent
model: openai/gpt-5
mcpServers:
  - https://example.com/mcp
```

## Environment overrides

`environments` maps an environment name (`production`, `development`, or any custom
name) to a block of overrides:

```yaml
name: my-agent
model: openai/gpt-5

environments:
  production:
    model: openai/gpt-5-mini
  test:
    model: mock/mock-model
```

The active environment resolves, highest wins: `--environment` CLI flag \>
`BX_AGENTS_ENV` env var \> `"development"` default. `bxAgents build --environment=production`
picks it up. Only the active block is applied, on top of the top-level keys. You'll use
this exact mechanism for the `mock` provider in your tests ([Lesson 19](/course/19-testing-your-agent/index.html)),
which is why `bxAgents new` already gives you a `test` block.

Full reference: [Agent.yaml](/conventions/agent-yaml/index.html).

## When you need code: Agent.bx

`Agent.yaml` covers almost every agent. Reach for the advanced class form, `Agent.bx`,
only when the definition itself needs code: hooks, dynamic instructions, tools
registered in code, an overridden method, or computing the environment with
`detectEnvironment()`. It is a real class extending bx-ai's `AiAgent`, which the build
instantiates:

```javascript
class extends="bxModules.bxai.models.runnables.AiAgent" {

	function init() {
		super.init(
			name        : "my-agent",
			description : "A helpful assistant",
			instructions: "You are a helpful assistant.",
			model       : aiModel( provider: "openai", params: { model: "gpt-5" } )
		)
		return this
	}

}
```

Scaffold one with `bxAgents new --class`, or start in YAML and switch later: create the
`Agent.bx`, move the settings across, and delete the `Agent.yaml`. Full reference:
[Agent.bx](/conventions/agent-bx/index.html).

Next: [Lesson 6 - instructions.md and the System Prompt](/course/06-instructions-and-system-prompt/index.html)

# instructions.md and the System Prompt

`instructions.md` is **optional** - `bxAgents new` scaffolds a starter one for you to
edit, but you have two equally valid choices for where your agent's system prompt
lives:

1. Set `instructions` inline in `Agent.yaml`.
2. Drop an `instructions.md` file beside `Agent.yaml` and let the build wire it in.

## Letting the file win

If `instructions.md` exists, the build emits:

```javascript
withInstructions( fileRead( "instructions.md" ) )
```

which wins over an inline `instructions` in `Agent.yaml` (or whatever a class set).
This is the more common pattern in
practice - it keeps the prompt as plain text you can edit without touching BoxLang
code, and it's easy to diff in a pull request.

```markdown
# instructions.md
You are a helpful assistant for a small hardware store. Be concise. If a customer
asks about a product you don't have information on, say so rather than guessing.
```

## Setting it inline instead

```yaml
name: my-agent
model: openai/gpt-5
instructions: |
  You are a helpful assistant.
  Keep answers short.
```

Do this for a short prompt, or when you'd rather keep everything about the agent in one
file. If both exist, `instructions.md` wins; if neither exists, the build fails and says
so. A prompt that must be generated or templated in code belongs in the advanced
class-based `Agent.bx` (see the end of [Lesson 5](/course/05-agent-bx/index.html)).

## Which one should you pick?

Start with `instructions.md` - it's what `bxAgents new` scaffolds, it's the simplest
mental model ("the system prompt is this file"), and it plays nicely with the rest of
this course, which assumes plain-text prompts throughout. Reach for the inline
`instructions` key only for a short prompt, and for code only once you have a concrete
reason to (templating, environment-specific prompts assembled from smaller pieces,
etc.).

## Try it

Open the `instructions.md` that [Lesson 4](/course/04-scaffolding-your-first-agent/index.html)'s
`bxAgents new` created and write a real system prompt for whatever kind of agent you
want to build in this course - a support bot, a code reviewer, anything. You'll build
and run it in the next two lessons.

Next: [Lesson 7 - Building Your Agent](/course/07-building-your-agent/index.html)

title: Lesson 7: Building Your Agent
body:
Building Your Agent With Agent.yaml and instructions.md in place, build your project: bxAgents build This runs the full build pipeline - config resolution, discovery, validation, code generation, manifest normalization - and writes a real ColdBox application to .build/app/ , plus .build/manifest.json . The five phases, in order flowchart TD A["1 · Resolve config"] --> B["2 · Discover"] B --> C{"3 · Validate"} C -->|"any error"| X["Build throws.
.build/app is never written"] C -->|"clean"| D["4 · Generate"] D --> E["5 · Normalize + write manifest"] E --> F[".build/manifest.json
+ .build/app"] style C fill:#fff3cd,stroke:#856404 style X fill:#f8d7da,stroke:#721c24 style F fill:#d4edda,stroke:#155724 Resolve config - loads Agent.yaml (or a class-based Agent.bx , calling its configure() ) and the active environment override, then deep-merges any boxlang.json / boxlang-{env}.json . Discover - walks the project and enumerates every convention folder into raw entries. Pure discovery - no interpretation of file contents yet. Validate - collects every error (never fails fast) plus warnings: duplicate tool/skill/model/subagent names, circular references, bad model/provider config, and more. If any errors were collected, the build throws here - .build/app is never written or touched. Generate - only reached once validation is clean. Interceptors, gateways, MCP, the router, the agent API handler, the web UI (if any), the core app skeleton, a verbatim copy of tools/ / skills/ , the bundled ColdBox libraries, and the scheduler, in that order. Normalize + write the manifest - produces the canonical .build/manifest.json . If your project fails validation build fails with every collected error, not just the first one - a duplicate tool name and an unknown model provider in the same project both get reported in one run. Idempotency Rebuilding an unchanged project produces byte-identical output, down to the manifest's per-file content hashes. This is the entire point of paying the assembly cost once, at build time, instead of deferring it into every request. Useful flag: --verbose bxAgents build --verbose Prints one line per build phase live as it runs - what got resolved/discovered/ validated, per-phase counts, which agents ended up registered in config/WireBox.bx and under which names, whether a scheduler was found, and a final timing line. Silent otherwise, so it costs nothing when you don't need it. Try it cd my-agent bxAgents build --verbose You should see a .build/app/ directory appear, and a manifest describing exactly what went into it. You'll talk to this built agent in the next lesson. Full reference: The Build Pipeline . Next: Lesson 8 - Talking to Your Agent

title: Lesson 8: Talking to Your Agent
body: Talking to Your Agent Once you've built your project ( Lesson 7 ), there are three ways to run it - all load the exact same GeneratedAgentFactory.bx and build the exact same agent tree, so they never diverge from each other. chat - a full-screen terminal chat bxAgents chat # fast, in-process bxAgents chat --server [--port=<port>] # full app, own throwaway server bxAgents chat --connect=http://127.0.0.1:8080 # full app, server you already run bxAgents chat --connect=https://agent.example.com --token=<token> # a server that wants a token At a terminal this draws a full-screen chat, not a bare prompt (the tour is in The terminal UI ). Finished turns are ordinary terminal text, so your scrollback and search keep working. Answers stream in as formatted Markdown, tool calls show their arguments and how long they took, and a run that needs approval asks in place. Add --no-tui , or run without a terminal, for the plain line-by-line prompt. What you can do in it: Keys. Enter sends, Alt+Enter adds a line, Up and Down walk your history, Esc stops the agent, and a message typed while it works steers it. ? or /keys lists every key, and you can rebind them in ~/.bxagents/bxAgents.yml . Slash commands. Type / for a menu: /help , /tools , /model , /info and more. Every command is listed in Slash commands . Sessions. Every chat is a conversation kept in data/chat.db , the same list the web chat shows. /sessions lists them, /resume goes back to one, /new starts another, /name names it, /fork copies it and carries on in the copy, and /export saves it as Markdown or HTML. bxAgents chat --continue reopens the latest one. The messages themselves last as long as the agent's memory does, so use a file memory if you want them after a restart. Notes. With a notes: block in Agent.yaml , /remember <text> and /notes keep short notes about you that the agent reads at the start of each conversation. Context. The hint row under the box shows how much of the model's window is used, such as ctx ~12.4k / 128k 9% . /context shows what it is made of. Files and pictures. @ lists files, and @notes.md puts a text file's content in your message. @picture.png or Ctrl+V sends a picture (refused when the profile says vision: false ). Recording. bxAgents chat --record=demo.cast , or /record inside the chat, saves the screen as an asciicast file for demos. The default mode loads the generated factory directly in this process - fastest, but without anything ColdBox brings (no scheduler, no interceptors, no gateway registry). When that matters, --server boots a real miniserver and drives the chat over HTTP against your project's agent API, and --connect does the same against a server you already have running. Both HTTP modes stream the reply token by token and carry the conversation across turns. If the server keeps its API somewhere else ( agentApi.path ), add --api-path=/where . If it wants a token ( Lesson 13 ), pass --token=<token> or set BXAGENTS_TOKEN . invoke - one non-interactive turn bxAgents invoke --message="What's the weather in Boston?" [--json] Exists for scripting and CI, where chat 's TTY requirement is a hard blocker. By default this loads the generated factory in-process, the same path chat uses internally, just without the chat screen - no serve prerequisite at all. --json prints {"response": "..."} instead of plain text. Add --server to instead launch a real, throwaway boxlang-miniserver process and send the message as a genuine HTTP request to your project's agent API - no gateways/ entry needed (those come in Lesson 13 ). Like serve , it needs boxlang-miniserver on PATH . serve - a real HTTP server bxAgents serve --port=8080 Requires a prior build and requires boxlang-miniserver on PATH (see Lesson 3 ). Launches a real server process pointed at .build/app , scoped to its own .build/runtime BoxLang home so each project's compiled-class cache stays isolated. Testing without a real API key Every one of these needs a real model to talk to a real provider - but you don't need one yet. ( bxAgents models test later sends each model one tiny question, so a wrong key or model name shows before a chat does.) Add a test environment override to Agent.yaml (covered fully in Lesson 19 ): environments: test: model: mock/mock-model then bxAgents build --environment=test && bxAgents chat runs entirely against bx-ai's built-in mock provider - no network call, no API key. Try it export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-... # or use the mock override above bxAgents chat Say hello to the agent you scaffolded and wrote instructions for in Lessons 4-6 . It's a real, running agent - you just haven't given it anything to do yet. That starts next lesson. Full reference: Quick Start , CLI Reference . Next: Lesson 9 - Giving Your Agent Tools

# Talking to Your Agent

Once you've built your project ([Lesson 7](/course/07-building-your-agent/index.html)), there are
three ways to run it - all load the exact same `GeneratedAgentFactory.bx` and build
the exact same agent tree, so they never diverge from each other.

## `chat` - a full-screen terminal chat

```bash
bxAgents chat                                  # fast, in-process
bxAgents chat --server [--port=<port>]         # full app, own throwaway server
bxAgents chat --connect=http://127.0.0.1:8080  # full app, server you already run
bxAgents chat --connect=https://agent.example.com --token=<token>   # a server that wants a token
```

At a terminal this draws a full-screen chat, not a bare prompt (the tour is in
[The terminal UI](/guides/terminal-ui/index.html)). Finished turns are ordinary terminal text, so
your scrollback and search keep working. Answers stream in as formatted Markdown, tool calls
show their arguments and how long they took, and a run that needs approval asks in place.
Add `--no-tui`, or run without a terminal, for the plain line-by-line prompt.

What you can do in it:

* **Keys.** Enter sends, Alt+Enter adds a line, Up and Down walk your history, Esc stops the agent, and a message typed while it works steers it. `?` or `/keys` lists every key, and you can rebind them in `~/.bxagents/bxAgents.yml`.
* **Slash commands.** Type `/` for a menu: `/help`, `/tools`, `/model`, `/info` and more. Every command is listed in [Slash commands](/guides/slash-commands/index.html).
* **Sessions.** Every chat is a conversation kept in `data/chat.db`, the same list the web chat shows. `/sessions` lists them, `/resume` goes back to one, `/new` starts another, `/name` names it, `/fork` copies it and carries on in the copy, and `/export` saves it as Markdown or HTML. `bxAgents chat --continue` reopens the latest one. The messages themselves last as long as the agent's memory does, so use a `file` memory if you want them after a restart.
* **Notes.** With a `notes:` block in `Agent.yaml`, `/remember <text>` and `/notes` keep short notes about you that the agent reads at the start of each conversation.
* **Context.** The hint row under the box shows how much of the model's window is used, such as `ctx ~12.4k / 128k 9%`. `/context` shows what it is made of.
* **Files and pictures.** `@` lists files, and `@notes.md` puts a text file's content in your message. `@picture.png` or Ctrl+V sends a picture (refused when the profile says `vision: false`).
* **Recording.** `bxAgents chat --record=demo.cast`, or `/record` inside the chat, saves the screen as an asciicast file for demos.

The default mode loads the generated factory directly in this process - fastest, but
without anything ColdBox brings (no scheduler, no interceptors, no
gateway registry). When that matters, `--server` boots a real miniserver and drives the
chat over HTTP against your project's agent API, and `--connect` does the
same against a server you already have running. Both HTTP modes **stream** the reply
token by token and carry the conversation across turns. If the server keeps its API
somewhere else (`agentApi.path`), add `--api-path=/where`. If it wants a token
([Lesson 13](/course/13-exposing-http-and-mcp/index.html)), pass `--token=<token>` or set `BXAGENTS_TOKEN`.

## `invoke` - one non-interactive turn

```bash
bxAgents invoke --message="What's the weather in Boston?" [--json]
```

Exists for scripting and CI, where `chat`'s TTY requirement is a hard blocker. By
default this loads the generated factory in-process, the same path `chat` uses
internally, just without the chat screen - no `serve` prerequisite at all. `--json`
prints `{"response": "..."}` instead of plain text.

Add `--server` to instead launch a real, throwaway `boxlang-miniserver` process and
send the message as a genuine HTTP request to your project's agent API -
no `gateways/` entry needed (those come in [Lesson 13](/course/13-exposing-http-and-mcp/index.html)). Like
`serve`, it needs `boxlang-miniserver` on `PATH`.

## `serve` - a real HTTP server

```bash
bxAgents serve --port=8080
```

Requires a prior `build` and requires `boxlang-miniserver` on `PATH` (see
[Lesson 3](/course/03-installing-bxagents/index.html)). Launches a real server process pointed at
`.build/app`, scoped to its own `.build/runtime` BoxLang home so each project's
compiled-class cache stays isolated.

## Testing without a real API key

Every one of these needs a real model to talk to a real provider - but you don't need
one yet. (`bxAgents models test` later sends each model one tiny question, so a wrong key or
model name shows before a chat does.) Add a `test` environment override to `Agent.yaml` (covered fully in
[Lesson 19](/course/19-testing-your-agent/index.html)):

```yaml
environments:
  test:
    model: mock/mock-model
```

then `bxAgents build --environment=test && bxAgents chat` runs entirely against bx-ai's
built-in mock provider - no network call, no API key.

## Try it

```bash
export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...   # or use the mock override above
bxAgents chat
```

Say hello to the agent you scaffolded and wrote instructions for in
[Lessons 4-6](/course/04-scaffolding-your-first-agent/index.html). It's a real, running agent - you
just haven't given it anything to *do* yet. That starts next lesson.

Full reference: [Quick Start](/getting-started/quick-start/index.html), [CLI Reference](/cli-reference/index.html).

Next: [Lesson 9 - Giving Your Agent Tools](/course/09-giving-your-agent-tools/index.html)

markdown:
# Giving Your Agent Tools

Any `.bx` file under `tools/` (searched recursively, so `tools/nested/Search.bx` works
too) that declares an `@AITool`-annotated function becomes a callable tool for your
agent.

```javascript
// tools/Greeter.bx
class {

	@AITool( "Say hello to someone by name." )
	function sayHello( name ) {
		return "Hello, " & arguments.name & "!";
	}

}
```

BxAgents doesn't scan or interpret `@AITool` annotations itself at build time - it
just discovers one entry per `.bx` file (for name-collision checking) and copies the
whole `tools/` folder **verbatim** into the generated app. At startup, the generated
app calls bx-ai's own scanner (`aiToolRegistry().scan( "tools" )`), which registers the tools
by name, and the agent factory loads each agent's own `tools/` folder through bx-ai, which
does the real reflection work. The scan statement is only emitted at all if your project
actually has a `tools/` folder with files in it.

## Whose tools are they?

An agent gets its own `tools/` folder and nothing else: a root agent's tools are not
given to its subagents, and the other way round. Tools that *modules* register with
bx-ai (its built-ins, `bx-playwright`, ...) are only attached when the agent asks for
them in `Agent.yaml`:

```yaml
tools:
  - now@bxai
  - "*@bxplaywright"
```

See [Agent.yaml](/conventions/agent-yaml/index.html#tools) for the details.

## Naming

The discovered entry name is the file's own base name - `Greeter.bx` becomes
`Greeter`. Two tool files with the same base name, even in different subfolders (since
discovery is flat by base name), fail validation with a duplicate-name error.

## What's excluded

Dotfiles are ignored by discovery, and `.env`/dotfiles inside `tools/` are never
copied into the build output even if present.

## Rebuilds are clean

`tools/` is copied with a wipe-then-write strategy on every `build` - a file you
delete from your project's `tools/` folder never lingers as stale output from a
previous build.

## Try it

Add a real tool to the agent you've been building:

```javascript
// tools/GetTime.bx
class {

	@AITool( "Get the current server time." )
	function currentTime() {
		return dateTimeFormat( now(), "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss" );
	}

}
```

Or let `bxAgents add tool GetTime --function=currentTime` scaffold the file with a typed `@AITool` function for you.
Rebuild and chat with it:

```bash
bxAgents build
bxAgents chat
> What time is it?
```

Full reference: [tools/](/conventions/tools/index.html).

Next: [Lesson 10 - Packaging Skills](/course/10-packaging-skills/index.html)

markdown:
# Logs

An agent writes what it does, and what goes wrong, to log files in the `logs/` folder of its [data home](/conventions/data/index.html). There is one file per area, so a broken chat app is not buried in the noise of a busy API:

    <data home>/logs/
      agent.log       startup, errors in a turn, tool failures
      gateways.log    every chat app: connect, disconnect, send failures. The gateway's name starts each line
      routines.log    routines: created, changed, run, skipped, failed, delivered
      heartbeat.log   each tick of the routine scheduler that did something
      api.log         refused calls and sign-in failures

A file appears when its first line is written. `routines.log` and `heartbeat.log` are written by [routines](/conventions/routines/index.html).

A line looks like this:

    [2026-11-09T09:15:11,300] [main] [ERROR] [GATEWAYS] [my-agent] [telegram] Could not start: Telegram rejected the configured bot token: Unauthorized

## What is never written

A log is for finding out what happened, not for keeping what was said.

* No message from a person, and no token, password or key. Callers do not pass them, and every line is cleaned all the same: bearer tokens, Telegram, Slack, GitHub and OpenAI style tokens, and the value after a name such as `password`, `secret`, `api_key` or `access_token` are replaced by `***`.
* Writing a log never stops the work it describes. A log that cannot be written is skipped.

## Rotation

The logs are written with BoxLang's own logging, so BoxLang rolls and removes them by its own rules: by default a file rolls at 100 MB, files are kept for 90 days and all logs together are capped at 5 GB. Change that with the `logging` settings of the BoxLang runtime (`maxFileSize`, `maxLogDays`, `totalCapSize` in `boxlang.json`). BX Agents adds no settings of its own for it.

`backup` does not include the logs.

## Reading them

**In the terminal:**

```bash
bxAgents logs                                     # which logs there are and how big
bxAgents logs gateways                            # the last 100 lines of the gateways log
bxAgents logs gateways --tail=500 --level=warn --grep=telegram
bxAgents logs api --json
```

`--level` shows that level and anything more serious (`debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`), `--grep` keeps the lines that contain the text (case does not matter), and `--tail` is how many lines, up to 1000. Only the end of a log is read, so a big log is as quick as a small one.

**In the web page** , for an admin, **Settings** has a **Logs** item and a **Chat apps** item (see [the web UI](/conventions/web-ui/index.html#logs-and-chat-apps)). A small red count on the Settings button says errors were logged since the app started.

**Over the API** , for an admin: `GET /logs` lists the logs and how many sources logged an error since the app started, and `GET /logs?area=gateways&tail=200&level=warn&q=text` gives lines. The client has `logs()`. See [the agent API](/conventions/agent-bx/index.html).

## Chat apps

`GET /gateways` (and **Chat apps** in the web page) says, for each chat app the project names:

* whether it is **connected** , **stopped** , **failing** (stopped, with an error logged) or **not registered**;
* which of its credentials are set, by the name of the environment variable and set or not set, never the value;
* when it last had a conversation, and its last error.

The chat apps themselves are still set up in `gateways/<name>.bx` and `.env`, and read when the app starts. See [gateways](/conventions/gateways/index.html).

See add . Consuming remote servers Declared directly on Agent.yaml (not a file under mcp/ ), via mcpServers : # Agent.yaml name: my-agent model: openai/gpt-5 mcpServers: - https://example.com/mcp - url: https://other.com/mcp name: other Each entry is either a bare URL string or a mapping. The server's address name A label for the file. It is not sent to the server token A bearer token. Must be an ${env.NAME} placeholder: a token written in the file is a build error password , user Basic authentication. password must be an ${env.NAME} placeholder headers Extra request headers. Values can use ${env.NAME} timeout Milliseconds oauth The server asks each person to sign in (mail, a calendar). oauth: true or a mapping. Needs a name . See connect allowedHosts The host names the server's address may have, for example [api.example.com, "*.example.com"] . *.example.com matches any subdomain, not example.com itself. A request to any other host is refused before anything is sent redirects false treats a redirect answer as a failure and never follows it maxResponseBytes Refuses an answer longer than this many characters handshake true sends the MCP initialize handshake before the first call prefix Tools are named prefix__tool , so two servers cannot clash toolFilter A list of tool names; only these are given to the agent Placeholders are replaced with the environment variable when the app starts , never at build time, so a secret stays out of the project and out of a packaged .bxa . A variable that is not set fails the agent at startup and names it; one that is set but empty lets the agent start, the server refuses the connection, and bx-ai logs that and carries on without that server's tools. Any other key is a build error that lists the valid ones. The entries are passed into the generated aiAgent(mcpServers: [...]) call. No network connection is ever attempted at build time - reachability is a runtime concern; an unreachable server at build time is not a build error. This section is for servers reached over the web; servers that run as a program on the agent's machine are next. bxAgents new offers GitHub, Stripe, Notion, Atlassian, Cloudflare, Supabase and Git and writes the entry and the .env stub for you. Subagents can declare their own mcpServers independently - each node in the agent tree gets its own resolved list. Servers that run as a program An entry with command starts an MCP server as a program on the machine that runs the agent, and talks to it over the program's standard input and output: mcpServers: - name: git command: [uvx, mcp-server-git] prefix: git toolFilter: [git_status, git_diff, git_log] - name: browser command: [bxplaywright, mcp] env: PLAYWRIGHT_API_KEY: ${env.PLAYWRIGHT_API_KEY} cwd: . Key Meaning command Required. A list: the program, then its arguments. It is never run through a shell name A label for the file env Environment variables for the program. A variable whose name contains KEY , TOKEN , SECRET , PASSWORD or CREDENTIAL must be an ${env.NAME} placeholder cwd The folder the program starts in inheritEnv false starts it with only env . Default true maxRestarts How many times in a row a program that died is started again. Default 2 timeout Milliseconds per request prefix , toolFilter As for web servers The program starts on the first call and is closed when the app stops. command cannot be combined with url , and the keys that only make sense for a web server ( token , headers , user , password , allowedHosts , redirects , maxResponseBytes , handshake ) are a build error on it. When the app starts, the programs your agents declare become bx-ai's mcp.stdio.allowedCommands setting, so the process starts only what the project declared. A list you set yourself (for example in .boxlang.json ) is left alone and must name the programs. bxAgents doctor warns when a program is not on the PATH. A program runs with your user's rights on the machine that hosts the agent. Read what you start, and use toolFilter to limit what the agent may call. Hosting a local server Each mcp/*.bx file is a local MCP server your project hosts, exposing a subset of your tools/ as MCP tools: // mcp/localServer.bx class { function configure() { return { description : "Internal tools MCP server", version : "1.0.0", cors : "*", // optional - CORS origin(s) allowed to call this server; omit for none tools : [ "sayHello" ] // names of tools already declared under tools/ }; } } The entry's discovered name is its filename ( localServer.bx → localServer ), not any name field inside its own configure() struct - a project may still set one for documentation, but it's ignored for naming/registration purposes. cors is optional and defaults to an empty string (no CORS header) when omitted - passed straight through as mcpServer() 's 4th positional argument. At build time, the file is copied verbatim into the generated app's mcp/ folder, and a registration statement is emitted into the generated base Application ( bxagents/Application.bx )'s onApplicationStart() : mcpServer( "localServer", "Internal tools MCP server", "1.0.0", "*" ) .registerTool( aiToolRegistry().get( "sayHello" ) ) mcpServer(name, ...) is a global, name-keyed singleton getter in bx-ai - registering it once at startup is all that's needed; there's no WireBox mapping involved (unlike the agent-exposure singleton used by toAi() ). Exposing a local server over HTTP A local mcp/* server isn't reachable over HTTP on its own - pair it with a gateways/ exposure entry naming it as the target : // gateways/expose-mcp.bx class { function configure() { return { exposes : "mcp", path : "/mcp/tools", target : "localServer" }; } } Validation An mcpServers entry (struct form) needs a url or a command , not both and not neither. An mcpServers entry that's neither a non-empty string nor a struct fails validation. A command must be a list of non-empty words. A key for the other kind of server, an env secret written in the file, and a mistyped allowedHosts , redirects , handshake , prefix or toolFilter fail validation. A gateways/ entry with exposes: "mcp" and a target that doesn't match any discovered mcp/* entry fails validation.

A program runs with your user's rights on the machine that hosts the agent. Read what you start, and use `toolFilter` to limit what the agent may call. ## Hosting a local server Each `mcp/*.bx` file is a local MCP server your project hosts, exposing a subset of your `tools/` as MCP tools: ```javascript // mcp/localServer.bx class { function configure() { return { description : "Internal tools MCP server", version : "1.0.0", cors : "*", // optional - CORS origin(s) allowed to call this server; omit for none tools : [ "sayHello" ] // names of tools already declared under tools/ }; } } ``` The entry's discovered name is its **filename** (`localServer.bx` → `localServer`), not any `name` field inside its own `configure()` struct - a project may still set one for documentation, but it's ignored for naming/registration purposes. `cors` is optional and defaults to an empty string (no CORS header) when omitted - passed straight through as `mcpServer()`'s 4th positional argument. At build time, the file is copied verbatim into the generated app's `mcp/` folder, and a registration statement is emitted into the generated base `Application` ([`bxagents/Application.bx`](/conventions/application-bx/index.html))'s `onApplicationStart()`: ```javascript mcpServer( "localServer", "Internal tools MCP server", "1.0.0", "*" ) .registerTool( aiToolRegistry().get( "sayHello" ) ) ``` `mcpServer(name, ...)` is a global, name-keyed singleton getter in bx-ai - registering it once at startup is all that's needed; there's no WireBox mapping involved (unlike the agent-exposure singleton used by `toAi()`). ## Exposing a local server over HTTP A local `mcp/*` server isn't reachable over HTTP on its own - pair it with a [`gateways/`](/conventions/gateways/index.html) exposure entry naming it as the `target`: ```javascript // gateways/expose-mcp.bx class { function configure() { return { exposes : "mcp", path : "/mcp/tools", target : "localServer" }; } } ``` ## Validation * An `mcpServers` entry (struct form) needs a `url` or a `command`, not both and not neither. * An `mcpServers` entry that's neither a non-empty string nor a struct fails validation. * A `command` must be a list of non-empty words. A key for the other kind of server, an `env` secret written in the file, and a mistyped `allowedHosts`, `redirects`, `handshake`, `prefix` or `toolFilter` fail validation. * A `gateways/` entry with `exposes: "mcp"` and a `target` that doesn't match any discovered `mcp/*` entry fails validation.

# Models and profiles

Which model an agent uses is written in `Agent.yaml`. The build maps it onto bx-ai's settings, so you never write a `boxlang.json` for it. The names are bx-ai's own: `provider`, `model`, `params`, `options`, `providers`, `profiles`.

```yaml
provider: openai                 # the default model
model: gpt-5
params: { temperature: 0.2 }

providers:                       # settings for another provider
  claude: { params: { max_tokens: 4000 }, options: { timeout: 90 } }

profiles:                        # named combinations
  fast:    { description: Cheap and quick, provider: openai, model: gpt-5-mini, params: { temperature: 0 } }
  planner: { description: Careful planning, provider: claude, model: claude-opus-4, apiKeyEnv: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }
defaultProfile: fast             # optional

embeddings:    { provider: openai, model: text-embedding-3-small }
speech:        { provider: openai, model: tts-1, voice: nova }
transcription: { provider: openai, model: whisper-1 }
image:         { provider: openai, model: gpt-image-1, size: 1024x1024 }
```

## The default model

`provider`, `model` and `params` are the model every agent uses when it says nothing else. `model: openai/gpt-5` still works as shorthand for `provider: openai` plus `model: gpt-5`. `params` are request parameters such as `temperature` and `max_tokens`. `options` (timeout and similar) apply to the default provider.

`contextWindow` and `vision` say what the default model can do, see [What the project knows about a model](#what-the-project-knows-about-a-model).

## Other providers

`providers` holds `params` and `options` for a provider by name, for the ones you use through a profile or a subagent. `bxAgents add provider` writes one for you. The key for each provider is read from its usual environment variable (`OPENAI_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, ...); `bxAgents doctor` tells you when one is missing.

## Profiles

A profile is a named combination: a provider, a model, params, options and the name of the environment variable that holds its key. It can carry a `description`.

|            Key            |                                                              Meaning                                                               |
|---------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `description`             | For people and the terminal and web pickers.                                                                                       |
| `provider`, `model`       | What it runs on. A profile without a provider uses the default provider.                                                           |
| `params`, `options`       | Layered on top of the provider's and the default's: `params` from the default, then the provider, then the profile.                |
| `apiKeyEnv`               | The **name** of the variable that holds the key. A key itself is never written in `Agent.yaml`; a profile that has one is refused. |
| `contextWindow`, `vision` | What the project knows about the model, see below.                                                                                 |

A profile cannot be named `default` or like a provider (`openai`, `claude`, ...), because both are selected by name. `defaultProfile` picks which profile is used when nothing asks for another one: it is the default model. If the file also has a top-level `model`, the profile wins and the build and `doctor` warn that the `model` line is ignored. Without a `defaultProfile`, the top-level `provider` and `model` are the default. `bxAgents add profile` writes a profile (and `--default` the `defaultProfile`) without touching the rest of the file; see [`add profile`](/cli-reference/index.html#add-profile).

## What the project knows about a model

bx-ai has no way to ask a model how much it can hold or whether it can see images, so you can say so, on the default model and on each profile:

```yaml
contextWindow: 128000      # tokens the default model can hold
vision: true               # the default model can see images
profiles:
  fast:
    provider: openai
    model: gpt-5-mini
    contextWindow: 400000
    vision: false
```

`contextWindow` is a whole number of tokens and `vision` is `true` or `false`; `build` refuses anything else. Both are optional and nothing is guessed: a model with no entry is simply unknown. bx-ai does not read them. The chat shows them in `/info` and `/model`, and uses `contextWindow` for the share of the window the context takes (`/context`, the status bar and the web header). `vision: false` makes the chat refuse a picture before it is sent, with a message instead of a provider error; when `vision` is not set the picture goes through.

## Testing a model

`/ping` in the chat and `bxAgents models test` send a model one tiny question through bx-ai and say whether it answered, and how long it took, so a wrong key or model name shows up before a conversation does. See [`models`](/cli-reference/index.html#models) and [Models in the chat](/cli-reference/index.html#models-in-the-chat).

## Which agent uses what

An agent uses its own `profile:`, else its own `model:` (a `provider/model` slug), else the default. Every subagent inherits the root's settings, and may set its own `model` or `profile`:

```yaml
# subagents/planner/Agent.yaml
name: planner
profile: planner
```

`providers`, `profiles`, `defaultProfile`, `params`, `options` and the capability keys apply to the whole app, so they belong in the project's own `Agent.yaml`; a subagent that sets them fails validation.

## Capability defaults

`embeddings`, `speech`, `transcription` and `image` set bx-ai's defaults for `aiEmbed()`, `aiSpeak()`, `aiTranscribe()` and `aiImage()`. They do not take profiles. Each takes `provider` and `model`; `speech` also `voice` and `format`, and `image` also `size`, `quality`, `style` and `instructions`. Any other key fails `build`. bx-ai has one audio provider, so `speech` and `transcription` must name the same one. `bxAgents add capability` writes one; see [`add capability`](/cli-reference/index.html#add-capability).

## Validation and tests

`bxAgents build` checks all of the above by bx-ai's own rules and names the file and the key. Under `bxAgents test` every profile runs on the `mock` provider, so a test never reaches the network.

## How it reaches bx-ai

The build writes the settings to `config/bxai-settings.json` in the app, and the app merges them into bx-ai's settings when it starts, before ColdBox boots and builds the agents. They travel with the app wherever it runs (`serve`, a `.bxa`, a container).

title: modules/
body: modules/ modules/ holds BoxLang module dependencies your agent needs - one immediate subfolder per module, discovered by folder name (not recursive - only the top level of modules/ is enumerated). modules/ └── my-extra-module/ ├── module.json └── ... Declaring dependencies between modules A module folder may include a module.json with a dependsOn array naming other modules/* entries by folder name: { "dependsOn": [ "some-other-module" ] } This is BxAgents' own dependency-declaration convention for validation purposes - it is independent of BoxLang's own module-loading mechanism. Info Today build validates modules/ and records each entry (with a content hash) in the manifest , but it does not copy the folders into the generated app or load them. To give the generated app a library, use the project lib/ folder described in Installation . Validation A module.json that isn't valid JSON fails the build with a parse error naming the offending module. A dependsOn entry naming a module that isn't itself a discovered modules/* folder fails validation ("depends on unknown module"). Circular dependencies are rejected the same way subagent cycles are - full cycle path reported, DFS-based detection, no code generation happens until the graph is acyclic. A module.json is entirely optional - a module folder with none is assumed to have no declared dependencies.

# modules/

`modules/` holds BoxLang module dependencies your agent needs - one immediate subfolder per module, discovered by folder name (not recursive - only the top level of `modules/` is enumerated).

    modules/
    └── my-extra-module/
        ├── module.json
        └── ...

## Declaring dependencies between modules

A module folder may include a `module.json` with a `dependsOn` array naming other `modules/*` entries by folder name:

```json
{
	"dependsOn": [ "some-other-module" ]
}
```

This is BxAgents' own dependency-declaration convention for validation purposes - it is independent of BoxLang's own module-loading mechanism.
> **Info**
>
> Today `build` validates `modules/` and records each entry (with a content hash) in the [manifest](/manifest/index.html), but it does not copy the folders into the generated app or load them. To give the generated app a library, use the project `lib/` folder described in [Installation](/getting-started/installation/index.html#adding-your-own-libraries).

## Validation

* A `module.json` that isn't valid JSON fails the build with a parse error naming the offending module.
* A `dependsOn` entry naming a module that isn't itself a discovered `modules/*` folder fails validation ("depends on unknown module").
* **Circular dependencies** are rejected the same way [subagent](/conventions/subagents/index.html) cycles are - full cycle path reported, DFS-based detection, no code generation happens until the graph is acyclic.
* A `module.json` is entirely optional - a module folder with none is assumed to have no declared dependencies.

# Quick Start

![A terminal session: bxAgents new scaffolds a project, bxAgents build assembles a ColdBox app, bxAgents inspect prints the agent, model and environment, and bxAgents serve starts it on http://127.0.0.1:8080](/assets/cli-quickstart.svg)

By the end you will have an agent you can chat with in the terminal and serve over HTTP. This walks through the full lifecycle of a BxAgents project: scaffold, edit, build, run.

## 1. Scaffold a project

```bash
bxAgents new my-agent
```

At a terminal this asks what the agent should do (its model, tools, MCP servers, channels, how people reach it, where it deploys) and writes the project to match; see [the new wizard](/guides/new-wizard/index.html). It ends by printing the one-line command that builds the same project without questions. To skip the questions, pass a model:

```bash
bxAgents new my-agent --model=openai/gpt-5
```

`--model` is a `provider/model` slug (written to `Agent.yaml` as separate `provider:` and `model:` lines) - see [the model slug](/conventions/agent-bx/index.html#the-model-slug) for how it's parsed. `--name` and `--description` are optional; `--name` defaults to the target directory's own name.

This creates:

    my-agent/
    ├── Application.bx
    ├── Agent.yaml
    ├── instructions.md
    ├── tools/
    ├── skills/
    ├── subagents/
    ├── gateways/
    ├── schedules/
    ├── mcp/
    ├── interceptors/
    ├── modules/
    ├── box.json
    └── tests/
        └── specs/
            └── AgentSpec.bx

Plus a root [`Application.bx`](/conventions/application-bx/index.html) that extends the class every build generates (add your own settings and hooks there), a `.env` (with `BOXLANG_HOME=.build/runtime`; secrets live here, so put your provider API keys in it and keep it out of source control), a `.gitignore` and a few dotfiles (`.editorconfig`, `.gitattributes`, `.bxlint.json`, `.markdownlint.json`, `.boxlang.json`). BoxLang loads the `.env` from the project root itself. The root `box.json` lists `testbox` as a development dependency.

This is the `minimal` starter - the default when `--template` is omitted. A template is a preset: the wizard (and flags such as `--with`, `--channels` and `--deploy`) add tools, channels and a deploy target on top of it. `new` can also scaffold one of 7 other built-in starters (`--template=webui-chat|slack-bot|telegram-bot|github-bot|mcp-server|scheduled|multi-agent`), each adding a bit of pre-wired content (a gateway, a scheduler) on top of the same skeleton, or skip scaffolding entirely and create the project from an existing GitHub repo (`--repo=owner/repo`) or a ForgeBox package (`--forgebox=<slug>`) instead - see the [CLI Reference](/cli-reference/index.html#new) for the full list and how each one works. The agent is defined by an `Agent.yaml` by default; pass `--class` to scaffold the advanced, class-based `Agent.bx` instead (see [Agent.bx](/conventions/agent-bx/index.html)).

`Agent.yaml` looks like this (`--description` adds a `description:` line):

```yaml
# Your agent. Most agents need nothing more than this file and instructions.md.
# For code in the definition (hooks, dynamic instructions), scaffold with --class.
name: my-agent
provider: openai
model: gpt-5

environments:
  # `bxAgents test` builds against this override by default (see
  # BaseAgentSpec.bx) so a fresh project's tests need no API key or
  # network access - swap the model to test against a real provider.
  test:
    model: mock/mock-model
```

The agent is just this file plus `instructions.md`. See [Agent.yaml](/conventions/agent-yaml/index.html) for every key.

Every convention folder is created empty - add files to the ones your agent actually needs and delete (or just ignore) the rest.

## 2. Edit

Open `instructions.md` and write the agent's system prompt, and adjust `name`, `description` or `model` in `Agent.yaml` as you like. Add a tool:

```javascript
// tools/Greeter.bx
class {

	@AITool( "Say hello to someone by name." )
	function sayHello( name ) {
		return "Hello, " & arguments.name & "!";
	}

}
```

See the [Conventions](/conventions/agent-yaml/index.html) section for every other folder (`skills/`, `subagents/`, `gateways/`, `schedules/`, `mcp/`, `interceptors/`, `modules/`). You do not have to write them by hand: `bxAgents add <kind>` (`tool`, `skill`, `subagent`, `gateway`, `schedule`, `interceptor`, `mcp`, `profile`, `provider`, `capability`, `extension`) asks a few questions and writes the files, and `--dry-run` shows them first.

## 3. Test it

```bash
box install        # once, to fetch testbox into lib/testbox (`new` already tried this for you)
bxAgents test
```

The scaffolded `tests/specs/AgentSpec.bx` passes out of the box - it builds your agent against the `mock` provider (no API key or network needed) and asserts on a scripted response. See [tests/](/conventions/testing/index.html) for `mockResponses()` and the custom matchers (`toHaveCalledTool`, etc.) available to your own specs.

## 4. Build

```bash
bxAgents build
```

Runs the full [build pipeline](/build-pipeline/index.html) - config resolution, discovery, validation, code generation, manifest normalization - and writes a real ColdBox application to `.build/app/`, plus `.build/manifest.json`. Run `bxAgents build --environment=production` to build against an `Agent.yaml` environment override (see [Agent.yaml](/conventions/agent-yaml/index.html#environments)).

If your project fails validation (duplicate tool names, an unknown model provider, a gateway entry with a bad path, ...) `build` fails with every collected error - not just the first one.

## 5. Run it

Two ways to talk to the built agent - both load the exact same `GeneratedAgentFactory.bx` and build the exact same agent tree, so they never diverge:

**Interactively, from the terminal:**

```bash
bxAgents chat
```

At a terminal this is a full-screen chat that keeps your scrollback: answers stream in as formatted Markdown, tool calls show as they run, Esc stops the agent, and typing `/` lists the commands (`/sessions`, `/resume`, `/name`, `/fork`, `/export`, `/notes`, `/context` and more). Type `@` to attach a file, or `@picture.png` to send a picture. Conversations are listed in `data/chat.db` (the messages last as long as the agent's memory does), so `bxAgents chat --continue` can pick up where you left off. See [the terminal UI](/guides/terminal-ui/index.html) and [Slash commands](/guides/slash-commands/index.html). To chat against the full app (schedulers, interceptors, gateways), use `bxAgents chat --server`, or `--connect=<url>` for a server that is already running (add `--token=<token>` if it wants one).

**Over HTTP** , via a real [`boxlang-miniserver`](https://boxlang.ortusbooks.com/getting-started/running-boxlang/miniserver) process:

```bash
bxAgents serve --port=8080
```

Every served agent has an HTTP API at `/__bxagents` (open on your own machine, behind tokens when you share it), and the web page, the terminal chat and chat platforms all use it. See [Call your agent from code](/guides/agent-api/index.html).

If your project also has a `gateways/*` entry with `{ exposes: "agent", path: "/api/chat" }`, the agent is reachable at `POST http://localhost:8080/api/chat/invoke` (and `/stream`, `/batch`, `/info` - see [gateways/](/conventions/gateways/index.html)). An `exposes: "webui"` entry adds the browser chat page.

## 6. Inspect, package, deploy

```bash
bxAgents doctor               # runtime, modules, project checks and unset environment variables
bxAgents inspect              # how the agent is composed: agents, tools, env vars, checks
bxAgents package --version=1.0.0   # writes dist/my-agent-1.0.0.bxa + .sha256
bxAgents deploy --destination=/path/to/somewhere   # copies the newest .bxa there
```

See [The Manifest](/manifest/index.html) and [Deployment \& Secrets](/deployment-and-secrets/index.html).

## 7. Clean up

```bash
bxAgents clean
```

Removes `.build/` and `dist/` only - your source conventions (`Agent.yaml`, `tools/`, etc.) are never touched.

## Next steps

* Walk through every convention folder in [Conventions](/conventions/agent-yaml/index.html).
* Look at the working sample projects in [`examples/`](https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/bx-agents/tree/development/examples).
* See every verb's flags in [CLI Reference](/cli-reference/index.html).

markdown:
# Routines

A routine is a prompt the agent runs on a schedule, as the person who made it. "Every weekday at 9, check the build and tell me what broke" is a routine. A person makes it by asking the agent, and the agent keeps it in the chat database. The answer can go to a chat app, and a routine can keep reports as files.

Routines are not [schedulers](/conventions/schedules/index.html). They are for the people who use the agent, not for the developer.

|                |       `schedules/*.bx` scheduler       |                       Routine                        |
|----------------|----------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|
| Who makes it   | The developer, in a file               | Anyone, by asking the agent                          |
| Where it lives | In the project, shipped with the agent | In the chat database, per person                     |
| Runs as        | The app                                | The person who made it, with their notes and volumes |
| Changed by     | Editing the file and rebuilding        | Asking the agent, while the app runs                 |
| Turned on by   | Existing                               | `routines.enabled: true`                             |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P[Person asks the agent] --> T[routine_schedule, approved by the person]
  T --> S[(routines table)]
  H[Heartbeat, every minute] --> S
  H --> R[Runner]
  R --> C[The routine's own conversation]
  R --> L[routines.log and heartbeat.log]
```

## Turn it on

Routines are off by default, so a published agent never grows automated work by surprise.

```yaml
routines:
  enabled: true
  minInterval: 5m
  timezone: Europe/Madrid
```

With the feature off there are no routine tools, no heartbeat and no routines capability. The settings:

|      Setting      |   Default    |                                                          Meaning                                                          |
|-------------------|--------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `enabled`         | `false`      | Turns the feature on                                                                                                      |
| `maxPerUser`      | `20`         | The most routines one person may have (1 to 200)                                                                          |
| `minInterval`     | `5m`         | The shortest a routine may repeat (`1m` to `1d`)                                                                          |
| `maxParallel`     | `2`          | How many routines the heartbeat starts in one beat (1 to 10)                                                              |
| `maxPromptLength` | `4000`       | The longest prompt, in characters (200 to 20000). Longer instructions belong in a [skill](/conventions/skills/index.html) |
| `approvalTimeout` | `24h`        | How long a run waits for a person to approve a tool (`5m` to `7d`)                                                        |
| `timezone`        | the server's | The time zone cron expressions are read in, an IANA name such as `Europe/Madrid`                                          |
| `summaryLength`   | `1500`       | How many characters of an answer are sent to a chat app (200 to 4000)                                                     |
| `maxReportSize`   | `256kb`      | The largest report file a routine may save (`1kb` to `5mb`)                                                               |
| `maxReportFiles`  | `500`        | The most files in one routine's results folder (10 to 5000)                                                               |

A duration is a whole number with `m`, `h` or `d`, and a size a whole number with `kb` or `mb`. A bad value stops the build and `doctor` names it.

## Making one

Ask the agent: "every weekday at 9, check the build". The agent calls `routine_schedule` and a person approves it, as for any tool that needs approval. The answer says when it first runs.

A schedule is stored in one of two forms:

* a 5 field cron expression, `minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week`, such as `0 9 * * 1-5`
* an interval, `every 30m`, `every 2h` or `every 1d`

The model turns plain words into one of these, and the tools answer with the English reading ("weekdays at 09:00") and the next run time, so a mistake is seen straight away.

## The tools

Every tool the agent gets from BX Agents is named `{type}_{action}`, so permissions can match them by pattern later.

|        Tool        |                                    Does                                     | Needs a person's approval |
|--------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------|
| `routine_schedule` | Makes a routine, and says where its answer goes                             | Yes                       |
| `routine_list`     | Lists yours, with when each runs next and how the last run went             | No                        |
| `routine_update`   | Changes the schedule, the prompt, where the answer goes, or any of them     | Yes                       |
| `routine_pause`    | Stops one without deleting it                                               | No                        |
| `routine_resume`   | Starts a paused one again, and clears its failures                          | No                        |
| `routine_run`      | Runs one at the next beat instead of waiting                                | No                        |
| `routine_delete`   | Deletes one. Its conversation and reports stay                              | Yes                       |
| `report_save`      | Saves a report file, for the routine that is running. Refused anywhere else | No                        |
| `report_list`      | Lists a routine's report files                                              | No                        |
| `report_read`      | Reads one                                                                   | No                        |

The tools act as the person in the conversation, never as an admin, and only the root agent has them. A routine's own run is refused the `routine_*` tools, so a routine cannot make or change routines. There is no tool that deletes a report.

## A run

Every minute the **heartbeat** , a scheduler the build adds, looks for routines that are due and starts them, at most `maxParallel` at once. Each run:

* is a normal turn as the person who owns the routine, so their notes, volumes and tool approvals all apply, and nothing extra is allowed
* happens in a conversation of its own, `routine-<name>-<id>`, which the person finds in their conversation list and reads like any other
* never overlaps itself: a routine still running is skipped, and the skip is logged
* stops for approval like any chat. The routine shows as waiting, the person answers in its conversation, and after `approvalTimeout` the run is cancelled and counts as a failure

Three failures in a row pause the routine. `routine_resume` starts it again. If the server was down when a routine was due, it runs once on start, never once per missed time.

An admin sees and manages every person's routines. Nobody else can see yours.

## Where the answer goes

Each routine has a destination, set when it is made:

|            Destination            |                                                      Meaning                                                      |
|-----------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| nothing said                      | The chat app chat the person is writing in, if that is where they asked. Otherwise the routine's own conversation |
| `routine`                         | The routine's own conversation only                                                                               |
| `gateway:telegram` (any chat app) | A chat on that [chat app](/conventions/gateways/index.html)                                                       |

Chat apps belong to the person who runs the agent. A person writing from a chat app may send a routine's answer to their own chat there. Anyone else is limited to the routine's own conversation, and the local user can choose a chat app, naming the chat when it has talked to more than one. A chat app can only write to a chat it has already heard from, because that is when the agent learns its address (and for Teams, the address it needs to reply). If the chat app has talked to nobody, the agent tells the owner to message the bot once.

What is sent is a summary: the answer cut to `summaryLength` characters, headed `Routine <name>:`, and a last line naming the reports the run saved. The whole answer is in the routine's conversation. A message that cannot be sent (the chat app is not connected, the chat is unknown, the platform refuses) counts as a failed run, so three in a row pause the routine, and `routines.log` says why. The log never holds the text.

A run that stopped for an approval is not sent anywhere once a person answers: its answer is in its conversation.

## Reports

A routine can save what it found as files: `report_save( file, content )` while it runs. They go in `<data home>/routines/<name>-<id>/`, are never overwritten (a name already used becomes `report-2.md`), and are never deleted automatically.

* A file name is letters, digits, `.`, `_` and `-`, up to 80 characters, ending in `.md`, `.txt`, `.json`, `.csv` or `.html`.
* A file is at most `maxReportSize`, and a folder holds at most `maxReportFiles`; at the limit the agent is told a person has to clean up.
* The agent reads reports back with `report_list` and `report_read` for the person's own routines. A long file is cut when read.
* The reports are in a [backup](/conventions/data/index.html).

## Logs

`routines.log` records each routine made, changed, run, skipped, failed, sent and paused, and each report saved (its name, never its text), and `heartbeat.log` the beats that started something. A prompt is never logged, only the routine's name and its owner. See [logs](/conventions/logs/index.html).

## Not yet

The `/routines` command, `bxAgents routines` (with a way to read and clean up reports), the API routes and a Routines section in the web page come next. Until then a person reads a routine's reports by asking the agent, and removes old ones in the data home folder.
