markdown:
# The terminal UI

Two commands draw a full terminal screen: [`bxAgents chat`](/cli-reference/index.html#chat), where you talk to your agent, and [`bxAgents new`](/guides/new-wizard/index.html), where you answer questions and get a project. This page is the tour. Every command and flag is in the [CLI reference](/cli-reference/index.html); every slash command is in [Slash commands](/guides/slash-commands/index.html); a guided first session is in [Chat walkthroughs](/guides/chat-walkthrough/index.html).

*A chat session: slash commands, a tool call and a formatted answer. The answers in these recordings come from a scripted demo model, so they are canned. Everything else is the real screen.*

## Start a chat

```bash
bxAgents build          # chat needs a built agent (not with --connect)
bxAgents chat
```

|                      Run                      |                     Talks to                      |                       Use it when                       |
|-----------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------|
| `bxAgents chat`                               | The agent, loaded in this process                 | You want to talk to the agent. Fastest.                 |
| `bxAgents chat --server`                      | A throwaway local server                          | You need interceptors, schedules or gateways to be real |
| `bxAgents chat --connect=<url> [--token=<t>]` | A server that is already running                  | You want to talk to a deployment                        |
| `bxAgents chat --no-tui`                      | Same as the first, in a plain line-by-line prompt | A terminal that cannot draw, or you just prefer it      |

`--continue` reopens your latest conversation, `--session=<number or id>` a particular one, `--user=<name>` chooses whose conversations and notes you see.

## The screen

Finished turns are printed as ordinary terminal text, so **your scrollback, search and copy keep working**. Only two things are redrawn: the message box at the bottom and the answer being written.

* **Answers** stream in as they are produced and are printed as formatted Markdown when complete: headings, lists, tables with rounded borders, and code blocks coloured by language.
* **Tool calls** are shown with their arguments and how long they took.
* **Thinking** is shown while the model works and is never kept.
* **Approvals.** When a run stops for a [human-in-the-loop](/conventions/gateways/index.html) decision, the screen asks in place: approve once, approve for the conversation, or reject.
* **The hint row** under the box lists the keys and starts with the size of the context, such as `ctx ~12.4k / 128k 9%`. It is an estimate (characters divided by four), refreshed before every prompt.

![The terminal chat after two answers, with the message box open for a new command](/assets/tui/chat-answer.png)

*Finished turns are ordinary terminal text. The answer is formatted Markdown, with the tool call above it and the message box below.*

## Keys

|                        Key                        |                                   Does                                   |
|---------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Enter                                             | Send the message                                                         |
| Alt+Enter, Shift+Enter, Ctrl+J, or `\` then Enter | New line                                                                 |
| Up / Down                                         | Earlier and later messages, from the first or last line of the box       |
| Tab                                               | Complete a `/command` or an `@file`                                      |
| Ctrl+A / Home, Ctrl+E / End                       | Start and end of the line                                                |
| Ctrl+U, Ctrl+W                                    | Delete to the start of the line, delete the word before the cursor       |
| Ctrl+V                                            | Add the picture on the clipboard                                         |
| Ctrl+C                                            | Clear the box. On an empty box, leave. While the agent works, stop it    |
| Ctrl+D                                            | Leave, on an empty box (otherwise delete the character under the cursor) |
| Esc                                               | While the agent works, stop it at its next step (not mid-word)           |
| Enter while the agent works                       | **Steer**: your message is added to the run                              |
| `?` alone, or `/keys`                             | Show the keys as bound right now                                         |

![The output of /keys, listing every key with its action name](/assets/tui/chat-keys.png)

*`/keys` lists every key, the action name to use in `bxAgents.yml`, and what it does.*

### Change a key

Keys live in a file that belongs to you, not to any project: `~/.bxagents/bxAgents.yml` (set `BXAGENTS_USER_CONFIG` to use another file).

```yaml
chat:
  keys:
    newline: [ ctrl+n, alt+enter ]
    stop: ctrl+x
```

Actions you can change: `submit`, `newline`, `historyPrevious`, `historyNext`, `clear`, `exit`, `deleteToStart`, `deleteWord`, `lineStart`, `lineEnd`, `complete`, `pasteImage` and `stop`. Keys are written the way people say them: `enter`, `alt+enter`, `shift+enter`, `ctrl+j`, `esc`, `tab`, `up`, `down`, `home`, `end`, or a letter with `ctrl` or `alt`.

A typo never leaves you stuck. An unknown action, an unreadable key, or a key another action in the same place already uses is reported when the chat starts, and that action keeps its default keys.

## Commands: type `/`

A `/` at the start of the box opens a menu of commands. Keep typing to narrow it, Tab or Enter to take one. All of them are listed in [Slash commands](/guides/slash-commands/index.html); the ones you will use first are `/help`, `/new`, `/sessions`, `/resume`, `/context`, `/model` and `/exit`. `/stats` shows the tokens the model calls used, once `usage: true` is set in `Agent.yaml`.

## Conversations

Every chat is a conversation, kept in the project's shared chat database next to the web page's own.

|            Do            |                                     How                                     |
|--------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Start where you left off | `bxAgents chat --continue`, or `--session=<number or id>`                   |
| See the list             | `/sessions` (numbered, newest first)                                        |
| Go back to one           | `/resume 2`; with no number, the most recent                                |
| Name or copy one         | `/name Quarterly plan`, `/fork Other approach`                              |
| Save one                 | `/export plan.html` (or `.md`); `--format=md\|html` overrides the file name |
| Start a clean one        | `/new`, or `/clear` to empty this one                                       |

From a shell, `bxAgents sessions list|rename|fork|delete` does the same. A step by step run is in [Chat walkthroughs](/guides/chat-walkthrough/index.html#2-pick-a-conversation-up-again).

## Extensions

Extensions in the project's `extensions/` folder, in your own `~/.bxagents/extensions/` and in installed modules add commands, keys and status text to this screen. `/extensions` lists what loaded and what went wrong; `/reload` loads them again after an edit (admins, which you are in your own terminal). Keys an extension adds show in `/keys` and can be rebound under `chat: keys:` like any other. See [Write your first extension](/guides/first-extension/index.html).

## Files, pictures and your own machine

|         Type         |                                                                 Does                                                                  |
|----------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `@`                  | Lists the files under the folder you started in. Keep typing to narrow it                                                             |
| `@path/to/file`      | Sends a text file's content with the message                                                                                          |
| `@picture.png`       | Sends a picture (png, jpg, gif, webp) as an image part. Up to 4 per message, 5 MB each. Refused when the profile says `vision: false` |
| `!command`           | Runs a shell command **on your machine**; its output goes with your next message so the agent sees what you saw                       |
| `!!command`          | Same, shown on screen only                                                                                                            |
| `#function( args )`  | Calls one BoxLang built-in, such as `#dateFormat( now(), 'yyyy-mm-dd' )`; the result goes with your next message                      |
| `##function( args )` | Same, shown on screen only                                                                                                            |

`!` and `#` run locally even when the chat is connected to a server. Switch them off, or narrow them, in the same user file:

```yaml
chat:
  shell: false                       # or a shell: "bash -c", "pwsh -Command"
  bifs: [ dateFormat, listLen ]      # or false to switch # off
```

![The output of /context and a conversation being renamed](/assets/tui/chat-context.png)

*`/context` shows what the context is made of. It is worked out locally, no model is called.*

Details and limits: [CLI reference](/cli-reference/index.html#files-and-pictures-in-the-message).

## The look of the message box

Five styles, each with a top bar that carries a label and small facts (widgets):

|      Style       |                                       Look                                       |
|------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `bars` (default) | A bar above and below the box, hints and bottom widgets under the lower bar      |
| `bars-hints`     | The same two bars, hints and bottom widgets inside the lower one                 |
| `rule`           | One coloured rule above, hints below                                             |
| `box`            | A rounded box                                                                    |
| `panel`          | A tinted panel with a thick left bar. Drawn as `rule` without 256 or true colour |

Widgets: `agent`, `profile`, `folder`, `user`, `clock`, `machine`, `git`, `date`, `session`, `elapsed`, `ctx`. A widget with nothing to show (`git` outside a repository) is left out, and the last ones drop off when the line is too narrow.

Set the start for the project in `Agent.yaml`:

```yaml
tui:
  prompt: bars
  widgets:
    top: [ agent, folder, user, clock ]
    bottom: [ ctx, profile ]
```

Or change it for one chat: `/prompt box`, `/prompt top +git -clock`, `/prompt bottom none`.

## Notes screen

`/notes` opens a screen with the notes the agent keeps about you and about its own work: `a` add, `e` or Enter edit, `d` remove, `t` or Tab switch between yours and the agent's, `s` stats, Esc back. Needs a [`notes`](/conventions/agent-yaml/index.html#notes) block in `Agent.yaml`.

## Record it

`bxAgents chat --record=demo.cast` (or `/record demo.cast` inside the chat, `/record stop` to finish) saves the screen as an [asciicast](https://docs.asciinema.org/manual/asciicast/v2/). Replay with `asciinema play demo.cast`. Keystrokes are not recorded, but what you typed in the box and everything the agent printed is, tool arguments included. It needs the terminal screen.

## Colours and fallbacks

* **True colour, 256 colours or 16 colours** depending on `COLORTERM` and `TERM`.
* **`NO_COLOR`** set, or `TERM=dumb`: no colour at all.
* **Not an interactive terminal** (a pipe, CI): the chat falls back to the plain REPL. For scripts use [`invoke`](/cli-reference/index.html#invoke).
* **`bxAgents new`** asks its questions only in a terminal and without `--model`. Pass `--model` (a script is calling) and it uses flags and defaults; without a terminal it needs `--model`. See [the new wizard](/guides/new-wizard/index.html).

## Troubleshooting

|                 You see                 |                                               Cause and fix                                               |
|-----------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| The chat cannot find the agent          | Run `bxAgents build` first, or use `--connect`                                                            |
| A key does nothing                      | Run `/keys` to see what is bound, and rebind in `bxAgents.yml` if your terminal keeps that key for itself |
| Colours look wrong                      | Set `COLORTERM=truecolor`, or `NO_COLOR=1` to switch colour off                                           |
| `--connect` says 401                    | The server wants a token: `--token=<token>` or `BXAGENTS_TOKEN`                                           |
| A picture is refused                    | The profile sets `vision: false`, or the file is not png, jpg, gif or webp, or is over 5 MB               |
| `/export` writes to an unexpected place | Without a name the file is dated and written to the folder you started in                                 |

title: The web chat UI
body: The web chat UI A gateways/*.bx entry with exposes: "webui" ships a complete browser chat client for the agent - a conversation sidebar, streaming with reasoning and tool calls, human-in-the-loop approvals, per-visitor theming, and a real SQLite store behind it. It lives under gateways/ because that is where exposures are declared, but it is a subsystem in its own right, which is why it has its own page. // gateways/chat.bx class { function configure() { return { exposes : "webui", path : "/chat", apiKeyEnvVar: "CHAT_UI_API_KEY" // optional - the agent API's shared secret, see Securing the API }; } } That generates a static <path>/index.html (served directly - no route needed). The page is a client of the agent API at /__bxagents , the same one the terminal chat and the gateways use, so there is no second API under <path> . The agent API must stay enabled ( agentApi.enabled: false with a webui entry is a build error). The screenshot above is the actual generated page - the real, unmodified template this repo ships - branded with examples/webui-agent 's own theme / title / icon config and populated with example conversation content for illustration; bxAgents build && bxAgents serve in that example reproduces it. The UI is dependency-free vanilla HTML/CSS/JS - no Bootstrap, AlpineJS or Vite build step - and is pre-built and vendored inside BxAgents itself : bxAgents build never runs npm install / npm run build , and a generated project never needs Node or npm installed at all. Everything the page needs is inlined into the single generated index.html . That constraint is about the build, not about scope. The page is a full client: conversation sidebar, streaming with reasoning and tool calls, approvals, compaction, server-side theming. What is genuinely still missing is listed under What is not here yet . The page talks to the agent API at /__bxagents via POST /__bxagents/stream ( Accept: text/event-stream ), using fetch() + a manual ReadableStream reader - not the browser's EventSource , which can't POST or set custom headers, both needed here. Warning toAi() forwards each bx-ai chunk verbatim - it does not wrap it. ColdBox's AI Routing docs show the stream as data: {"token":"..."} lines, but its own source ( Router.cfc , toAi() 's stream sub-route) does emitter.send( chunk, "chunk" ) - so every frame carries the full normalized bx-ai envelope : event: chunk data: {"object":"chat.completion.chunk","choices":[{"delta":{"role":"assistant","content":"Ray","reasoning":"...","tool_calls":[...]}}]} event: done data: [DONE] There is no token key anywhere. A client written against that docs page - including this UI's own first version - reads undefined and renders nothing at all. Read choices[0].delta.content instead. Because the whole envelope arrives, reasoning and tool calls are already on the wire with no extra endpoint needed: delta.reasoning (normalized across every provider by bx-ai) renders as a collapsed "Thinking" strip, and delta.tool_calls as collapsed per-call chips. Tool-call arguments stream as partial JSON fragments keyed by index , so the page accumulates per index rather than assuming any single chunk holds a complete call. Walkthrough A minute and a half through the whole page: the password form, suggestions, a formatted answer, a tool call, a code block with its Copy button, the Settings menu, dark mode, notes and the access tokens panel. The voice is Kokoro (an Apache 2.0 model), and the page's answers come from a scripted demo model, so they are canned. Captions are on. Sign in. Accounts come from users . The header. Chats, the context ring and a Settings gear; everything else is in the Settings menu. The picker shows when the entry lists profiles . Streaming. Replies render Markdown as they arrive. Model picker. The pick is sent with each message, in the same conversation. Tools. Each call shows its name and arguments. Conversations. Saved per account, and still there after a reload. Notes. What the agent should remember, with the size it adds. Theme. Light or dark, remembered, with your theme accent. Context. The ring fills as the conversation grows; click it for the breakdown. Commands. Type / for the menu. Suggestions. An empty conversation can offer suggestions that send with one click. Code. Each block shows its language and copies the code itself. Settings. One gear holds the conversation actions, your notes, appearance and the server items. Appearance. Mode, accent, text size and density, kept in this browser. Access tokens. An admin makes and revokes named tokens; the secret is shown once. What a streaming turn actually looks like sequenceDiagram autonumber participant B as browser (generated index.html) participant H as handlers/AgentApi.bx participant A as the agent participant D as the shared store (SQLite) B->>H: POST /__bxagents/stream, Accept: text/event-stream H->>D: resolve the conversation for this session H->>A: agent.stream( ... ) H-->>B: event: thread - the threadId, sent BEFORE the first chunk loop for every chunk bx-ai emits A-->>H: a full normalized bx-ai envelope H-->>B: event: chunk - choices[0].delta.content / .reasoning / .tool_calls end H->>D: persist the turn H-->>B: event: done - [DONE] The thread event goes first because a response header cannot be read before the body starts arriving, and the page needs that threadId to be able to POST /cancel mid-turn. The API the page calls The page has no API of its own. Everything it does goes through the agent API's routes, documented under The always-on agent route : turns ( /stream , /cancel , /steer , /resume , /pending ), conversations ( /sessions , /history , /clear , /compact , /export ), /preferences , /notes , /commands and /command , and the capability routes ( /agent , /context , /status , /slots , /profiles , /tools ). Anything the page can do, a script can do with the same calls. Each call carries three headers: Header Why x-bxagents-source: web Marks conversations the page starts, so the API's ?source= filter ( GET /__bxagents/sessions?source=web ) can tell them from terminal and gateway ones x-bxagents-token The password typed in the Password form (opened from Password in the Settings menu, or by itself when the server answers 401 ), when one is set (see Securing the API ) x-bxagents-csrf: 1 Sent on every request. A request made with the sign-in cookie that changes something must carry it, so another site cannot make your browser do it Identity is the API's: with no users the page is the one open local user, shared with the terminal chat on the same machine, and with users it is the signed-in account. Slash commands Type / in the message box and a menu of commands appears (arrow keys, Tab to complete, Esc to close). They are the same commands as in the terminal chat : /help , /new , /tools , /volumes , /sessions , /resume , /clear , /compact , /model , /info , /context , /remember , /notes , /name , /fork , /export , /ping and /keys . Pressing Enter runs the line on the server with POST /command and draws the answer: text, a table, or buttons to pick from. /new , /resume and /fork move the page to the conversation they name, /clear reloads the transcript, and /export [file] [--format=md|html] hands the conversation to the browser to save ( Fork this conversation and Export in the Settings menu run /fork and /export ). The reply is data, so any client can use it: { "success": true, "conversationId": "...", "blocks": [ { "type": "table", "layout": "keyvalue", "rows": [ [ "Agent", "helper" ] ] } ], "effects": [ { "type": "conversation", "id": "..." } ] } Blocks are text , table , choose (options, each with the command line to run), transcript and file ( { name, mime, text } , which the page saves); effects say what happened to the conversation ( reset , conversation ). /info leaves out where the database file is. A command that only makes sense on your own machine ( /copy , /record , /profile ) is not offered, and a server never switches the shared agent's model: the page picks a profile per message instead. threadId is server-authoritative: taken from the request when supplied, minted otherwise, and always echoed back - as an X-Thread-Id response header on /invoke and /batch , and as a thread SSE event sent before the first chunk on /stream (a header can't be read before the body starts arriving). That's the same contract ColdBox 8.1's own toAi() adopted, so a client written against one works against the other. Warning Stop must go through /cancel , not just an aborted fetch. Aborting the HTTP request only stops the browser listening - the server keeps running the turn, calling tools and spending tokens. The page therefore sends a threadId with every turn and posts it to /cancel before aborting, so agent.cancelRun() can signal the run at its next checkpoint. /clear and /compact are both careful about scope. /clear goes through each memory's own clear( userId, conversationId ) rather than AiAgent.clearMemory() , which takes no arguments and would wipe every visitor's history; /compact goes through summarize( config, userId, conversationId ) for the same reason. Compaction replaces this conversation's older messages with an AI-written summary and keeps the most recent few, touching nothing outside the caller's (userId, conversationId) pair. Info /compact needs a summary model, and reports whether it has one. summarize() is a silent no-op unless the memory has both summaryProvider and summaryModel configured, and also when the conversation is already at or under keepRecent . Neither is an error, so /compact returns { compacted, before, after } and lets the caller see for itself, and /info 's capabilities.compact reports whether a summary model is configured at all - so a page can hide a button that would do nothing rather than look broken. Only keepRecent is taken from the request. summarize() also honours model / provider overrides, but accepting those here would let any visitor aim a summarization call at a provider and model of their choosing on your credentials - the memory's own config decides that instead. # Agent.yaml - what makes /compact functional memory: type: cache summaryProvider: openai summaryModel: gpt-4o-mini summaryThreshold: 10 Choosing the model By default the page talks to the agent's own model and offers no choice. List profiles in the entry and the header gets a model picker: // gateways/chat.bx return { exposes : "webui", path : "/chat", profiles : [ "fast", "planner" ] }; GET /profiles returns only the listed profiles: name, description, provider, model and which is the default. Never a key. The page sends the pick with each message as options.profile and remembers it in the browser. "Default model" sends none. A request that names any profile that is not listed is a 400 , whether or not Agent.yaml declares it. A profile is a model your server pays for, so the browser never chooses one you did not offer. Without a list, every options.profile is refused. Each name must be a profile Agent.yaml declares, or default . Web UI entries share one handler, so entries that list different profiles are a build error. An agent entry (a toAi() route) forwards the caller's own params and options , so it has no list to offer. The always-on route has its own: agentApi.profiles . Users and sign-in By default the web UI has no accounts and no gate - it is open, and every visitor is anonymous. That is the zero-ceremony bxAgents serve experience, and it is not a deployment posture. Declaring users on a webui entry turns on a real sign-in gate backed by cbauth and the same SQLite store everything else uses. Without accounts, the UI is one shared workspace There is no per-visitor identity, on purpose. Every visitor to an accountless web UI reads and writes the same conversations, preferences and agent memory (the local user, which the terminal chat on that machine shares) - whoever can reach the page sees everything in it. That is the point of running without accounts rather than an oversight: an open UI is a single shared tool (a laptop, a trusted internal box), not a multi-tenant service. Handing each browser its own slice would only fragment one workspace into per-browser copies nobody asked for, and any client-side id doing the fragmenting would be forgeable anyway. Warning An open UI has no privacy between visitors. Anyone who can reach the URL sees every conversation in it, and can continue or delete any of them. If that is not what you want - anywhere the page is reachable by more than the people who should see the transcripts - declare users . // gateways/chatUi.bx users : [ { username: "ada", passwordEnvVar: "ACME_ADA_PASSWORD", displayName: "Ada Lovelace" }, { username: "grace", passwordHash: "pbkdf2$210000$...", displayName: "Grace Hopper" } ] Passwords are never written in config An account names the environment variable holding its password ( passwordEnvVar ), or carries an already-hashed value ( passwordHash ). A literal password key is a build error, not a warning - silently ignoring it would leave you believing you had set a password when you had only committed one. A passwordHash is safe to commit precisely because it cannot be reversed. Generate one with the same hasher the app uses: bxAgents hash-password --password="<your-password>" Danger Hashed, not encrypted. Encryption is reversible, and a stolen database file almost always travels with whatever could decrypt it - so a reversible scheme turns one file leak into every user's password, including any they reused elsewhere. Passwords here go through PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with a per-user random salt and are never recoverable from the database. (BoxLang ships no bcrypt or argon2 BIF; PBKDF2 is the strongest primitive available without adding a dependency.) The iteration count is stored inside each hash ( pbkdf2$<iterations>$<salt>$<digest> ), so it can be raised later without invalidating anything already stored. What sign-in changes Everything user-scoped re-keys to the real account. The agent API reads the signed-in account from cbsecurity (which wraps cbauth) in one place ( models/api/Authenticator ), and agent memory, the conversation index, preferences and pending-run ownership all key off the id it gives. Accounts also close the API: with users , a request to /__bxagents needs the sign-in cookie or a token, whatever agentApi.access says. A page with accounts must never sit in front of an API anyone can call. A visitor who is not signed in is sent to <path>/login.html . The practical difference: conversations and preferences follow the person across browsers and devices, and clearing cookies no longer creates a brand-new "user". No users With users Identity One shared workspace The signed-in account Conversations visible to Everyone who can reach the UI Only their owner Follows the person across browsers/devices n/a - nothing is per-person Yes Reachable without signing in Everything Only the login form Lifecycle Accounts are reconciled from config on every boot, in this order: ChatDb migrates the schema, the seeder writes accounts, then the login gate starts enforcing. Adding a user to config creates them. Changing their password updates it. The seeder re-hashes only when the configured password no longer matches what is stored, so an unchanged password costs one verification rather than a fresh hash. Removing them from config deactivates the account rather than deleting it. Their conversations reference their id, so deleting the row would orphan that history instead of revoking access. They can no longer sign in; their data stays intact and returns if the account is restored. A passwordEnvVar whose variable is unset skips that account entirely and logs a warning to webui-auth . This fails closed on purpose - creating the account with an empty password would be far worse than it not existing. Admins and members Every account is either an admin or a member . A member talks to the agent and sees only their own conversations, notes and preferences. An admin can also do what the operator of the app does: manage access tokens, see everyone's conversations, change the agent's own notes and secrets, see where the agent keeps its data ( GET /data ), and choose who else is an admin. The flag is a boolean on the account: users : [ { username: "ada", passwordEnvVar: "ACME_ADA_PASSWORD", admin: true }, { username: "grace", passwordEnvVar: "ACME_GRACE_PASSWORD" } ] Config seeds it, the database keeps it. admin: true sets the flag when the account is created, or when no account is an admin yet (how an account that existed before the flag gets its first admin). After that the database value wins, so a change made later survives a restart. Take admin: true out of config and the account stays an admin. No admin set means no admin. A server with accounts and none of them an admin has no one who can manage the others; the terminal and the server secret are still admins. Changing it. An admin can call POST /users/admin with { "username": "grace", "admin": true } , list accounts with GET /users , or run bxAgents users . The last admin cannot be demoted. The change applies on the account's next request. The server secret ( agentApi.tokenEnvVar ), an issued token with admin scope and the terminal are admins as before; an open server with no accounts is one shared admin. What this is not This is a fixed roster of operator-provisioned accounts, not a user-management system. There is no self-registration, no password reset, no roles beyond admin and member, and no per-user rate limiting or spend cap. If you need federated identity instead, edit resolveUserId() in the generated handler to return your own authenticated principal - the rest of the web UI neither knows nor cares where the id came from. Human-in-the-loop When the agent pauses for approval, the stream emits a middleware_stop chunk that carries no detail. The page therefore asks GET /pending?threadId= what is being requested, renders it with Approve / Reject , and answers via POST /resume - which streams the continuation of the same turn , so the outcome lands in the conversation rather than starting a new one. decidedBy is filled from the session server-side, never from the request body: who approved something is exactly the kind of claim a caller should not get to make about itself. Warning A suspended run belongs to the session that started it, and both routes enforce that. Deriving decidedBy server-side only stops a caller lying about who decided - on its own it does nothing about whose run they are deciding on. Unlike every other action, /pending and /resume are addressed by threadId rather than by conversation, so without an ownership check a visitor holding someone else's threadId could read their pending tool calls and their arguments, and approve or reject on their behalf. The owner needs no extra bookkeeping: the handler stamps the session-derived userId into the run options, and the agent checkpoints those options alongside the suspension - so the saved state already knows who it belongs to. /pending answers as though nothing is pending when the caller is not the owner, so it cannot be used to probe whether a threadId exists at all; /resume refuses with a 403 . History and reload The transcript lives in the DOM; the conversation lives in the agent's memory. Without rehydration a reload shows an empty screen while the agent still remembers everything - so the page would look blank and then answer follow-ups about messages the user cannot see. On load the page therefore calls GET /__bxagents/history and replays the stored messages (markdown and all), falling back to the welcome message when the conversation is empty or the fetch fails. New starts a fresh conversationId . It does not delete anything - the previous conversation stays on the server under its own id and appears in the sidebar, which is what the conversations table exists for. What the page does The shipped page is a real chat client, not a demo shell. It reads GET /info first and shapes itself to what the server actually reports, so a control only appears where the capability exists. Area Behaviour Conversation sidebar Lists this visitor's conversations newest-first, with message counts. Switch, rename (✎), delete (×), or start a new one. Titles render through textContent - a title is whatever the user typed first, so it is never parsed as markup Steer while streaming The composer stays live during a turn. Send becomes Steer , and the message splices into the run already in flight rather than starting a new one Stop Posts /cancel before aborting the fetch, so the server actually stops spending tokens, then keeps whatever already streamed Clear / Compact Clear empties this conversation; Compact appears only when a summary model is configured, and reports what it actually did ( Compacted 12 messages down to 3 , or Nothing to compact yet ) Reasoning + tool calls Collapsed disclosures fed from delta.reasoning and delta.tool_calls on the same envelope Approvals A human-in-the-loop pause renders an Approve/Reject card from GET /pending , answered via /resume , which streams the continuation of the same turn Theme Stored server-side in preferences , so it follows the identity rather than the browser. localStorage keeps a local copy so the choice survives a failed request Model /info 's model name sits in the header, so it is always clear what answered Context size A ring in the header that fills as the context does (amber from 70 percent, red from 90), from GET /context , refreshed after each turn, command, clear, compaction, conversation switch and change to the notes. Click it for the breakdown: the total, each part with its share (system prompt, tool definitions, notes, messages), the tools, and a button to compact the conversation. The ring fills only when the model's contextWindow is set; without it the panel still shows the sizes Attachments An Attach button (shown when /info reports capabilities.attachments ) picks pictures and text files; you can also paste a picture or drop files on the page. Chips show what waits, each with a remove button. Pictures go as base64 attachments of the stream request, text files are inlined in the message. At most 4 pictures, 5 MB each; /info also reports vision , and a picture to a profile without it is refused with the reason Shortcuts Enter sends, Shift+Enter adds a line. ? alone (or /keys ) lists them Recovery matters more than it sounds. The last-opened conversation is remembered in localStorage , but the conversations themselves live on the server. If that id no longer exists - deleted in another tab, or a fresh store - the page falls back to the newest remaining conversation instead of rehydrating into an empty screen with no active row. Narrow screens get a real layout rather than a squeezed one: under 40rem the sidebar overlays the transcript instead of stealing its width, and prefers-reduced-motion is honoured. The SQLite store Every webui project gets a SQLite database. It isn't optional and there's no flag to turn it off. The reason is a real gap, not a preference: bx-ai's IAiMemory has no enumeration API. It's a per- (userId, conversationId) bucket - you can read, write and clear one, but nothing in it answers "which conversations does this user have." A conversation list, per-user preferences, and anything else relational needs real storage alongside the memory, not inside it. Piece What it is bx-sqlite The JDBC driver, bundled with BxAgents as a nested module qb QueryBuilder for the sign-in accounts in ChatDb ChatStore In the BxAgents module, shared with the terminal chat. Owns the tables and their versions, in plain SQLite SQL models/ChatDb.bx Generated, only the sign-in accounts. Hands out query builders; its migrate() calls ChatStore A start-up statement in the generated base Application Generated. Builds ChatDb at boot so migration runs then, not on whichever request touches the database first The datasource is registered in the generated base Application ( bxagents/Application.bx ) and the grammar is pinned in config/ColdBox.bx : // bxagents/Application.bx (generated) this.datasources[ "bxagents" ] = { "driver" : "sqlite", "database": expandPath( "./data/chat.db" ) } this.datasource = "bxagents" // NOT this.defaultDatasource - see below // config/ColdBox.bx (generated) qb : { defaultGrammar : "SQLiteGrammar@qb", defaultOptions : { datasource : "bxagents" } } Both are optional to override, per entry: Key What it does Default database.datasource The ColdBox datasource name bxagents database.path The database file, relative to the app root ./data/chat.db An absolute database.path fails the build : it's resolved with expandPath() inside the generated app, so an absolute path silently escapes the app directory and breaks a packaged .bxa deploy. One file for the web chat and the terminal chat. On a developer's machine, bxAgents serve starts the app with the environment variable BXAGENTS_DB set to data/chat.db in the project folder, and bxAgents chat opens the same file. The generated app uses BXAGENTS_DB when it is set and database.path otherwise, so a deployed app keeps its file inside the app unless you set BXAGENTS_DB there too (for example to a mounted volume). New projects git-ignore data/chat.db* . The file is in WAL mode, so the terminal chat and a running server can use it at the same time. Schema is versioned and forward-only. ChatStore.migrate() (called by ChatDb.migrate() ) records what it has applied in a bxagents_schema_version table and applies only what's newer, so booting against an existing store is a no-op. v1 creates conversations and preferences ; v2 adds users , v3 tokens , v4 notes and v5 usage ; v6 adds where a conversation started, v7 the vault and v8 the admin flag of an account. Evolve it by adding a step to the store's migration list - never by editing a migration that has shipped, because SQLite cannot modify or drop a column . A database made by an earlier version of the generated app is recognised and left as it is. Warning Two things here are counter-intuitive, and both were established the hard way against a real ColdBox boot rather than read off a docs page. The default-datasource setting is this.datasource , not this.defaultDatasource . The registration key is plural ( this.datasources[ "name" ] ), so the singular default reads like it should match - and BoxLang accepts this.defaultDatasource silently and does nothing with it. The failure it produces names the very datasource you are trying to select ( No default datasource defined in the application or globally or in the query options. Registered datasources are: [bxagents] ), which reads as a broken selection mechanism rather than a misspelled setting. Name the datasource on every qb builder; do not rely on moduleSettings.qb.defaultOptions . qb's ModuleConfig.cfc maps QueryBuilder@qb with .initArg( name = "defaultOptions", value = settings.defaultOptions ) in onLoad() , so the setting looks like it covers you. It did not arrive in a real boot - the datasource was registered and the builder still had empty options. ChatDb.query() therefore calls .mergeDefaultOptions( { datasource : static.DATASOURCE } ) on every builder it hands out. The moduleSettings.qb block is still generated - it is right for any other qb use in the app - but the generated store does not depend on it. If you extend ChatDb , name the datasource on whatever you add. One more, unchanged: the datasource must be a named datasource, never an inline struct - qb's own appendSqlComments() types that argument as string , so a struct throws before any SQL runs. The store is SQLite. ChatDb reads and writes go through qb, but the tables are created by ChatStore with SQLite SQL, so another database later means a new ChatStore , not only a grammar change. Conversations and preferences These are what the SQLite store exists for, and both are scoped by the same server-derived userId as everything else. Conversations. Every turn through the agent API's /invoke , /stream , /events or /batch records itself against the index: the row is created on first use, updatedAt moves, and the first user message becomes the title (collapsed to one line, truncated to 60 characters) unless one is already set - so a rename is never silently undone by the next turn. messageCount is a display counter , bumped by two per turn; a turn that dies midway can leave it one high, and /clear resets it. The agent's own memory remains the authority on what was actually said. POST /sessions/delete removes the index row and clears the agent's messages for that conversation. Dropping only the row would leave the conversation invisible while still sitting in the model's context the moment anyone reused the id. Warning Why touchConversation() is not a qb upsert. An upsert targets the primary key alone, so a caller who guessed another visitor's conversationId would have their own userId written onto that row and take the conversation over. The store reads first and refuses when the row belongs to someone else. setPreference() does upsert, and safely - its target is the (userId, prefKey) composite key, so the caller's own identity is part of what it matches on. Preferences. Server-side rather than localStorage , so they follow the identity instead of the browser. With users declared, a person's preferences follow them across browsers and devices. Branding and theming The entry needs only exposes and path . All the other keys are optional. These are not about looks and are described elsewhere on this page: Key What it does exposes "webui" . path Where the page is served, for example /chat . Rooted, plain segments, unique among the gateways/ entries, and not under the agent API's path. apiKeyEnvVar The name of the variable holding the API's shared secret, see Securing the API . users Named accounts, see Users and sign-in . profiles The profiles people may pick, see Choosing the model . database { datasource, path } , see The SQLite store . These keys brand the page: Key What it does title Browser title and header heading subtitle Small line under the heading icon An emoji (rendered into an inline-SVG favicon and the header) or an image URL/path ( /logo.svg , https://… , data:image/… ). With none, the header shows a robot. Or phosphor:<name> for an icon from the page's own set ( phosphor:lightning , phosphor:robot , phosphor:chat-circle-text , ...), used for the header and the tab; a name the set does not have is shown as plain text. welcome Empty-state message shown before the first turn suggestions Up to four short texts shown as buttons under the welcome message on an empty conversation. One click sends it. placeholder Composer input placeholder footer Small note under the composer - disclaimers, links showReasoning Show the "Thinking" strip. Default true showToolCalls Show tool-call chips. Default true theme Design tokens - see below themeFile Path to a CSS override, relative to the project root. Default resources/webui/theme.css theme maps directly onto the page's CSS custom properties: accent , accentFg , bg , fg , muted , border , surface , inputBg , bubbleUser , bubbleUserFg , bubbleAssistant , bubbleAssistantFg , bubbleError , reasoningFg , reasoningBg , toolFg , toolBg , radius , radiusSm , font , fontMono , fontSize , maxWidth . accent also drives the page's tints and icon color ( --accent-soft , --accent-ink and the focus glow are worked out from it), so one color is enough to brand the page. A nested theme.dark block overrides any of the same tokens for dark mode. An unknown token fails the build rather than being silently ignored, so a typo surfaces immediately instead of leaving you wondering why your brand color never showed up. // gateways/chat.bx theme: { accent : "0f766e", radius : "10px", font : "Inter, system-ui, sans-serif", dark : { accent : "rgb(45, 212, 191)" } } Info Write hex colors bare, with no leading hash. BoxLang begins string interpolation at # in both single- and double-quoted strings, so a literal hex color in a .bx config is a parse error unless the hash is doubled - a footgun nobody remembers. The generator adds it back for you, so "0f766e" just works. rgb() , hsl() and named colors need nothing special either way. For anything the tokens don't cover - custom fonts, layout, per-element rules - drop a resources/webui/theme.css into the project. It's inlined last into the page's <style> , so it beats both the shipped defaults and the theme tokens; and being a real .css file, ordinary #rrggbb hex works there normally. (A literal </style in that file fails the build, since it would terminate the page's style block early.) Securing the API Warning apiKeyEnvVar is a shared secret, not a login system. It is the same thing as the agent API's agentApi.tokenEnvVar (a name in Agent.yaml wins if both are set). Left unset, the API is open (fine on your own machine, not for a public deployment; serve warns when an open API listens on every interface). Set it, and every call to /__bxagents must carry a matching x-bxagents-token header, compared in constant time. The static shell ( <path>/index.html ) is not gated , because a browser's plain page navigation can't send a custom header; the page asks for it in a form: a Password box that opens by itself when the server answers 401 and again from Password in the Settings menu. The password is kept in localStorage and sent on every call; a wrong one shows "That password was not accepted." For several people use issued tokens or users . Logs and chat apps For an admin, the Server group of the Settings menu has two more items when the server keeps a data home: Logs opens a panel with a tab for each log that exists (agent, gateways, routines, heartbeat, API). Each line shows its time, its level (error, warn, info or debug, in words as well as colour), who it is about and what happened. Filter by level, search for a word, pick how many lines, and tick Refresh every 5 s to follow a log as it grows. See logs . Chat apps lists each chat app the project names with its state (connected, stopped, failing or not registered), which of its credentials are set (the names only, never a value), when it last had a conversation, and its last error with a button that opens that gateway's lines in the log. The chat apps are still set up in gateways/ and .env : the page only shows how they are doing. A small red count on the Settings button says how many sources logged an error since the app started. Settings and appearance The header keeps only what you use every minute: the Chats button, the context ring, the model picker and a Settings gear. The gear opens one menu, in three groups: Conversation (Fork this conversation, Export as Markdown, Clear messages, Compact older messages), You (Notes, Appearance, Dark or Light theme) and Server (Password, Access tokens). An item shows only where the server offers it, and a group with nothing in it is left out. Settings , then Appearance , opens the panel where a visitor picks, for this browser only: Setting Choices Mode System, Light or Dark (the same choice as the Dark theme or Light theme item, and it follows the account when the page has preferences) Accent color The gateway's own accent (the Default swatch), eight presets, or any hex value. The panel shows the contrast of the button text on it and warns under 4.5 : 1 Text size Small, Medium or Large Density Comfortable or Compact The choice is stored in the browser ( localStorage , key bxagents_webui_appearance ) and Reset to defaults clears it. It never changes what the operator wrote in theme : that stays the default every visitor starts from. A picked accent also sets --accent-fg to white or near black, whichever reads better, and the tints and focus glow follow it. Extension scripts and styles can rely on --accent , --accent-fg , --accent-soft , --accent-ink , --ring , --bg , --fg , --muted , --border and --surface and so follow the visitor's choice too. Conversation identity Every memory an agent holds is keyed by (userId, conversationId) - and an agent can hold several at once ( AiAgent 's memories is an array; loadMemoryMessages() iterates all of them with the same pair). AiAgent.run() / .stream() fall back to "" for both when nothing supplies them, so a server-side identity has to come from somewhere. The agent API supplies it on every turn route ( invoke , stream , events , batch ): No users declared and an open API: the one local user, as described in Users and sign-in . A shared secret: admin . An issued token: the token's name. users declared: the signed-in account's id, read from cbsecurity (which wraps cbauth). A signed-out request is refused with a 401 . Either way the id is derived on the server and never taken from the request body, so a caller cannot name themselves someone else. conversationId still comes from the client, and that's deliberate: it distinguishes several conversations belonging to the same identity - it's what the New button rotates. It is not the isolation boundary; the userId is. A project with a webui exposure also gets session management on in the generated base Application - this.sessionManagement = true , this.setClientCookies = true , a 60-minute sessionTimeout - because the sign-in is session-backed. Cookies are load-bearing there: no cookie, no session. A project with no webui keeps sessions off - an API/gateway-only app has no browser to track, and a session there is overhead plus a cookie nobody asked for. Info Why not toAi() ? ColdBox 8.1's toAi() lets a caller-supplied userId win over the server-derived one, and ColdBox route middleware does not reach its routes. The agent API's own handler derives the identity server-side only and never looks at body.userId , and sits behind one gate. No memory type is forced. Choose one (or several) per agent with a memory key on Agent.yaml , same shape as checkpointer : # Agent.yaml memory: type: cache maxMessages: 50 Reply rendering Assistant replies render as full Markdown: headings, lists, tables, quotes, strikethrough, links and fenced code, with code coloured by language (BoxLang, CFML, Java, JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Go, Rust, Kotlin, SQL, JSON, YAML, TOML, XML/HTML, CSS, shell, Dockerfile, diff and Markdown). The page carries its own copy of marked , DOMPurify and highlight.js , so it still works offline and loads nothing from a CDN. What the model writes is never trusted: raw HTML in an answer is escaped and shown as text, the result is sanitized, images are not loaded (a remote one would tell its server the page was opened), and a javascript: link is not turned into a link at all. Info The composer is a textarea - Enter sends, Shift+Enter adds a newline, and it grows to about six lines before scrolling. A turn in flight can be halted with Stop (an AbortController ), which keeps whatever already streamed rather than discarding it. The transcript only auto-scrolls when you're already at the bottom, so scrolling up to re-read something mid-stream doesn't yank you back down. Notes When the agent has a notes block, the Settings menu has a Notes item. It opens a panel with two tabs, About you and About the agent , how full each is (characters of the limit, and about how many tokens that adds to every conversation), and the notes with their ids. Add, edit in place and remove work on your own notes. The page and the terminal chat share the same database, so a note added in one shows in the other. About you belongs to the same identity as your conversations: your account with users , or the shared workspace without accounts. About the agent is shared by everyone who uses the agent, so anyone using the page may add or edit one, but the page has no Remove button for it and /notes/remove answers 403 . Removing a note of the agent takes an admin token on the agent's own /__bxagents/notes/remove route, or bxAgents notes remove --scope=agent where the agent runs. Without a notes block the button is not shown and the routes answer 404 : /info 's capabilities.notes says which. Connections When an mcpServers entry has oauth , the Settings menu has a Connections item ( /info 's capabilities.connections says whether). It opens a panel with a row for each service: its name, its address, Connected or Not connected , and a Connect or Disconnect button. Connect opens the provider's sign in in a new tab (a link is also shown, in case the browser blocks the tab) and the panel checks again every two seconds until it works. The page never sees a token. What is not here yet The page is complete against its own API - every route it needs exists and is exercised. These are the gaps: Missing Note Retry / regenerate A failed turn has to be re-sent by hand Edit and resend No editing a message already sent Token / cost display The page shows none. usage: true in Agent.yaml records tokens for bxAgents stats , and /stats shows them in the terminal chat only

# The web chat UI

A `gateways/*.bx` entry with `exposes: "webui"` ships a complete browser chat client for the agent - a conversation sidebar, streaming with reasoning and tool calls, human-in-the-loop approvals, per-visitor theming, and a real SQLite store behind it.

It lives under [gateways/](/conventions/gateways/index.html) because that is where exposures are declared, but it is a subsystem in its own right, which is why it has its own page.

```javascript
// gateways/chat.bx
class {
	function configure() {
		return {
			exposes     : "webui",
			path        : "/chat",
			apiKeyEnvVar: "CHAT_UI_API_KEY"   // optional - the agent API's shared secret, see Securing the API
		};
	}
}
```

That generates a static `<path>/index.html` (served directly - no route needed). The page is a client of the [agent API](/conventions/agent-bx/index.html#the-always-on-agent-route) at `/__bxagents`, the same one the terminal chat and the gateways use, so there is no second API under `<path>`. The agent API must stay enabled (`agentApi.enabled: false` with a `webui` entry is a build error).

![The generated web chat UI: a conversation sidebar, a multi-turn transcript, and a themed header/composer](/assets/webui-chat-light.png)

The screenshot above is the actual generated page - the real, unmodified template this repo ships - branded with [`examples/webui-agent`](https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/bx-agents/tree/development/examples/webui-agent)'s own `theme`/`title`/`icon` config and populated with example conversation content for illustration; `bxAgents build && bxAgents serve` in that example reproduces it.

The UI is dependency-free vanilla HTML/CSS/JS - no Bootstrap, AlpineJS or Vite build step - and is **pre-built and vendored inside BxAgents itself** : `bxAgents build` never runs `npm install`/`npm run build`, and a generated project never needs Node or npm installed at all. Everything the page needs is inlined into the single generated `index.html`.

That constraint is about the build, not about scope. The page is a full client: conversation sidebar, streaming with reasoning and tool calls, approvals, compaction, server-side theming. What is genuinely still missing is listed under [What is not here yet](#what-is-not-here-yet).

The page talks to the agent API at `/__bxagents` via `POST /__bxagents/stream` (`Accept: text/event-stream`), using `fetch()` + a manual `ReadableStream` reader - not the browser's `EventSource`, which can't `POST` or set custom headers, both needed here.
> **Warning**
>
> **`toAi()` forwards each bx-ai chunk verbatim - it does not wrap it.** ColdBox's [AI Routing docs](https://coldbox.ortusbooks.com/the-basics/routing/routing-dsl/ai-routing) show the stream as `data: {"token":"..."}` lines, but its own source (`Router.cfc`, `toAi()`'s stream sub-route) does `emitter.send( chunk, "chunk" )` - so every frame carries the **full normalized bx-ai envelope**:
>
>     event: chunk
>     data: {"object":"chat.completion.chunk","choices":[{"delta":{"role":"assistant","content":"Ray","reasoning":"...","tool_calls":[...]}}]}
>
>     event: done
>     data: [DONE]
>
> There is no `token` key anywhere. A client written against that docs page - including this UI's own first version - reads `undefined` and renders nothing at all. Read `choices[0].delta.content` instead.

Because the whole envelope arrives, **reasoning and tool calls are already on the wire** with no extra endpoint needed: `delta.reasoning` (normalized across every provider by bx-ai) renders as a collapsed "Thinking" strip, and `delta.tool_calls` as collapsed per-call chips. Tool-call arguments stream as partial JSON fragments keyed by `index`, so the page accumulates per index rather than assuming any single chunk holds a complete call.

## Walkthrough

A minute and a half through the whole page: the password form, suggestions, a formatted answer, a tool call, a code block with its Copy button, the Settings menu, dark mode, notes and the access tokens panel. The voice is [Kokoro](https://github.com/thewh1teagle/kokoro-onnx) (an Apache 2.0 model), and the page's answers come from a scripted demo model, so they are canned. Captions are on.
